Introduction
These release notes cover vSphere Supervisor 9.1 and related 9.1.x releases.
For vSphere Supervisor 9.0.x release notes, see VMware vSphere Supervisor Release Notes on the VCF Service
Administration and Development 9.0 site.
The release notes include product enhancements and notices, bug fixes, and resolved issues.
About vSphere Supervisor Releases
vSphere Supervisor is a control plane built in vSphere that integrates desired state and a single consistent API directly
in the hypervisor. vSphere Supervisor enables native deployment and management of Kubernetes clusters, declarative
virtual machines, and vSphere Pods alongside traditional workloads. It transforms vSphere to an extendable platform
by providing a declarative API for self-service provisioning of modern infrastructure services in a resource boundaries
enabled by vSphere Namespaces.
These release notes provide details for each release of VMware vSphere Supervisor. Refer to the vSphere Supervisor
documentation for more information.
VMware by Broadcom 7

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
vSphere Supervisor 9.1.1
Important:
When upgrading vCenter from 8.0 Update 3 and later, 9.0.0, 9.0.1, or 9.0.2 to 9.1.0 or 9.1.1, Supervisor data
can potentially be lost if the vLCM database was previously reset. To avoid data loss, you must determine if your
environment if affected and take mitigation steps. See Broadcom KB article 455737 for more information.

What's New
vSphere Supervisor 9.1.1 introduces the following new features and enhancements:
• Simplified Air-Gapped VKS Deployments
Deploy VKS clusters, Supervisor services, and VKS add-ons in air-gapped environments using the VCF Download
Tool to download all required artifacts and upload them to the Software Depot. This new method replaces the previous
manual registry relocation workflow. For more information, see Deploying VKS in Air-Gapped Environments.
• Enhanced Certificate Trust Chain Support for Supervisor Certificates
Supervisor certificate management is enhanced to support full trust chain certificates for Supervisor Virtual IP (VIP)
and NSX Load Balancer (NSX-LB), delivering full end-to-end trust chain validation, visibility, and enforcement.
• Custom SAN Support for Supervisor CSR Generation
You can now specify Subject Alternative Name (SAN) attributes directly when generating Certificate Signing Requests
(CSRs) through the Supervisor CSR generation API to better manage and control certificate fields in accordance with
security policies.
• VM-VM Anti-Affinity and Affinity Rules Through Compute Policies
You can use compute policies to create VM-VM anti-affinity rules that distribute VMs across separate hosts for
resiliency, and VM-VM affinity rules that collocate VMs on the same host for low latency. This functionality applies to
traditional virtual machines and to virtual machines created through VM Service. In the VM spec file, you can configure
the strictness of a rule as either required (hard) or preferred (soft) during initial VM placement. However, only the
preferred setting is supported during runtime.
Argo CD Service What's New
Until VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1, Argo CD was available only as a Supervisor Service. With VCF 9.1.1, Argo CD is
available in the following two forms:
• Argo CD Supervisor Service
Deploy and manage the Argo CD Supervisor Service in vCenter. After you deploy the Supervisor Service, use the
CLI to create an Argo CD instance in a vSphere Namespace. An Argo CD instance manages workloads in vSphere
Namespaces and VKS clusters. This capability is available with VCF 9.1.With VCF 9.1.1, Argo CD Supervisor
Service reduces the manual toil and introduced a policy to automatically discover and attach VKS clusters to the
ArgoCD instances enabling quick start managing workloads in VKS clusters. For more information, see Installing and
Configuring Argo CD. The Argo CD version that is currently release is 1.2.0, check the release notes.
• Argo CD as a VCF Service
VMware by Broadcom 8

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
VCF 9.1.1 introduces installation of the Argo CD service through the Service Management option in the VCF
Automation Provider Management UI. The VCF Automation organization UI enables organization admin to deploy
Argo CD instances to their vSphere Namespaces and then log in to the deployed Argo CD instance by using thier VCF
Automation credentials to quickly start managing workloads in vSphere Namespaces and VKS clusters. See Installing
and Configuring Argo CD.
Note:
In the VCF Automation organization UI, as an organization admin you can use the GitOps Service to deploy Argo
CD instances. You can manage up to 30 vSphere Namespace across all deployed Argo CD instances in the VCF
Automation. For VCF 9.1.1, Argo CD as VCF Service is release as a tech preview.
VKr Support for Argo CD
Argo CD Service support for new Kubernetes minor versions lags VKS by 2–4 months. Based on current upstream
schedules, a June VKr receives Argo CD support in October, an October VKr receives Argo CD support in January, and a
February VKr receives Argo CD support in April.
Known Issues
kubectl exec, attach, logs, and port-forward operations against workloads running in vSphere Pods might fail
temporarily during Supervisor upgrades
During Supervisor upgrades from Kubernetes 1.33.11 or earlier to Kubernetes v1.33.13 or v1.34.9 shipped in this release,
, , , and operations against workloads
kubectl exec kubectl attach kubectl logs kubectl port-forward
running in vSphere Pods can fail temporarily. The failures occur when the Supervisor control plane VMs are upgraded,
but one or more ESX hosts are still running the previous spherelet version. The operations fail with an HTTP 403
Access
error.
denied
vSphere Pod scheduling, networking, storage, and running workloads are not affected. The issue resolves on each host
after its spherelet upgrade completes.
Workaround: Wait for the affected ESX host to complete its spherelet upgrade, or retry the operation after the upgrade
progresses beyond the temporary version-mismatch window.
Take Snapshot page in the Local Consumption Interface keeps loading when taking a snapshot of a VM created
by using the VM Service
When you take a snapshot of a VM created by using the VM Service from the Local Consumption Interface, the Take
Snapshot page continues to load and does not complete, even after waiting for more than 2 minutes. The snapshot does
not render in the UI.
Workaround:
To work around this issue, do one of the following:
From the UI:
1. Navigate back to the namespace.
2. Navigate to the VM.
3. Click the Snapshots tab to view the snapshot.
From the backend, apply the following YAML:
apiVersion: vmoperator.vmware.com/v1alpha5
kind: VirtualMachineSnapshot
metadata:
name: sn-1
namespace: test
spec:
vmName: <name of vm to snapshot>
memory: true
description: "snapshot"
VM Service VM reports PoweredOff on Supervisor while running in vCenter, and reconciliation pauses
VMware by Broadcom 9

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
A VM Service VM can report a PoweredOff state on the Supervisor even though vCenter shows the virtual machine
actively running. The VM loses its IP address assignment, becomes unreachable on the network, and ignores
configuration changes. When you inspect the VM by running
kubectl get vm <vm-name> -n <namespace> -o
, the metadata includes the following annotation:
yaml
vmoperator.vmware.com/paused: "true"
This issue occurs rarely, and only when auto-registration runs on a Supervisor before the incremental restore support
check completes. For example, shortly after a Supervisor control plane service restart, or when a VM is restored from a
snapshot through the vCenter UI, which is an unsupported operation.
Workaround:
To restore normal operation and resume VM reconciliation, manually remove the pause annotation and power on the VM
through the Supervisor API:
1. Remove the pause annotation.
Note the trailing - which deletes the key:
kubectl annotate vm -n <namespace> <vm-name> vmoperator.vmware.com/paused-
2. Confirm annotation removal.
kubectl get vm -n <namespace> <vm-name> -o=jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}'
3. Power on the VM by running and updating the
kubectl edit vm -n <namespace> <vm-name>
field to .
spec.powerState PoweredOn
spec:
powerState: PoweredOn
Once updated, the VM operator automatically resumes normal management and reconciles the powered-on status.
MinIO PVCs remain in Pending state and the MinIO tenant fails to reach Running state when the cluster uses
remote vSAN datastores
MinIO PVCs can remain in a Pending state with the error
failed to provision volume with StorageClass:
. The
rpc error: code = Unknown desc = fail to find a StoragePool passing all criteria
MinIO tenant fails to reach a Running state. MinIO requires host-local datastores, so if the cluster contains remote vSAN
datastores, MinIO workloads do not come to a Running state.
Workaround: Ensure that host-local vSAN datastores are present in the cluster to provision MinIO workloads.
VPCs assigned to Supervisor Namespaces without load balancer or AutoSNAT support have limited functionality
In VCF 9.1.x, you can assign a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) to a Supervisor Namespace without load balancer or
AutoSNAT support. This configuration is intentional and supported, but some functionality might not be available.
• If the VPC does not have load balancer support, VKS clusters, LoadBalancer services, and Ingress resources cannot
resolve a public IP and do not function.
• If the VPC does not have AutoSNAT support, workloads on private subnets (the default for VMs) cannot egress from
their VPC, and workloads on private TGW subnets (the default for vSphere Pods) cannot egress from their NSX
project. VKS clusters cannot be deployed with AutoSNAT disabled unless the VKS VMs are on a public subnet.
Workaround: If network connectivity does not work as expected, verify the NSX configuration for the VPC to ensure that
load balancing and AutoSNAT are configured, if those capabilities are required.
Signature verification fails for Supervisor Services that use a private container image registry addressed by a
private IP
When a Supervisor Service pulls images from a private container image registry addressed by a private IP address,
signature verification can fail permanently. The Supervisor reports that it cannot verify connectivity to the image, indicating
that the registry authentication address is a private or link-local address, and the service is not marked as trusted. The
image itself remains reachable and can be pulled.
The failure occurs because an upstream server-side request forgery (SSRF) protection in the go-containerregistry library
rejects a registry whose token-authentication endpoint advertises a private IP address that differs from the registry's own
address.
VMware by Broadcom 10

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Workaround:
Choose one of the following:
• Configure the registry with a routable IP address that is not in a private or link-local range.
• Use a DNS hostname for the registry.
• Align the registry's token endpoint with its address. If you must use an IP address, configure the registry so that its
external endpoint and token-authentication URL advertise the exact same host and port notation that you registered in
vCenter.
Supervisor upgrade may fail with a WorkloadClientUpgrade timeout in large-scale deployments
In large-scale deployments, a Supervisor upgrade might fail with the error
Component WorkloadClientUpgrade
. The failure occurs because the
upgrade did not finish within 360 seconds timeout deadline
WorkloadClientUpgrade component has a fixed 6-minute timeout, and under scale conditions with a high volume of
concurrent operations, the reconciliation of the workload CLI plugins can exceed this timeout.
This is not a functional defect but a timing limitation that can occur whenever the environment is sufficiently large.
Workaround: Navigate to Supervisor Management → Updates in the vSphere Client, select the Supervisor, and re-apply
the update.
The update succeeds on retry because the pending reconciliation has typically completed by the time the update is re-
applied.
Supervisor might get permanently stuck after decommissioning a compute cluster from a vSphere Zone
After you decommission a compute cluster from a vSphere Zone, the associated Supervisor can get permanently stuck.
The Supervisor fails to configure the API server agent VM and reports errors indicating that the cluster may be
decommissioned. The Supervisor's wait logic does not recognize a task that has already completed. It blocks indefinitely
waiting for an operation that has already finished. This leaves the Supervisor stuck on stale data for the decommissioned
cluster.
Workaround: Restart the Supervisor control plane service on the affected vCenter to clear the stale state and unblock
reconciliation.
Resolved Issues
In VPC-mode deployments, LoadBalancer services in Supervisor Service namespaces could experience periodic
VIP flapping approximately every 10 minutes, causing brief connectivity disruptions
This issue has been fixed and AKO's annotations are now preserved by the platform across reconcile cycles.
In Monitoring, the certificate used by telegraf agents in VKS clusters could expire, preventing metrics from being
streamed from VKS clusters to VCF Operations
This issue has been fixed.
In pure DHCP environments, the ports required for the Supervisor Management Proxy could fail to open
This issue has been fixed.
Supervisor or VKS control plane services with Avi Load Balancer could frequently go down and come up with
new IP addresses
An NCP pod restart caused internal resources to be deleted and re-created, which in turn caused Avi virtual services to be
deleted and recreated. This issue has been fixed.

environment if affected and take mitigation steps. See Broadcom KB article 455737 for more information.

What's New

• Local Consumption Interface (LCI) with VKS 3.7
You can now use the Local Consumption Interface (LCI) on the Supervisor with VKS version 3.7.
Upgrade Considerations
CAUTION:
A known pre-check issue allows vCenter upgrades to proceed even if Supervisor Kubernetes versions are
incompatible. Upgrading without matching versions can cause severe production outages. Before upgrading,
manually confirm that the target vCenter supports the same Supervisor Kubernetes minor version as your
source vCenter. For example, If your source vCenter uses Supervisor 1.29.x, the target vCenter must also
support Supervisor 1.29.
Upgrade From Upgrade To Upgrade Path Condition - Source Supervisor

What's New
vSphere Supervisor 9.1.0.0100 introduces bug fixes and security patches to maintain platform stability.
Upgrade Considerations
CAUTION:
A known pre-check issue allows vCenter upgrades to proceed even if Supervisor Kubernetes versions are
incompatible. Upgrading without matching versions can cause severe production outages. Before upgrading,
manually confirm that the target vCenter supports the same Supervisor Kubernetes minor version as your
source vCenter. For example, If your source vCenter uses Supervisor 1.29.x, the target vCenter must also
support Supervisor 1.29.

Known Issues
Removal of Endpoints write access from default edit and admin roles
To mitigate CVE-2021-25740 and align with upstream Kubernetes security standards, the Supervisor cluster no longer
overrides the default Kubernetes RBAC behavior for the edit and admin ClusterRoles. Previously, a custom ClusterRole
injected Endpoints write permissions back into these roles. This override has been removed.
Following this upgrade, users or service accounts relying solely on the default edit or admin ClusterRoles will receive a
error when attempting to manually create, update, or patch Endpoints. Standard Kubernetes Services that
Forbidden
use a selector remain unaffected, as the control plane automatically manages their endpoints.
For complete details on the vulnerability and the upstream remediation strategy, see the Kubernetes Security Advisory for
CVE-2021-25740 at https://discuss.kubernetes.io/t/security-advisory-cve-2021-25740-endpoint-endpointslice-permissions-
allow-cross-namespace-forwarding/16700.
Workaround:
Use one of the following options:
• If your workloads rely on manually created Endpoints to route traffic, for example, selector-less Services, use a
Kubernetes Service of type instead.
ExternalName
• If a specific deployment strictly requires manual Endpoint editing, a Cluster Administrator must create a purpose-built
Kubernetes Role granting endpoints write access and bind it explicitly to the User or ServiceAccount that requires it.

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Release Snapshot

following Supervisor Kubernetes Versions.

What's New
• Supervisor deployment update
Starting with VCF 9.1, the vSphere Client UI no longer supports deploying a Supervisor with classic NSX Segment
Networking. Deployment remains fully supported through the API.
• The software depot support for Supervisor and VKS
The software depot now provides comprehensive support for Supervisor, Supervisor Services, VKS releases, and
standard packages, thereby consolidating all essential components into a single, central repository. This enhancement
facilitates streamlined lifecycle management by establishing a unified, trusted source of truth for all requisite VCF
artifacts, alongside improved content distribution and a more efficient patching process across your VCF environment.
• vSphere Zones scaling
To meet the high-capacity needs of enterprise and CSP customers, vSphere Zones can now scale beyond single-
cluster limits to include multiple ESX clusters. This enhancement allows you to increase resource capacity for tenants
and application teams dynamically without altering the zone objects used by vSphere Namespaces. Additionally, a
new cluster decommission workflow enables the removal of specific ESX clusters for maintenance without impacting
consumer workloads or causing application downtime.
Container Service
• Container Service
The new Container Service enables the seamless deployment of individual containers without the complexity of
managing or deploying a full Kubernetes cluster. By utilizing a dynamic and isolated runtime, the service ensures that
only containers within a specific vSphere Pod share resources, including the system kernel. This architecture provides
a high-security environment that maximizes resource efficiency while simplifying the transition from virtual machines to
containerized workloads.
VM Service
• Consumer VM snapshots
In VCF 9.1, tenants can now take, manage, and delete snapshots on their VM Service VMs via VCF Automation.
• Edit VM Service VM Network Configuration
In VCF 9.1, VM Service VMs can now be configured with multiple network interfaces during VM creation, and network
configuration can be edited during day-2.
• VM affinity/anti-affinity via infrastructure policies
Initial placement of VMs as part of VM group can be defined via infrastructure policy which maps to the affinity and
anti-affinity compute policy in vCenter. Tenants can then define affinity/anti-affinity for VMs to VMs, nodes, and zones.
• VM groups
VM Service VMs can be added to VM groups or created as part of VM groups that allow consumers to batch VMs to
apply placement policies and define power-on order.
• Non-disruptive VM import onto Supervisor
As a vSphere administrator, you can import an existing VM that runs in vSphere to a vSphere Namespace on vSphere
Supervisor. You can then have this VM managed by the VM Service. In VCF 9.1, customers can use the VCF-A VCD
Migration Tool or migrate VMs via the API to non-disruptively import VMs onto the Supervisor, import VMs in batches
with defined import order, and roll back the operation while in progress.
• Integration to automate adding a VM to an Active Directory
Tenant Admins get the ability to define an integration that automatically joins VM Service VMs to an Active Directory
and joins it to a specific domain.

Known Issues
VM fails to reconfigure and reports an error when you switch between Native and External Key Providers on an
encrypted live VM with volume attached
When you attempt to change the EncryptionClass of a VM from a Native Key Provider (NKP) to an External KMS (BYOK),
or vice versa, the operation fails in environments where boot disks are managed as First Class Disks (FCDs). You might
observe the following error:
Invalid virtual machine configuration
This issue occurs because the VM Operator skips FCDs during the encryption reconciliation process, causing a mixed
mode state. In this mode, the VM home attempts to use the new key type while the disks remain on the old one. This
triggers a vCenter validation failure because VMs do not support simultaneous encryption keys from different provider
types.
Workaround: None.
During Supervisor upgrades, hosts in the cluster enter maintenance mode
When you perform a Supervisor upgrade, all ESX hosts within the cluster enter maintenance mode one at a time. This
process is required to install the Spherelet on each host. This has been the standard behavior since vSphere 7.0 and
continues through VCF 9.1.x and vSphere 9.1.x.
Workaround: None. This process is expected to change in one of the next releases to reduce host impact during
upgrades.
In high-scale VKS environments, NSX-NCP pods might run out of memory and restart
During high-scale testing of VKS clusters, NSX-NCP pods might run out of memory at a scale of 400 or more clusters.
Restart counts might increase after back-to-back upgrades of vCenter and the Supervisor. When NSX-NCP runs out of
memory, network-related updates are not applied to NSX as quickly or reliably as expected.
You can notice the following symptoms:
• New applications or updates take longer to become ready.
• Connections fail or require a retry to succeed.
• Security or network rules appear out of sync with recent deployments.
• System alerts and restarts occur, which can make the platform appear unstable.
Workaround: With tenant administrator access, manually patch the NSX-NCP deployment.
You must increase the memory requests and limits. The default 1000Mi limit might be insufficient for environments
reaching approximately 450 clusters or 3,200 VMs.
The special characters ":", "?", "#", "[" and "]" are not supported in the Supervisor
VMware by Broadcom 15

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
You cannot use NSX resources with policy IDs containing special characters like "?", "#", "[" and "] wih the Supervisor.
Examples are resources like VPCs or Subnets.
Workaround:
Create the NSX resources with policy IDs without "?", "#", "[" and "]".
After NSX restore, VPC that is associate with a vSphere Namespace is missing from NSX
After taking an NSX backup, if you create an NSX VPC and associate that VPC with a vSphere Namespace, after NSX
restore, that VPC will not exist on NSX. If any SubnetPort, VM, Subnet or IPAddressAllocation were created under that
namespace between NSX backup and NSX restore, the Supervisor restore process will be blocked because the VPC
does not exist.
Workaround:
Re-create the missing VPC on NSX. The Supervisor will restore the other resources under this namespace, and then you
can do modifications on the namespace like creating more resources or deleting the namespace.
VMs on DHCP Subnet created right before an NSX restore might fail to be restored
The MAC address of VMs on a DHCP Subnet is synchronized to the SubnetPort CR by a polling thread that runs every 10
minutes. This MAC address is required to successfully restore a VM after an NSX restore operation. If an NSX restore is
triggered before this synchronization occurs, the Supervisor fails to restore the affected VMs.
Workaround: After creating a VM on a DHCP Subnet, wait at least 10 minutes to allow for MAC address synchronization
before starting an NSX restore.
NCP pod restarts during an NSX restore can cause workload network reconfiguration failures
In vSphere 9.1, the Supervisor supports the automatic recovery of workload networks created between an NSX backup
and an NSX restore. However, if an NSX Container Plugin (NCP) pod crashes or restarts after it recreates the NSX
SubnetPort but before it notifies Spherelet or the VM Operator, the network reconfiguration might fail. This results in the
affected vSphere pod or VM failing to recover its network connectivity.
Workaround: To resolve this issue, manually recreate the affected vSphere pod or VM.
You cannot re-enable a Supervisor on a decommissioned vSphere cluster
If you enable a Supervisor on a vSphere cluster and then decommission that cluster, attempts to enable a different
Supervisor on the same decommissioned cluster fail. You see the following error:
Supervisor cannot be enabled
.
on cluster <cluster-id>, which was previously backing Supervisor <supervisor-id>
Workaround:
To resolve this issue, perform the following steps:
1. Create a new vSphere cluster.
2. Add the hosts from the decommissioned vSphere cluster to the new cluster.
3. Enable the Supervisor on the new cluster.
VPC for the vmware-system-vks-public namespace is not deleted after switching to a system VPC
After upgrade, the namespace switches the CR from
vmware-system-vks-public VPCNetworkConfiguration
the default to the system one, then it starts using the system VPC. However, the previous VPC created for namespace
is not automatically deleted. This remaining VPC does not impact for workload
vmware-system-vks-public
deployment because namespace is a system namespace, and pods under this
vmware-system-vks-public
namespace are mode that are deployed on the Supervisor control plane VMs.
hostNetwork
Workaround:
To remove the remaining VPC, use one of the following methods:
• Disable the Supervisor to delete this VPC.
• Manually delete this VPC by using the REST API with header ' '.
X-Allow-Overwrite: true
vSphere Namespace creation fails when using an existing VPC and NSX IPBlocks with the parameter
cidr_list
VMware by Broadcom 16

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
In NSX 9.1, IPBlock introduces a the parameter to set a list of CIDRs. If your Supervisor is 9.0, it consumes
cidr_list
the old parameter instead of .
cidr cidr_list
Workaround:
Create with for Supervisors 9.0, or upgrade the Supervisor to 9.1 to consume new IPBlock
NSX IPblock cidr
parameter .
cidr_list
Failure to evacuate vSphere Pods from ESX host causes unsuccessful Supervisor upgrade
The Supervisor upgrade process might be unsuccessful because vSphere Pods fail to evacuate from the ESX host. This
prevents the host from entering maintenance mode (EMM).
Workaround: Evacuate the vSphere Pods manually.
1. Log in to the ESX node where the Enter Maintenance Mode task is stuck.
2. Identify the VM IDs for the vSphere Pods:
vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms
3. Shut down the vSphere Pods:
vim-cmd vmsvc/power.shutdown <VMID>
4. If the shutdown fails, force power off:
vim-cmd vmsvc/power.off <VMID>
5. Wait for the host to enter maintenance mode and the upgrade to resume.
vSphere Pod log streaming fails when the syslog server address is provided as host name rather than an IP
address
You configure vSphere Pod log streaming trough a Kuberenetes Custom Resource, where you specify the destination
for the logs. In VCF 9.1, this destination must be in the form of an IP address. If given as a host name, vSphere Pod log
streaming fails.
Workaround: Specify the syslog server address with an IP address. This can also be a Service or ClusterIP if needed.
During scale, some of the VKS cluster pods go into OOM state
VKS clusters pods might go into OOM (Out of Memory) state when being scaled for VKS 3.6 and VCF 9.1.
Workaround: Upgrade VKS to 3.6.1.
Supervisor upgrade fails when running Kubernetes version 1.32
If the upgrade order specified in KB 390634 is not followed, the upgrade of the Supervisor fails.
Workaround: Stop the spherelet on the ESX host to proceed with the upgrade.
Traffic from vSphere Pod to Load Balancer service fails when endpoints are outside the Virtual Private Cloud
If a Load Balancer service is deployed inside a Virtual Private Cloud but the service endpoints are located outside of it,
traffic fails. This occurs because the Load Balancer virtual machines use private network addresses that cannot reach
endpoints outside the Virtual Private Cloud.
Workaround: To enable connectivity, the administrator of the Virtual Private Cloud must configure automatic Source
Network Address Translation (auto-SNAT) rules within that Virtual Private Cloud.
vSphere Pod ephemeral storage does not support namespace-level storage quotas
In VCF Automation multi-tenancy mode, vSphere Pod ephemeral storage consumption is not counted toward namespace
storage quota limits. This occurs because storage for the VM home directory and ephemeral disks is allocated as a
cluster-wide resource rather than at the namespace level. As a result, Cloud Service Providers cannot enforce tenant
storage limits or track consumption for chargeback. Persistent volumes and standard enterprise deployments are not
impacted.
Workaround: None.
Supervisor disablement fails because associated Content Library is in use
VMware by Broadcom 17

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Supervisor disablement fails and remains stuck in a removing phase if an associated Content Library cannot be deleted.
This issue occurs if a vSphere Namespace fails to clean up properly, leaving the Content Library associated with it. This
triggers a deletion guardrail that prevents the Supervisor disablement process from completing.
Workaround: Follow these steps to remove the Content Library usage association, so that the disablement can proceed.
1. Obtain a valid .
vmware-api-session-id
2. Find the active usage ID holding the lock by running a GET request:
curl -X GET -H 'vmware-api-session-
id: <session-id>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 'http://localhost:1080/api/
.
content/library/<library-id>/usages'
3. Manually delete the usage association using the usage ID returned in step 2:
curl -sS -X DELETE -H
'vmware-api-session-id: <session-id>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 'http://
.
localhost:1080/api/content/library/<library-id>/usages/<usage-id>'
Supervisor restore is stuck if reinvoked immediately after cancellation
During a Supervisor restore, control plane VMs are destroyed and redeployed. If a restore is canceled and reinvoked
within ten seconds, the task to destroy the previous control plane VMs might become stuck. This occurs because the
Supervisor control plane does not process the VM lifecycle hooks raised by ESX Agent Manager, which blocks the task.
Workaround: Manually mark the VM lifecycle hooks as processed to unblock the stuck task from the previous restore
operation.
Overlapping subnets between VCF Automation and Supervisor prevents management communication
If VCF Automation is deployed on a VPC public subnet that overlaps with the Supervisor workload networks, management
communication between VCF Automation and the Supervisor fails. This prevents the successful creation of Namespaces.
Currently, there is no validation in the workflow to prevent this subnet overlap.
Workaround: In NSX, create a new Distributed Transit Gateway (DTGW) with a unique external CIDR and VLAN external
connection. Use this new connectivity profile when creating the Supervisor workload networks to ensure they do not
overlap with the subnet used by VCF Automation.
Default VKS content library requires VCF Software Depot configuration on vCenters
Starting with VCF 9.1, the public CDN (wp-content.vmware.com or wp-content.broadcom.com) is no longer used to create
the default VKS content library. Only on vCenter instances where VCF Software Depot is configured in a VCF or VVF
deployment, the default VKS content library is automatically created based on the VCF Software Depot endpoint upon the
first Supervisor enablement in vCenter.
Workaround: None.

About the vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.7 Release Notes
vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) provides components for provisioning and managing the lifecycle of Kubernetes
clusters in the vSphere Supervisor environment.
These release notes provide details for each VKS release. Refer to the Managing vSphere Kubernetes Service with
vSphere Supervisor documentation for usage information.
Prerequisites for VKS 3.7 Upgrade
• Service YAML Selection Warning - Ensure you select the correct VKS 3.7 service YAML based on your vCenter
version and network connectivity:
– vsphere-kubernetes-service-legacy-3.7.0+v1.36.yaml: Points to the public 'projects.packages.broadcom.com'
instance via its imgpkgBundle. This must only be used for vCenter versions 9.0 and lower, or within air-
gapped vCenter 9.1 (or newer) environments.
– vsphere-kubernetes-service-3.7.0+v1.36.yaml: Points to the VCF Operations Software Depot via
its imgpkgBundle. This must be used for internet-connected vCenter versions 9.1 and newer.
Deploying the incorrect YAML configuration will result in image registry resolution failures.
• vSphere Kubernetes Release (VKr) Version - VKS 3.7 drops compatibility for VKr v1.32. Before upgrading, ensure
all VKS clusters run at least VKr 1.33. Refer to the interoperability matrix upgrade path tool for upgrade path details.
• VKS Version - To upgrade to VKS 3.7, ensure the Supervisor runs VKS version 3.4.0 or later.
• vCenter 8.0 P07 and Supervisor Kubernetes Version - VKS 3.7 requires a minimum Supervisor Kubernetes version
of 1.32. Refer to the interoperability matrix.
• DSM - Please review interoperability matrix as you upgrade to VKS 3.7.
Deprecation Announcements
• Introduction of builtin-generic-v3.7.0 ClusterClass - With the release of VKS 3.7, VMware at Broadcom introduces
and recommends using the builtin-generic-v3.7.0 ClusterClass. Existing clusters must rebase to builtin-generic-v3.7.0
as a part of, or prior to, any upgrade to Kubernetes v1.36 or later. For more information, see the clusterclass variable
reference. Additionally, the builtin-generic-v3.6.0 ClusterClass is deprecated and will be removed in a future release.
• Discontinuation of TKC-based Clusters - VKS 3.7 drops support for TanzuKubernetesCluster (TKC) API-based
clusters. Because vSphere Kubernetes Release (VKr) v1.32 was the final version to support the TKC API, clusters that
rely on this API are no longer compatible with this release.
• Removal of Kubernetes Service management UI: In VKS 3.7.1, the Kubernetes Service management UI is no
longer supported as this was used to configure default CNI for TanzuKubernetesCluster (TKC) API-based clusters.
Since TKC API-based clusters are not supported starting VKS 3.7.0, the Kubernetes Service menu underneath the
Supervisor Management ---> Supervisor menu has been removed.

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
What's New
This release includes bug fixes and security patches.
• Updated default AddonRepository - The default AddonRepository has been updated to the latest standard
packages, VKS Add-ons version 3.7.0-20260723. Any new clusters you provision will automatically use these up-to-
date definitions, while existing clusters will remain safely unchanged.
• Enhanced error messaging for the SystemChecksSucceeded Cluster condition - SystemChecksSucceeded error
messages have been improved for various scenarios, including dry run check and misconfigured tools, to be more
clear and helpful.
Fixed Issues
Containerd TLS verification failure and image pull errors after certificate rotation in VKS which were set via
additionalTrustedCAs variable
In VKS 3.6.0 and later versions, certificates configured through the Cluster variable additionalTrustedCAs are propagated
in-place to the machines. If a certificate is rotated and the variable is updated, pods may reach a state of failure
accompanied by image pull errors. Inspecting the events or logs of the affected pods will show the following containerd
error:
trust: tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority.
The in-place mechanism used to update certificates does not restart the containerd service after the system certificates
have been updated on the machine. Consequently, containerd retains the previous certificate context in memory and
rejects connections utilizing the newly rotated certificates.
This issue affects VKS 3.6.x and VKS 3.7.0. Please see https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/448971 for
details. This issue is fixed in this release, VKS 3.7.1.
Kube-proxy remains running despite being disabled after cluster creation
If you provision a cluster without explicitly setting the variable, the system
kubernetes.kubeProxyConfiguration
improperly allows you to mutate the enabled flag to false after creation. Doing so results in a misleading cluster status that
reports kube-proxy as disabled, even though the kube-proxy pods continue to run.
This issue occurs due to a validation gap that allows an otherwise immutable variable
( ) to be modified after creation if it was left unset during the initial
kubernetes.kubeProxyConfiguration.enabled
cluster provisioning phase.
This issue affects VKS 3.7.0 and is fixed in this release, VKS 3.7.1.
Known Issues
VCFA Attach or Regional Harbor Setup Triggers In-place Update Might Lead to Supervisor Instability
Performing a VMware Cloud Foundation Automation (VCFA) Attach operation or configuring a Regional Harbor registry
pushes global configuration changes to VKS clusters. When these updates hit clusters utilizing the
builtin-generic-
ClusterClass, they trigger an in-place update workflow that provisions spare nodes to maintain availability,
v3.7.0
leading to a heavy resource load on the Supervisor.
The severity of this issue depends directly on the combined scale of clusters and node pools using the 3.7.0 ClusterClass.
Because an in-place update is triggered per cluster and per node pool, environments will experience simultaneous spike
in resource creation. This can exhaust the default ETCD database size limit on the Supervisor control plane VMs before
the next scheduled database compaction occurs.
Workaround: Contact Broadcom Support for a resolution.
Rollout of Nodes When Using Harbor Supervisor Service with Custom Certificates
When you use VKS alongside a Harbor Supervisor Service configured with a custom certificate, clusters on
ClusterClasses builtin-generic-v3.2.0, builtin-generic-v3.3.0, or builtin-generic-v3.4.0 might undergo a node rollout after
an upgrade. This rollout occurs because the ordering of trusted certificates is now deterministic, ensuring that subsequent
cluster reconciliations by VKS always add the same certificate with a consistent ordering. This behavior is a one-time
rollout, and existing clusters will not undergo automatic rollouts in the future. This issue is observed only when using a
Harbor Supervisor version earlier than 2.11.2+vmware.1-tkg.2.
VMware by Broadcom 20

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Workaround: Use the KB article to patch your current service to fix the labeling of secrets, or upgrade the Harbor
Supervisor Service to version 2.11.2+vmware.1-tkg.2 or later. Both workarounds initiate a rollout on all existing clusters.
VKS cluster rollouts stall indefinitely when bootstrapping failure leaves the machine without a nodeRef
This issue occurs during a rollout when a new machine fails to bootstrap (specifically, failing to join the cluster and
thus missing a nodeRef). Eventually, this machine is marked for remediation according to the configured health check
conditions. Because the machine is part of an in-place update process, the controller attempts to move the machine to a
new revision rather than simply deleting it. However, because the move mechanism requires a valid nodeRef to proceed,
and standard deletion is disabled for machines pending an in-place update, the controller enters a deadlock. It cannot
update, move, or delete the machine, causing the rollout to stall indefinitely.
Workaround: Contact Broadcom Support for a resolution.
Automatic Control Plane Rollout When Using Custom ClusterClass After Upgrading to VKS v3.5 and Later
Existing VKS clusters created with a custom ClusterClass (CC) that uses the builtin-generic-v3.4.0 class experience an
automatic rollout of their control plane nodes after an upgrade to VKS 3.5.0 or later.
This unscheduled rollout affects only the control plane nodes; workloads running on the cluster remain unaffected.
Workaround: No workaround is available for this issue because it stems from an incorrect inference of the base version of
the custom ClusterClass (in this case, 3.4.0).
Mixed-OS Clusters That Use Cilium CNI Fail to Reach a Ready State
When you deploy a VKS cluster with mixed worker nodes (Windows OS and Photon OS), the Windows worker nodes
remain in a Not Ready state. This issue occurs because the Cilium Container Network Interface (CNI) does not provide
support for Windows operating systems.
Workaround: If your workloads require Windows worker nodes, use a different supported CNI. If you must use the Cilium
CNI, provision the cluster exclusively with supported Linux worker nodes, such as Photon OS.
VKS Cluster Creation with OIDC Configuration Fails When Initiated from the VCFA UI
When you attempt to provision a VKS cluster with OIDC authentication via the VCFA UI, the cluster creation process fails.
This issue blocks administrators from using the graphical interface to configure OIDC for the Kubernetes API server.
The UI generates an improperly formatted cluster YAML file during the submission process. Specifically, it incorrectly
populates the field under as a single
audiences apiServerConfiguration.extraAuthentication.jwt.issuer
string, rather than the required YAML list or array format.
Workaround: To successfully provision a VKS cluster with OIDC configuration, bypass the UI and use the CLI or API to
submit the cluster deployment. Ensure that the field in your payload is formatted as a list:
audiences
issuer:

vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.7.0+v1.36

vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.7.0+v1.36 June 18 2026
What's New
Lifecycle and Upgrades
• Support for Kubernetes v1.36 - VKS 3.7 introduces compatibility for vSphere Kubernetes Release 1.36 (v1.36),
consuming Cluster API v1.13 and Cluster API Provider vSphere (CAPV) v1.16. VKS 3.7 drops support for VKr 1.32.
VMware by Broadcom 21

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
• Improvements to Configuring FIPS on Ubuntu Nodes - VKr 1.36 Ubuntu nodes now come bundled with FIPS. You
can enable FIPS on Ubuntu nodes without a Canonical Pro Subscription.
• Webhook Allowlist for Upgrade Precheck - VKS 3.6 introduced pre-upgrade checks to detect misconfigured
(Gatekeeper, Kyverno, Rancher, k8tz, Dynatrace, Linkerd, OpenTelemetry).
ValidatingWebhookConfigurations
In 3.7.0, cluster administrators can now configure a per-cluster allowlist of webhook names to exclude from the
misconfigured-software check. When all detected webhooks of interest are allowlisted,
SystemChecksSucceeded
resolves to and the cluster upgrade proceeds without requiring the blanket
True kubernetes.vmware.com/
annotation. The allowlist is set via a Cluster
dangerous-skip-misconfigured-software-check-for-update
annotation and is fully backward-compatible. Ommiting an allowlist leaves existing behavior is unchanged.
For information, see Bypassing Misconfigured Software Checks.
Configuration and Security
• Enhanced Control Plane Resilience with 5-Node Control Planes - To support environments that require extreme
resilience, you can configure VKS clusters with 5 control plane nodes. This expanded high-availability configuration
ensures greater fault tolerance and control plane stability for your critical Kubernetes workloads. To ensure clusters
with 5 control plane nodes can recover from a simultaneous loss of 2 control plane nodes, use VKr version 1.36.1+,
1.35.5+, or 1.34.8+.
• Read-only /usr Partition for Workload Cluster Nodes (Photon OS Only) - Added the
osConfiguration.immutability.usrPartitionMode variable to the builtin-generic-v3.7.0 ClusterClass. When you set this
variable to ReadOnly, the system mounts the /usr partition as read-only for the duration of the node lifecycle, which
enhances defense-in-depth against DaemonSet tampering. The default setting remains read-write.
• Expanded In-place Node Updates - VKS 3.7 can apply a broad set of node configuration changes directly to running
nodes, which significantly reduces disruption and upgrade time for large fleets. These in-place updates flow through
Cluster API and respect your configured maxUnavailable and maxSurge settings. By default, VKS briefly adds spare
nodes to preserve availability during the update. You can opt into a fully in-place update for a node pool by setting
maxUnavailable to 1 or higher. Note that maxUnavailable also governs disruptive rolling updates such as version
upgrades. Raising this value increases the importance of well-defined PodDisruptionBudgets and multi-replica, well-
spread workloads. Changes outside the supported set, such as Kubernetes version or VM class, continue to use the
standard rolling update. For more information about in-place-eligible and ineligible changes, refer to Understanding the
Update Model for VKS Clusters and the clusterclass variable reference. Clusters automatically pick up this behavior
when they rebase onto the builtin-generic-v3.7.0 ClusterClass during a cluster upgrade, or explicitly when you change
the ClusterClass.
• API to Disable kube-proxy for CNIs Bringing Their Own Proxy Implementation - VKS 3.7 introduces a mechanism
to provision new workload clusters with kube-proxy disabled, targeted at enterprise customers who deploy CNIs (such
as Cilium) that natively replace kube-proxy. This feature is supported with Kubernetes Release versions 1.35.0 or later.
• Configurable TLS Profiles for Kubernetes Components - New ClusterClass variables
and are available on the builtin-generic-v3.7.0
security.minimumTLSProtocol security.tlsCipherSuites
ClusterClass. These variables allow you to enforce a minimum TLS version (TLS 1.2 or 1.3) and specify custom cipher
suites across control plane and node components (kube-apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler, etcd, and kubelet).
The system automatically ignores custom ciphers under TLS 1.3 per Go standards.
• Automated Node Pool Configuration for Cluster Autoscaler Scale-from-Zero - The Cluster Autoscaler
automatically detects Windows node pools and inherits custom labels and taints when scaling from zero, eliminating
the need for manually maintained MachineDeployment annotations.
– Windows OS detection - Windows node pools no longer require the
capacity.cluster-
annotation.
autoscaler.kubernetes.io/labels: "kubernetes.io/os=windows"
– Custom labels and taints - Custom node labels and taints defined via cluster variables automatically propagate to
the Cluster Autoscaler by the cluster webhook, removing the need to duplicate them as a separate annotation.
• Configurable RuntimeClasses - VKS 3.7 provides the ability to add custom RuntimeClasses to ContainerD for use
with workloads. The initial support allows for the configuration of ulimits on Linux, which addresses common database
workload requirements such as memory lock and file open limits.
• Control Plane Scale Tuning (Etcd Customization) - You can adjust the default maximum request size for etcd
via cluster variables to prevent large ConfigMaps and Secrets from causing transaction failures in heavy GitOps
workflows.
– New VKS 3.7 Clusters - Utilize these advanced configuration variables natively out-of-the-box by using the
standard ClusterClass framework.

• Enhanced Validation to Prevent CIDR Overlaps During Cluster Creation - VKS 3.7 includes a validation check
that rejects new cluster creations if the Pod or Service CIDRs overlap with Supervisor-managed IP ranges. This
validation applies to cluster creations only and supports all Supervisor network topologies, such as VDS, NSX
Segment Networking, and NSX-VPC.
Identity and Access Management
• Native OIDC Authentication for VKS Clusters - VKS supports native OpenID Connect (OIDC) authentication for
VKS workload clusters as an alternative to the existing Pinniped-based identity flow. This feature enables enterprise
platform teams to implement standard, direct identity mechanisms across multi-provider environments. By leveraging
Kubernetes structured authentication configuration, operators can use customizable Common Expression Language
(CEL) expressions for advanced user, group, and attribute claims mapping. This capability natively unblocks
pass-through JWT authentication for popular Kubernetes dashboards and tooling (such as Headlamp and Tekton
Dashboard) and ensures seamless tenant isolation for environments that lack network access to the Pinniped
supervisor endpoint.
• Workload Identity Federation - VKS supports configuring the service account issuer URL, which allows workloads
to authenticate with their service account tokens to external services such as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud
Platform, and Microsoft Azure.
Add-ons and Add-on Management
• Support for Multiple AddonRepositoryInstalls for VKS Add-ons - Starting with VKS 3.7.0, VKS Add-ons shifts
from a single, continuously updated to a version-specific, additive model. The system
AddonRepositoryInstall
creates a new and for the current release on every VKS installation
AddonRepositoryInstall AddonRepository
or upgrade, which adds the new resources alongside existing ones and allows multiple VKS Add-ons repositories
to coexist simultaneously on VKS clusters. When you upgrade from VKS 3.5 or 3.6, the existing
default-addon-
is deprecated. It remains functional to prevent workload disruption, but VKS no longer updates it.
repo-install
Administrators are responsible for manually deleting unused and
AddonRepositoryInstall AddonRepository
resources when they are no longer needed.
• Core and Standard Packages Rebranded to VKS Add-ons - Starting with VKS 3.7.0, Broadcom formally
transitioned from the legacy "Core" and "Standard" package terminology to a unified VKS Add-ons framework.
VKS Add-ons are a collection of validated software components that extend the core functionality of VKS clusters,
deployable via the UI, CLI, or API. All add-ons are organized into four support tiers based on ownership, engineering
commitment, and integration depth:
– Product - Curated, packaged, and validated by Broadcom engineering. Broadcom Global Support (GS) provides
full support for deployment, lifecycle management, and runtime troubleshooting.
– Partner - Curated and validated by Independent Software Vendors (ISVs). Broadcom GS supports deployment and
lifecycle management; runtime troubleshooting escalates to the partner.
– Ecosystem - Broadcom-curated open-source software (OSS) validated for base VKS infrastructure compatibility.
Broadcom support is limited to packaging, signing, and lifecycle management issues.
– Community - Unverified or user-built OSS packages managed outside the official VKS portfolio. Broadcom does
not provide a support channel, lifecycle management, or runtime troubleshooting.

CLI and Tooling
• New CLI Command: vcf clusterclass explain - The command retrieves detailed information about a ClusterClass,
including available variables, default values, and documentation. This command reduces the need to manually inspect
ClusterClass YAML for day-2 configuration tasks.
Scale and Performance
• Increased Maximum Worker Node Scale for VKS Clusters - VKS supports up to 250 worker nodes in a single
cluster, which increases the previous maximum limit of 150. To ensure performance and stability when operating at this
new 250-node scale, you must apply the following cluster configuration adjustments:
– Control Plane Node Sizing - Minimum VM class requirements depend on your CNI and ingress configuration:
• Antrea + AVI - Minimum 4 vCPU / 12 GiB.
• Calico + Multus + AVI - Minimum 6 vCPU / 12 GiB.
– ETCD Database Size - Increase the ETCD database limit to at least 4 GB. The default 2 GB limit is insufficient for
250-node clusters executing high-concurrency rollouts.
– Pod CIDR Allocation - Configure the podCIDR mask based on your maxPods setting. Use a /15 mask for the default
maxPods limit of 110. If your configuration requires a larger maxPods limit, use a /14 mask.

– Multus Memory Limit - If using Multus, set the memory limit to 1.5 Gi or higher to prevent OOMKilled errors.
Note: If you perform high-concurrency rollouts (maxSurge > 20) in a 250-node cluster with approximately 11,000

Fixed Issues
• Windows Worker Nodes Fail to Join Active Directory Domain During VKS Cluster Deployment - When you
deploy a VMware Kubernetes Service (VKS) cluster, Windows worker nodes might fail to join the Active Directory (AD)
domain, which prevents the configuration of Windows Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) webhooks. This
issue occurs when the Kubernetes secret used for AD credentials contains unexpected newline (\n) characters. This
issue is resolved.
• Intermittent Control Plane Provisioned and Deleted During VKr Version Upgrades - Clusters created with VKS
v3.4.0 or earlier see an intermittent control plane provisioned and deleted during VKr version upgrades. This issue is
fixed for clusters that use the builtin-generic-v3.7.0 ClusterClass. Existing clusters that use builtin-generic-v3.4.0 or
earlier automatically update to use this class when you update the Kubernetes version, unless you add the skip-rebase
annotation to the cluster. Clusters that use older ClusterClass versions continue to experience the extra rollout.
Known Issues
Containerd TLS verification failure and image pull errors after certificate rotation in VKS which were set via
addiiotnalTrustedCAs variable
In VKS 3.6.0 and later versions, certificates configured through the Cluster variable additionalTrustedCAs are propagated
in-place to the machines. If a certificate is rotated and the variable is updated, pods may reach a state of failure
accompanied by image pull errors. Inspecting the events or logs of the affected pods will show the following containerd
error: trust: tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. The in-place mechanism used
to update certificates does not restart the containerd service after the system certificates have been updated on the
machine. Consequently, containerd retains the previous certificate context in memory and rejects connections utilizing the
newly rotated certificates.
This issue affects VKS 3.6.x and VKS 3.7.0. Please see https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/448971 for
details. This issue is fixed in VKS 3.7.1.
VKS cluster rollouts stall indefinitely when bootstrapping failure leaves the machine without a nodeRef
This issue occurs during a rollout when a new machine fails to bootstrap (specifically, failing to join the cluster and
thus missing a nodeRef). Eventually, this machine is marked for remediation according to the configured health check
conditions. Because the machine is part of an in-place update process, the controller attempts to move the machine to a
new revision rather than simply deleting it. However, because the move mechanism requires a valid nodeRef to proceed,
and standard deletion is disabled for machines pending an in-place update, the controller enters a deadlock. It cannot
update, move, or delete the machine, causing the rollout to stall indefinitely.
Contact Broadcom Support for a resolution.
VCFA Attach or Regional Harbor Setup Triggers In-place Update Might Lead to Supervisor Instability
Performing a VMware Cloud Foundation Automation (VCFA) Attach operation or configuring a Regional Harbor registry
pushes global configuration changes to VKS clusters. When these updates hit clusters utilizing the
builtin-generic-
ClusterClass, they trigger an in-place update workflow that provisions spare nodes to maintain availability,
v3.7.0
leading to a heavy resource load on the Supervisor.
The severity of this issue depends directly on the combined scale of clusters and node pools using the 3.7.0 ClusterClass.
Because an in-place update is triggered per cluster and per node pool, environments will experience simultaneous spike
in resource creation. This can exhaust the default ETCD database size limit on the Supervisor control plane VMs before
the next scheduled database compaction occurs.
Workaround: Contact Broadcom Support for a resolution.
Rollout of Nodes When Using Harbor Supervisor Service with Custom Certificates
When you use VKS alongside a Harbor Supervisor Service configured with a custom certificate, clusters on
ClusterClasses builtin-generic-v3.2.0, builtin-generic-v3.3.0, or builtin-generic-v3.4.0 might undergo a node rollout after
an upgrade. This rollout occurs because the ordering of trusted certificates is now deterministic, ensuring that subsequent

cluster reconciliations by VKS always add the same certificate with a consistent ordering. This behavior is a one-time
rollout, and existing clusters will not undergo automatic rollouts in the future. This issue is observed only when using a

Workaround: Use the KB article to patch your current service to fix the labeling of secrets, or upgrade the Harbor

Automatic Control Plane Rollout When Using Custom ClusterClass After Upgrading to VKS v3.5 and Later
Existing VKS clusters created with a custom ClusterClass (CC) that uses the builtin-generic-v3.4.0 class experience an
automatic rollout of their control plane nodes after an upgrade to VKS 3.5.0 or later.
This unscheduled rollout affects only the control plane nodes; workloads running on the cluster remain unaffected.
Workaround: No workaround is available for this issue because it stems from an incorrect inference of the base version of
the custom ClusterClass (in this case, 3.4.0).
Mixed-OS Clusters That Use Cilium CNI Fail to Reach a Ready State
When you deploy a VKS cluster with mixed worker nodes (Windows OS and Photon OS), the Windows worker nodes
remain in a Not Ready state. This issue occurs because the Cilium Container Network Interface (CNI) does not provide
support for Windows operating systems.
Workaround: If your workloads require Windows worker nodes, use a different supported CNI. If you must use the Cilium
CNI, provision the cluster exclusively with supported Linux worker nodes, such as Photon OS.

About the vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.6 Release Notes
vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) provides components for provisioning and managing the lifecycle of Kubernetes
clusters in the vSphere Supervisor environment.
These release notes provide details for each VKS release. Refer to the Managing vSphere Kubernetes Service with
vSphere Supervisor documentation for usage information.
Versioning and Upgrades
vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) point releases deliver the same base ClusterClass of the major release, bundled with
cumulative bug fixes and underlying improvements. They do not introduce a new or different ClusterClass. For example,
vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.6.x+v1.35 delivers bug fixes for the major VKS 3.6.0+v1.35. This means that the core
major release requirements, upgrade prerequisites, and deprecations apply to each point release.
To ensure cluster stability and receive critical bug fixes, always install or upgrade to the latest available point release, for
example, VKS 3.6.x+v1.35.
For the core requirements, refer back to the respective major baseline section, such as vSphere Kubernetes Service
3.6.0+v1.35, vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.5.0+v1.34, and so on.
Prerequisites for VKS 3.6 Upgrade
• vCenter and Supervisor Kubernetes version - VKS 3.6 requires Supervisor Kubernetes version 1.30 or later.
Supervisor Kubernetes version 1.30 is available with vCenter 9.0 and vCenter 8.0 Update 3g and above. You must
upgrade the Supervisor Kubernetes version in vCenter to at least version 1.30. Refer to the interoperability matrix for
more details.
• VKr Version - VKS 3.6 drops compatibility for VKr v1.31. Before upgrading to VKS 3.6, you must ensure all your VKS
Clusters are running at least on VKr 1.32.
• VKS version - To upgrade to VKS 3.6 directly, the VKS version installed on the Supervisor must be at least VKS 3.3.
Refer to the upgrade path tool in the interoperability matrix for more details.
VMware by Broadcom 27

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1

vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.6.3+v1.35
Release Snapshot
vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.6.3 is generally available for use with vSphere 9.x and vSphere 8.x.
Name Release Date
vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.6.3+v1.35 JUN 16 2026
What's New
• This release focuses on upgrade reliability, air-gapped support fixes, webhook guardrail enhancements, addon
framework correctness, and essential security patches.
Lifecycle and Upgrades
• Webhook Allowlist for Upgrade Precheck - VKS 3.6 introduced pre-upgrade checks to detect misconfigured
ValidatingWebhookConfigurations (Gatekeeper, Kyverno, Rancher, k8tz, Dynatrace, Linkerd, OpenTelemetry). In 3.6.3,
cluster administrators can now configure a per-cluster allowlist of webhook names to exclude from the misconfigured-
software check. When all detected webhooks of interest are added to allowlist, SystemChecksSucceeded resolves
to True and will not block upgrades. The allowlist is set via a Cluster annotation and is fully backward-compatible, no
allowlist means existing behavior is unchanged.
• Published addons.kubernetes.vmware.com API Resources in Developer Documentation - The full
addons.kubernetes.vmware.com API group resources including AddonConfig, AddonInstall, AddonRelease, and
related types are now published in developer.broadcom.com. This provides an official reference for operators and
integrators building on the VKS addon framework.
• Updated Embedded Add-on Repository to 3.6.0+20260416 - The default AddonRepository embedded in VKS
3.6.3 has been updated to the Standard packages release 3.6.0+20260416. After upgrading to VKS 3.6.3, the default
AddonRepositoryInstall for standard packages will automatically switch to this release. To skip the auto-update, use the
annotation addons.kubernetes.vmware.com/skip-vks-managed-addon-repository-update.
• machineadm Service Logs Added to VKS Support Bundle - The machineadm systemd service runs on all VKS
guest cluster Linux nodes and is responsible for critical node bootstrap operations. Its logs are now included in the
VKS support bundle alongside kubelet and containerd logs, captured with the same head-10M / tail-10M size cap. This
significantly improves supportability and root-cause analysis for node-level issues.
Fixed Issues
Provisioning a VKS cluster with an additional volume on Ubuntu fails on some nodes
When creating or scaling a VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) cluster using Ubuntu-based images with
additional storage volumes (specifically /var/lib/containerd or /var/lib/kubelet), the worker nodes may fail to initialize. These
VMware by Broadcom 28

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
nodes will appear stuck in a "NotReady" state because the system fails to format the additional partition The issue has
been fixed in this release.
Antrea AddonConfig validation error didn't sync to ClusterAddon
When an Antrea AddonConfig had a validation error, the error status was not propagated to the corresponding
ClusterAddon resource, leaving operators without visibility into the misconfiguration. Validation errors are now correctly
reflected in the ClusterAddon status. The issue has been fixed in this release.
VKS upgrade precheck errored when non-VKS images were present in the VKS Content Library
The Upgrade Compatibility System (UCS) precheck failed with an error when it encountered images in the VKS Content
Library that were not managed by VKS (e.g. user-added custom images). The precheck now correctly ignores non-VKS
images and only validates VKS-managed entries. The issue has been fixed in this release.
Control-plane only clusters on VKS 3.6 ClusterClass never become available
Clusters provisioned with the VKS 3.6 ClusterClass without worker node pools would complete infrastructure provisioning,
but never become available. The Antrea add-on configuration template failed to render because spec.topology.workers is
absent from the Cluster resource when no workers are defined, preventing cluster networking from starting. The issue has
been fixed in this release.
Failed to inject additional CA certificates to windows worker nodes
Windows nodes were incorrectly classified as eligible for in-place updates when configuration changes were applied,
preventing the expected rolling replacement. In VKS 3.6.3, Windows nodes are correctly identified as requiring rollout
when node-level configuration changes.
VKS cluster upgrade stuck due to non-deterministic AddonRelease selection
This occurs when there are multiple AddonReleases with the same spec.version. This can happen for different KR
patches with the same CNI version. The AddonRelease selection was not deterministic, which caused cluster upgrade to
get stuck on the upgrade hook. This issue has been fixed in this release.
MaxPods validation did not account for the ClusterClass version in use
The admission webhook validating maxPods > 110 was applied unconditionally, without checking which ClusterClass
version the cluster was using. Clusters using older ClusterClass versions that legitimately support higher maxPods values
were incorrectly rejected. The validation now correctly inspects the ClusterClass version before enforcing the limit. The
issue has been fixed in this release.
Fix kapp Reconciliation Deadlock for Air-Gapped Upgrades
Customers upgrading VKS in air-gapped environments using a pull/push bundle relocation workflow (instead of imgpkg
copy) experienced a kapp reconciliation deadlock. After an initial failed relocation followed by a correct imgpkg copy, kapp
would block indefinitely on no-op PackageInstall resources (stuck in FAILED state), preventing the fixed Package from
reconciling. The issue has been fixed in this release.
Accurate Upgrade Version Filtering for TKC Clusters
VKr 1.33.1 was incorrectly displayed as a compatible upgrade path for TanzuKubernetesCluster objects running 1.32.x.
Since VKr 1.33.1 only supports Cluster API and not TKC API, this version is now excluded from the compatible upgrades
list for TKC objects, preventing user confusion.
Known Issues
Clusters created with VKS v3.4.0 or earlier will see an intermittent control plane provisioned and deleted during
VKr version upgrades.
After VKS upgrades from v3.4.x or below, existing clusters triggering a Kubernetes version upgrade and/or ClusterClass
version update, will observe the first newer control plane machine's Up-To-Date condition be marked as False almost
immediately after it starts to be provisioned. This means that the first control plane machine will be rolled out twice during
the upgrade.
This machine eventually moves to the Ready state and is instantly deleted to be replaced by another up-to-date control
place machine. The rollout of the cluster progresses successfully after.
VMware by Broadcom 29

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Steps to reproduce:
1. Create a cluster using VKS v3.4.1 (or below) using any of the shipped ClusterClass versions, say, builtin-generic-
v3.4.0
2. Upgrade VKS to version v3.6.0
3. Update the VKr version in use by the Cluster by updating the spec.topology.version field.
No manual intervention is necessary, the first newer control plane machine gets deleted and recreated. The rest of the
Cluster upgrade progresses successfully.
Creating a VKS cluster fails due to Velero webhook failures
When creating a VKS cluster, the process fails, and you observe the following error:
failed to create
or update VirtualMachine: Internal error occurred: failed calling webhook
"cbt.mutate.virtualmachine"
The Velero vSphere Operator webhook monitors VM creation for VKS clusters and enables the Changed Block Tracking
(CBT) flag on the VM Custom Resource (CR) if required. If the Velero vSphere Operator webhook is unavailable, cluster
creation fails with the error mentioned above.
Workaround: Identify the cause of the webhook failure by inspecting the Velero vSphere Operator logs.
Rollout of nodes when using Harbor Supervisor Service with custom certificates
When using VKS alongside Harbor Supervisor Service configured with a custom certificate, Clusters on ClusterClasses
builtin-generic-v3.2.0, or builtin-generic-v3.3.0, or builtin-generic-v3.4.0, may undergo a node rollout post upgrade. This
happens because the ordering of trusted certificates has now been made deterministic such that subsequent reconciles of
the Cluster by VKS will always add the same certificate with the same consistent ordering. This is a one time rollout and
existing clusters should not undergo any such automatic rollouts in the future. This issue is observed only when using a
Harbor supervisor version < 2.11.2+vmware.1-tkg.2.
Either use the KB article to patch your current service to fix the labeling of secrets or consider upgrading Harbor
Supervisor Service to a version >=2.11.2. Both these workarounds will initiate a rollout on all existing Clusters. This issue
is observed only when using a Harbor supervisor version < 2.11.2+vmware.1-tkg.2.
VKS 3.5.0 and VKS 3.6.0 are not compatible with Data Services Manager 9.0.0 and 9.0.1.
Upgrading VKS to version 3.5.0 or VKS 3.6.0 will cause Data Services Manager versions 9.0.0 and 9.0.1 to become
inoperable. Refer to the interoperability matrix for more details.
Workaround: N/A
Resolution: Customers using DSM 9.0.0 and DSM 9.0.1 are advised not to upgrade to VKS 3.5.0 /or VKS 3.6.0 due to
known incompatibility.
Automatic Control Plane Roll-out when using Custom ClusterClass post upgrade to VKS v3.5 and higher
Existing VKS clusters created with a custom Class (CC) using the builtin-generic-v3.4.0 class will experience an automatic
rollout of their control plane nodes after upgrading to VKS 3.5.0.
Note: This unscheduled rollout only affects the control plane nodes, and workloads running on the cluster should remain
unaffected
Workaround:
There is no workaround available for this issue, as it stems from an incorrect inference of the base version of the custom
CC (in this case, 3.4.0).
VMware by Broadcom 30
