Antrea Hybrid inter-subnet traffic disrupted after Node lifecycle operations
In VKS clusters where Antrea hybrid mode is enabled, Pod-to-Pod traffic between nodes in different subnets may be
disrupted following Node lifecycle operations. These operations include VM Class updates, Node scaling and the reuse of
Pod CIDRs. This issue specifically affects clusters where nodes are distributed across multiple subnets.
Note:
Antrea Hybrid mode is available on VKS 3.6 running VKr version 1.35 or higher.
As a temporary workaround, restarting the antrea-agent Pods on the affected Nodes may temporarily restores Pod-to-
Pod traffic, This workaround does not address the underlying issue, and the traffic disruption may reoccur if the triggering
conditions are met again.
Known Issues
After an ESX reboot, time drift could cause some of the VKS nodes to be in state
NotReady
Following an ESX host reboot, VKS nodes scheduled on the rebooted host, may experience clock drift. While VKr relies
on the chrony service to synchronize time with an NTP server, a race condition can occur: if the kubelet initializes before
chrony finishes correcting the time, the kubelet will generate service tokens with past timestamps, rendering them
invalid.
Workaround:
Deleting the problematic node, the node will be recreated with correct time and the pods will be scheduled and running.
After upgrade, application pods will be stuck in ContainerCreating state with warning
FailedAttachVolume
If a pod is stuck in state, execute the following command -
ContainerCreating
kubectl get pods -A | grep ContainerCreating"
Describe the pod, and if you find the following warning pattern, execute the workaround
2m9s (x59 over 104m) attachdetach-controller AttachVolume.Attach failed for volume
Warning FailedAttachVolume
"pvc-1f46ebd4-2606-4800-aa70-af8bdb75fdb8" : CSINode vks361-ph-336-calico-11ns5-c5-np1-worker-rf5zx-ttrqp-6qc7j
does not contain driver csi.vsphere.vmware.com
Workaround:
restart the csi-node pods
kubectl delete pod vsphere-csi-node-<xyz> -n vmware-system-csi
After worker node scale-up and scale-down operation on large VKS cluster with 3CP/150W, around 70 pods went
into OutofPods/Pending state
This is caused due to a race condition in a scenario where auto-scaler is increasing the number of nodes, while there are
a larger number of pods waiting to be scheduled. And scheduler assigns the pods to the first few nodes available.
Work around:
Delete the pods marked with the error "OutOfPods".
Autoscaler is unable to scale up windows nodes in a cluster containing multiple node pools with mixed OS types.
In autoscaler-based guest clusters having hybrid node pools with different OS (Photon, Ubuntu, Windows), when scaling
up applications on the clusters, Windows nodes are not scaled up even though Windows pods are in a pending state.
Workloads are stuck in a pending state and new nodes will not be deployed. The autoscaler pod logs show the error
can't schedule pod : predicate "NodeAffinity" didn't pass (predicateReasons=[node(s)
didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector];
When the cluster contains multiple node pools, the autoscaler will try to automatically scale up the node to handle pending
pods. When the pod contains nodeSelector, the autoscaler will simulate the node to be created based on the annotation
VMware by Broadcom 83

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
of the current node pool to evaluate whether it meets the needs of the current pod. Windows pods need nodeSelector to
schedule to Windows nodes, so this problem will be encountered.
Add the annotation ( : "key1=value1,key2=value2") in
capacity.cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/labels
machine deployment to inform the autoscaler that this node pool can create nodes with this label.
After VKS cluster upgrade a failed Antrea upgrade job remains in the cluster
Sometimes, when the upgrades take longer you will notice an Antrea upgrade jobs in error state. These errors do not
impact the functionality of the Antrea. These are transient errors that occur while the cluster is upgrading.
Workaround: You can use the to clean up the failed jobs.
kubectl delete
Packages are in 'Reconcile failed' state after upgrade due to caBundle certificate mismatch
After the cluster upgrades to this version, you may sometimes see that the packages are in 'Reconcile Failed' state. Due
to this the upgrade is flagged as failed. This may happen because the kapp-controller from the old cluster still exists
due to a possible race condition during the upgrade. Both the old and the new kapp-controller attempt to update the api
service with their CA bundle causing this issue.
1. Try restarting the kapp-controller pod in the cluster, the correct CABundle content gets synced to the api-service and all
packages get reconciled.
2. If the above workaround doesn't work, edit the CA bundle of the api service manually with the content of upgraded
kapp-controller self signed cert.

• Pre-requisites for VKr 1.35 upgrade

Kubernetes v1.35 or later.
• Support for Kubernetes version 1.35.0 -
– Pre-built node images for Photon OS 5.0, Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS
– Custom Node Images Support - RHEL 9, Microsoft Windows Server 2022
– vSphere Kubernetes v1.35 and all subsequent patch releases are supported for 24 months from GA, through
February 2028.
– CNI configurations (such as Antrea and Calico) are now managed through the VKS Addon Framework using the
custom resource.
AddonConfig
• Support for Antrea Hybrid mode - Starting with release VKr 1.35, Antrea (v2.5.1) introduces a dynamic traffic
encapsulation capability known as Hybrid mode, specifically for NSX VPC based deployments. When configured, this
feature significantly improves pod-to-pod network performance by disabling encapsulation for traffic between pods on
the same subnet, while continuing to utilize tunnels for cross subnet traffic. This capability reduces CPU usage and
lowers latency, providing significant performance gains for latency-sensitive applications. Refer documentation.
• Key Upstream K8s Capabilities available with VKr 1.35
VMware by Broadcom 84

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
– In Place update of Pod resources (stable in v1.35, enabled-by-default in v1.33) enables dynamic adjustment
of pod resources without restarting the pods. In compute-intensive workloads like Stateful Applications and AI/ML
workloads, interruptions due to restarts can trigger expensive cold starts and loss of continuity, requiring rebuilding
of cache, rebalancing of distributed data and restarting of batch jobs. This capability significantly minimizes
the performance penalty and operational overheads, preventing cost escalations associated with pod restarts.
(upstream blog)
– OCI Image is now a first class Volume Service (stable, enabled by default in v1.35) - Kubernetes 1.35 enables-
by-default the new field image in the Pod Volume specifications that allows you to point directly to an OCI image
or artifacts. This eliminates the need for InitContainers and ensures the volume is mounted by runtime before
the application starts. This significantly reduces the size and threat surface of the application container image. The
mounted volume is immutable and artifacts cannot be modified (upstream announcement).
– Fine-grained Container restart rules (beta, enabled-by-default in v1.35) - Kubernetes v1.35 enables granular
control over container lifecycles by decoupling them from the Pod-level restart policy. Users can now define
restartPolicy for individual containers that can operate independently of the overall Pod’s setting. This is particularly
valuable for Pods configured with restartPolicy: Never, as it allows specific containers encountering transient
errors to attempt recovery by restarting, ensuring critical workloads are not terminated prematurely. (upstream
announcement)
Deprecations Announcements
• support has now been removed - All node images shipped as part of VKS are already oncgroupsv2
cgroupv1

After the cluster upgrades to 1.33.3, you may sometimes see that the packages are in 'Reconcile Failed' state. Because of
this the upgrade is flagged as failed. This may happen because the kapp-controller from the old cluster still exists due to
a possible race condition during the upgrade. Both the old and the new kapp-controller attempts to update the api service
with thier CA bundle causing this issue.

all the packages get reconciled.

kapp-controller self signed cert.

What's New
• Support for Kubernetes version 1.34.1 for Photon OS 5.0, Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. To be able
to upgrade to VKr 1.34.1, you must upgrade to vSphere Kubernetes Service version v3.5+1.34. See the VKS 3.5
Release notes for more information
• Change in naming convention of the Release Name: From vSphere Kubernetes release 1.34.1 onwards, we are
dropping the use of the string ‘.fips’ in the release name. This change is limited to the release string only and does not
have any impact on the status of FIPS-enabled components in the build.
– Kubernetes and other open source components will continue to be FIPS-enabled by default
– User will have to continue to manually enable the OS FIPS Mode (see documentation)
Example
– Release name string in the past → v1.33.1---vmware.1-fips-vkr.2
– Release name string from VKr 1.34.1 onwards → v1.34.1---vmware.1-vkr.2
("fips" keyword in the string is dropped)
• Dynamic Resource Allocation
– Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) feature has been graduated to stable in upstream Kubernetes 1.34. DRA
provides a flexible way to categorize, request, and use devices such as GPUs in your cluster. Workloads can now
perform fine-grained filtering for specific device attributes and share devices across pods, enabling more efficient
utilization of resources.
Upgrade Instructions
• VKr 1.34 only works with cluster-class with
builtin-generic-v3.5.0.
•
Important:
etcd Version in VKr 1.34.1
When upgrading from 1.32.0 -->1.33.1 --> 1.34.1, specifically involving etcd versions less than 3.5.20, an upgrade
issue is observed (Bug #20793).
This was attributed to an upstream issue involving etcd. To protect users from encountering this issue VKr 1.34.1
will ship etcd version 3.5.23, instead of the newer etcd version 3.6.4. We are collaborating with the etcd
community to fix the issue in the upcoming patches.
•

Mandatory Step: VKr 1.34 supports both Ubuntu 24.04 and Ubuntu 22.04. Whether you are creating a new v1.34
cluster, you must update the annotation in the cluster object configuration to reflect the
resolve-os-image
required Ubuntu version number. Cluster object definitions with Ubuntu nodes will require an explicit field for
os-
and in the ClusterClass topology annotations to resolve to either Ubuntu 22.04 or Ubuntu
name os-version
24.04. Please note, not performing this step will result in failure to create a new cluster.
The recommended configuration is to have ClusterClass topology annotations in the following format:
run.tanzu.vmware.com/resolve-os-image: "os-name=$osname,os-version=$osversion"
VMware by Broadcom 93

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Example 1: To create VKr 1.34 with Ubuntu 22.04 use the following:

Example 2: To create VKr 1.34 with Ubuntu 24.04 use the following:

Known Issues
Packages are in 'Reconcile failed' state after upgrade due to caBundle certificate mismatch
After the cluster upgrades to 1.33.3, you may sometimes see that the packages are in 'Reconcile Failed' state. Due to
this the upgrade is flagged as failed. This may happen because the kapp-controller from the old cluster still exists due to
a possible race condition during the upgrade. Both the old and the new kapp-controller attempt to update the api service
with their CA bundle causing this issue.
1. Try restarting the kapp-controller pod in the cluster, the correct CABundle content gets synced to the api-service and all
packages get reconciled.
2. If the above workaround doesn't work, edit the CA bundle of the api service manually with the content of upgraded
kapp-controller self signed cert.

What's New

| Operating System  | OS Version       |     | Kernel Version |
| ----------------- | ---------------- | --- | -------------- |
| Photon OS         | Photon 5.0       |     | 6.1.136-2.ph5  |

• Support for Kubernetes minor release 1.33. To be able to upgrade to VKr 1.33, you must upgrade to vSphere
Kubernetes Version 3.4. See the VKS 3.4 Release notes for more information.
• Support for Ubuntu 24.04. In addition to Photon OS 5.0 and Ubuntu 22.04, VKr 1.33 supports Ubuntu 24.04.  Please
refer to the important upgrade recommendations below before upgrading to VKr 1.33.
Important:
FIPS 140-3 modules for Ubuntu 24.04 LTS kernel are currently undergoing assessment by CMVP, pending FIPS
Validation (see update). If you are using VKr 1.32 (Ubuntu OS 22.04) with Ubuntu Pro for FIPS-140-3 enabled for
your OS, you must upgrade to VKr 1.33 (Ubuntu OS version 22.04) to continue utilizing Ubuntu Pro FIPS 140-3
validated kernel modules. In such case, you must not choose Ubuntu 24.04 when you upgrade to VKr 1.33
•
Container runtime is upgraded to use containerd 2.0.
• Calico is upgraded to 3.30.0. In addition to adding several new features, calico 3.30 has updates on policy naming.
• VKr core packages are configured with Priority Classes to ensure the system services are not evicted under
resource pressure.

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
• Upstream Kubernetes 1.33 has several updates . Some key items that require your attention in terms of
deprecation are:
– The pod field is now deprecated and will no longer be set. The status of a pod resize will be
status.resize
exposed under two new conditions: and instead.
PodResizeInProgress PodResizePending
– The hints field has graduated to GA. The beta annotation
EndpointSlice service.kubernetes.io/
is now considered deprecated. Users are encouraged to use the
topology-mode spec.trafficDistribution
field in the Service API for topology-aware routing configuration.
– The feature flag is deprecated and can no longer be enabled
WatchFromStorageWithoutResourceVersion
– Removed support for v1alpha1 version of and
ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
API kinds
ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
– In addition, the following APIs have newer versions of them available in 1.33. Review and update your applications
accordingly.
• certificates.k8s.io/clustertrustbundles
• coordination.k8s.io/leasecandidates
• authentication.k8s.io/selfsubjectreviews
• networking.k8s.io/ipaddresses
• networking.k8s.io/servicecidrs
• resource.k8s.io/deviceclasses
• resource.k8s.io/resourceclaims
• resource.k8s.io/resourceclaimtemplates
• resource.k8s.io/resourceslices

Known Issues
Consumption Interface 1.02 GA can't create Ubuntu based VKr 1.33 Cluster
VKr 1.33 offers a choice of Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. This requires the OS-name and OS-version to
be specified for VKS to resolve the same. Consumption Interface 1.02 will not be able to make the resolution. It will be
available in future releases
Use the CLI to specify the OS-name and OS-version as instructed above in the 'Important Upgrade Recommendation'
section
After VKS cluster upgrade a failed Antrea upgrade job remains in the cluster
In some cases, when the upgrades take longer you will notice an Antrea upgrade jobs in error state. These errors do not
impact the functionality of the Antrea. These are transient errors that occur while the cluster is upgrading.
Workaround: You can use the to clean up the failed jobs.
kubectl delete
VKS clusters with Ubuntu v1.32.x and FIPS enablement can't be upgraded to v1.33.1 with Ubuntu 24.04 as OS
version
If you select Ubuntu 24.04 as a target version for 1.33.1 for FIPS enabled Ubuntu clusters of v1.32.x, the upgrade gets
stuck. Ubuntu 24.04 does not yet support FIPS enablement at the moment.
Workaround: Use Ubuntu 22.04 as a target since Ubuntu 24.04 doesn't support FIPS Kernel updates via Ubuntu Pro.

Known Issues
After VKS cluster upgrade a failed Antrea upgrade job remains in the cluster
In some cases, when the upgrades take longer you will notice an Antrea upgrade jobs in error state. These errors do not
impact the functionality of the Antrea. These are transient errors that occur while the cluster is upgrading.
Workaround: You can use the  kubectl delete  to clean up the failed jobs.

What's New
VKr 1.30.11 includes the following new features:
• Log rotation to avoid pod eviction due to increased disk pressure: Improved the management of the system-
generated logs to avoid pods getting evicted due to disk pressure, causing workload degradation. With log rotation, the
system-generated logs up to 500 MB are retained before the log rotation kicks in. Journal Log has been set to grow up
to a max size of 2GB so as to avoid increase of disk pressure due to build up of Journal Logs.
• Improved timesync: This release also addresses possible race condition on startup between   and
chronyd
. This leads to lack of synchronization of time on the nodes resulting in time drift in the pods.
systemd-timesyncd
chronyd  is now used for NTP timesync and ensures that  timesyncd  doesn't stop  chronyd  from running.

Known Issues
During upgrade from 1.28.7 to 1.29.15 - antrea package could get stuck in Reconcile failed state.
As part of the upgrade, antrea packages launches an upgrade job. If the upgrade job is scheduled on older version node,
the job fails and doesn't auto-reconcile.
VMware by Broadcom 107

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Manually delete the job and let kapp resync the antrea pkgi succeed(wait 10min).
kubectl delete job -n vmware-system-antrea register-placeholder

Upgrade Recommendations
• If you are upgrading from Kubernetes release 1.27 - It is highly recommended to upgrade to VKr 1.28.15 and
above. While the system allows to upgrade from VKr 1.27.16 to VKr 1.28.8, this would result in a back in time upgrade
and will cause the upgrade to get stuck. If you have already initiated an upgrade from 1.27.16 to 1.28.8, follow KB
378212 to revert the cluster back to 1.27.16 and then upgrade to 1.28.15.
• If you are upgrading to Kubernetes release 1.29 - It is highly recommended to upgrade to VKr 1.29.15 or later
patches. While the system allows upgrade from VKr 1.28.15 to VKr 1.29.4, this would result in a back in time upgrade
for some of the packages and will cause the upgrade to get stuck. If you have already initiated an upgrade from VKr
1.28.15 to VKr 1.29.4, follow KB 378212 to revert the cluster back to VKr 1.28.15 and then upgrade to VKr 1.29.15.
Please note that VKr 1.29.15 is compatible with VKS 3.3.3+. Therefore the recommended upgrade path from VKr
1.28.15 to VKr 1.29.15 is as follows:
– Upgrade to VKS 3.3.3.
– Upgrade the VKr 1.28.15 clusters to VKr 1.29.15.

What's New
VKr 1.32.0 includes the following new features:
VMware by Broadcom 110

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
• Support for Kubernetes release v1.32. To be able to run Kubernetes release v1.32, you must upgrade your VKS to
v3.3. Please refer VKS 3.3 Release notes.
• vSphere CSI driver release 3.4 ships with an enhanced CSI snapshotter version. After upgrading to Kubernetes
release v1.32, you no longer need to install the snapshot validation webhook into the guest cluster using standard
packages. After you upgrade to v1.32 and if you had previously installed the snapshot validation webhook, you can
follow these steps to remove it.
a. Check if the snapshot validation webhook is installed from standard packages.
• Run following command from the jumphost/external-gateway VM with tanzu CLI installed and check for package
"external-csi-snapshot-webhook" in the package list.
#
tanzu package installed list
b. Remove the redundant snapshot validation webhook if found installed.
• Run the following command from the jumphost/external-gateway VM with tanzu CLI installed to delete package
"external-csi-snapshot-webhook" in the guest cluster.
#
tanzu package installed delete external-csi-snapshot-webhook
Other improvements include:
• Log rotation to avoid pod eviction due to increased disk pressure: Improved the management of the system-
generated logs to avoid pods getting evicted due to disk pressure, causing workload degradation. With log rotation, the
system-generated logs up to 500 MB are retained before the log rotation kicks in. Journal Log has been set to grow up
to a max size of 2GB so as to avoid increase of disk pressure due to build up of Journal Logs.
• Improved timesync: This release also addresses possible race condition on startup between and
chronyd
. This leads to lack of synchronization of time on the nodes resulting in time drift in the pods.
systemd-timesyncd
is now used for NTP timesync and ensures that doesn't stop from running.
chronyd timesyncd chronyd

Known Issues
Autoscaler is unable to scale up windows nodes in a cluster containing multiple node pools with mixed OS types.
In autoscaler-based guest clusters having hybrid node pools with different OS (Photon, Ubuntu, Windows), when scaling
up applications on the clusters, Windows nodes are not scaled up even though Windows pods are in a pending state.
Workloads are stuck in a pending state and new nodes will not be deployed. The autoscaler pod logs show the error
can't schedule pod : predicate "NodeAffinity" didn't pass (predicateReasons=[node(s)
| didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector]; |     |     |     |
| ------------------------------------------- | --- | --- | --- |
When the cluster contains multiple node pools, the autoscaler will try to automatically scale up the node to handle pending
pods. When the pod contains nodeSelector, the autoscaler will simulate the node to be created based on the annotation
of the current node pool to evaluate whether it meets the needs of the current pod. Windows pods need nodeSelector to
schedule to Windows nodes, so this problem will be encountered.
| Add the annotation ( |     | : "key1=value1,key2=value2") in  |     |
| -------------------- | --- | -------------------------------- | --- |
capacity.cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/labels
machine deployment to inform the autoscaler that this node pool can create nodes with this label.

This VKr 1.32 release fixes the issue described in Important Upgrade Requirements for VKr 1.31.1 for vSphere 8.x. You
no longer need to migrate the objects of Antrea CRDs to the latest storage versions before upgrading VKS clusters from
VKr 1.27.

• Highly recommended to upgrade to VKr 1.31.7 (requires upgraded to VKS 3.3.3) or VKr 1.31.4.
• Upgrade to 1.31.1 are known to get stuck causing downtime.
Update: [20th Dec 2024]
Some customers reported issues while upgrading VKS clusters from VKr 1.27
When upgrading VKS clusters from VKr 1.27 and earlier to VKr1.31.1 with Antrea 2.1.0, you must migrate all existing
objects of Antrea CRDs to the latest storage version. Follow the steps to perform the migration correctly:
1. Go to https://github.com/antrea-io/antrea/releases/tag/v2.1.0 and download the antctl tool.
2. Run the following commands to migrate the objects from the old versions to the latest storage versions:
# antctl upgrade api-storage --dry-run
# antctl upgrade api-storage

Known Issues
Upgrade of VKS clusters hangs when upgrading from 1.27 or earlier to 1.31.1 with Antrea
This manual step is required becauseVKr 1.31.1 comes with Antrea 2.1, where deprecated CRDs are removed and CRDs
with new storage versions are introduced. If you have missed performing the migration steps described in the Important
Upgrade Requirements section of these release notes, the following error will be displayed in the clusterbootstrap status
of the Supervisor and upgrade will hang:
status:
conditions:
lastTransitionTime: "2024-11-26T09:04:15Z"
message: |-
kapp: Error: update customresourcedefinition/tiers.crd.antrea.io (apiextensions.k8s.io/v1) cluster:
Updating resource customresourcedefinition/tiers.crd.antrea.io (apiextensions.k8s.io/v1) cluster:
API server says:
CustomResourceDefinition.apiextensions.k8s.io "tiers.crd.antrea.io" is invalid: status.storedVersions[0]:
Invalid value: "v1alpha1": must appear in spec.versions (reason: Invalid)
VMware by Broadcom 116

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Follow the steps in KB 384095 to resolve the error.
Fixed Issues
VKr 1.31.1 for vSphere 8.x has the following fixed issue:
When VC public keys are renewed, after you authenticate with Kubernetes cluster successfully, you will get the following
error with  kubectl  command:
$ kubectl get pod -A error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)
The issue is fixed in 1.31.1. Public keys will be auto reloaded.

Resolved Issues
After a power outage or other repeated I/O failures, the VKS cluster is unhealthy and the workloads are
unavailable
With VKr versions earlier than 1.27.11, repeated I/O failures, triggered by a power outage or datastore path change,
can cause the control plane and worker node disks to be mounted as ReadOnly. As a result, the VKS cluster becomes
unhealthy and its workloads unavailable.
Workaround:
• To resolve this issue on VKr versions earlier than 1.27.11, restart the VMs.
• On VKr version 1.27.11 and later, this issue is resolved.

What's New
TKr 1.26.5 includes the following new features.
• Support for Kubernetes version 1.26.5 for PhotonOS and Ubuntu.
– Photon OS Kernel version: photon-4.19.288-2.ph3
– Ubuntu Kernel version: ubuntu-20.04.1
• With TKr 1.26.5, VKS on Supervisor will enforce PSA by default on VKS clusters.
– Sample command to update pod security on a TKr 1.26 Kubernetes namespace:
•
kubectl label --overwrite ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/
enforce=privileged
Note:
PSA policies on system namespaces cannot be changed.
– For more information, refer to the PSA documentation:
• Pod Security Admission
• Pod Security Standards
• Migrate from PodSecurityPolicy to the Built-In PodSecurity Admission Controller
– See also:
• TKr 1.25 Release Notes
• TKG on Supervisor documentation
• Tanzu Kubernetes Grid Image Builder 0.3.0 for vSphere 8.x is available on Github.
– This release adds support for building custom Photon and Ubuntu images for Kubernetes 1.26.5.

Fixed Issues
TKr 1.26.5 for vSphere 8.x has the following fixed issues.
Iptables fails with exit code 3 (no child processes) due to bpfilter kernel bug
Verify naming length issue due to kapp is fixed
Verify that the name length issue is fixed and available from v0.45.0 of kapp controller.
Consume linux kernel package for photon images instead of linux-esx
The linux-esx kernel package lacks some of the features supported by the generic linux kernel package. Because there is
no specific requirement to support linux-esx kernel, moving to the linux kernel package is preferred.
TKr 1.25.7 for vSphere 8.x
Release Snapshot
TKr 1.25.7 is generally available for use with vSphere 8.x.
Name Release Date vCenter Server 8.0
v1.25.7---vmware.3-fips.1-tk 7/27/2023 vSphere 8.0 U1c and later
g.1
What's New
TKr 1.25.7 includes the following new features.
• Support for Kubernetes version 1.25.7 for PhotonOS and Ubuntu.
• Support for Pod Security Admission (PSA) controller to replace Pod Security Policies (PSP).
– With TKr 1.25, VKS supports applying pod security standards of type privileged, baseline, and restricted using the
Pod Security Admission (PSA) controller. By default, for a VKS cluster created with 1.25 TKr, all namespaces have
their pod security warn and audit modes set to restricted. This is a no-force setting: the PSA controller may generate
warnings about pods violating policy, but the pods will continue to run. Some system pods running in kube-system,
tkg-system, and vmware-system-cloud-provider require elevated privileges. These namespaces are excluded from
pod security.
– With 1.26 TKr, VKS will enforce PSA by default on VKS clusters. TKr 1.25 users should plan to migrate their VKS
cluster workloads to PSA in anticipation of uprading VKS clusters to TKr 1.26.
– PSA configuration for VKS:
• TKr 1.25.7 - warn mode: restricted, audit mode: restricted, enforce mode: not set
• TKr 1.26 and later - enforce mode: restricted
– Sample commands to update pod security on a TKr 1.25 Kubernetes namespace:
•
kubectl label --overwrite ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=privileged
•
kubectl label --overwrite ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=privileged
Note:
PSA policies on system namespaces cannot be changed.
– For more information, refer to the PSA documentation:
• Pod Security Admission
• Pod Security Standards
• Migrate from PodSecurityPolicy to the Built-In PodSecurity Admission Controller
• Tanzu Kubernetes Grid Image Builder 0.2.0 for vSphere 8.x is available on Github. This release adds support for
building Photon and Ubuntu images for Kubernetes 1.25.7.

Known Issues
TKr 1.25.7 for use with vSphere 8.x has the following known issues.
For Clusters provisioned using the v1beta1 API, upgrading the Kubernetes version from TKr v1.24.9 to TKr
v1.25.7 can result in an inconsistent cluster state if you couple the version upgrade with a scale up of the number
of nodes in a node pool.
For clusters provisioned using the v1beta1 API, attempting to perform a version upgrade from TKr v1.24.9+vmware.1-
tkg.4 to TKr v1.25.7+vmware.3-fips.1-tkg.1 in the same operation as a scale up of the number of replicas in a node pool
can lead to the cluster upgrade failing. The control plane will upgrade, but the node pool scale up operation fails causing
the cluster upgrade to roll back.
NOTE: This issue has been observed only on v1beta1 Clusters with Supervisor running Cluster API (CAPI) version less
than 1.5.0. Supervisor running CAPI 1.5.0 or above will not face this issue.
If this issue does occur, scale in the node pool to 0 and wait for the cluster to complete the upgrade. Once the upgrade is
successful then scale out the nodes to desired value.
NOTE: As a general practice, it is recommended that you perform a cluster version upgrade first and separately. Once
the version upgrade completes successfully, you can then perform a second operation and scale in or out the number of
nodes in a node pool.
Fixed Issues
TKr 1.25.7 for use with vSphere 8.x has the following fixed issues.
VKS clusters on Supervisor do not display pod metrics
1.23.15 and 1.24.9 VKS VKr's were using cgroupfs as cgroupdriver for containerd. With 1.25 containerd uses systemd as
cgroupdriver.
Online volume expansion on restored pvc failed
Fixes issue in online expansion of persistent volume in workload cluster.

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Regression in performance of pvc creation
Fixes performance issue caused by regression in pvcsi-driver shipped with VKr 1.24.9.

Verify Compatibility
In addition to reviewing the compatibility matrix, you should independently verify compatibility before using or upgrading
to a particular VKr. You must also verify compatibility before upgrading Supervisor. Note that upgrading Supervisor may
initiate a rolling update of provisioned VKS clusters.
Compatibility with Supervisor
To verify VKr compatibility with Supervisor, switch context to the target vSphere Namespace and run the command
. The COMPATIBLE column displays a Boolean value showing the compatibility of each VKr with
kubectl get tkr
Supervisor. True means the release is compatible with Supervisor. False means it is not.
Important:
For the VKr to be compatible, Supervisor must be upgraded to the latest patch version shipped with the
corresponding vCenter release.
Compatibility with vSphere 8.x and 7.x
There are two types of VKr formats: non-legacy VKrs and legacy VKRs.
• Non-legacy VKrs are purpose-built for vSphere 8.x and are only compatible with vSphere 8.x
• Legacy VKrs use a legacy format and are compatible with vSphere 7.x, and also with vSphere 8.x but for upgrade
purposes only.
To verify VKr compatibility with vSphere, run the command (or
kubectl get tkr TKR_NAME --show-labels
). To list only the VKrs that do not contain the legacy label, run the command
kubectl get tkr TKR-NAME -o yaml
. See examples below.
kubectl get tkr -l '!run.tanzu.vmware.com/legacy-tkr'
If the release includes the label annotation , the image is based on the vSphere
run.tanzu.vmware.com/legacy-tkr
7.x format. You can run a legacy VKr on vSphere 8.x, but you will not be able to take advantage of vSphere 8.x features
such as class-based clusters and Carvel packaging until you upgrade to a non-legacy VKr. For more information, refer to
the Using TKG Service with vSphere Supervisor documentation.
The following example shows that v1.24.11---vmware.1-fips.1-tkg.1 is a legacy VKr because the label is
legacy-tkr
present.
kubectl get tkr v1.24.11---vmware.1-fips.1-tkg.1 -o yaml
apiVersion: run.tanzu.vmware.com/v1alpha3
kind: TanzuKubernetesRelease
metadata:
creationTimestamp: "2023-07-14T04:25:04Z"
finalizers:
- tanzukubernetesrelease.run.tanzu.vmware.com
generation: 1
labels:
os-arch: amd64
os-name: photon
os-type: linux
os-version: "3.0"
run.tanzu.vmware.com/legacy-tkr: ""
name: v1.24.11---vmware.1-fips.1-tkg.1
The following example shows that v1.25.7---vmware.3-fips.1-tkg.1 is a non-legacy VKr because the label is
legacy-tkr
absent.
kubectl get tkr v1.25.7---vmware.3-fips.1-tkg.1 -o yaml
apiVersion: run.tanzu.vmware.com/v1alpha3
kind: TanzuKubernetesRelease
metadata:
creationTimestamp: "2023-07-27T04:20:13Z"

List Components and Packages
The VKr for vSphere 8.x are updated to a package-based framework for VKS components, such as the container storage
interface (CSI) and container network interface (CNI). To view the components and packages comprising a release, run
the command .
kubectl get tkr TKR_NAME -o yaml

Introduction
VMware vSphere Kubernetes releases | 11 February 2026
Check for additions and updates to these release notes.
vSphere Kubernetes releases
VMware vSphere Kubernetes releases (VKrs) provide you with Kubernetes software distributions signed and supported
by VMware for provisioning vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) clusters in the vSphere Supervisor environment. VMware
VKrs follow the upstream Kubernetes versioning.
This document contains release notes for VKrs version 1.24.x and earlier. For release notes for later VKr releases, see
VMware VKr Release Notes.
Content Library
The availability of VKrs depends on the vCenter content library and its synchronization frequency. Use the command
to list the VKr that are available in your environment. If a release is not synchronized with your library,
kubectl get kr
that release will not appear in the list returned by the command. Refer to the Managing vSphere Kubernetes Service with
vSphere Supervisor documentation for more information.
VMware by Broadcom 138

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
About vSphere Kubernetes releases
Historically, vSphere Kubernetes releases (VKr), formerly known as Tanzu Kubernetes releases (TKrs) have been
distributed in two distinct formats: legacy and non-legacy. Each format was designed for compatibility with specific
vSphere versions and was clearly labeled to communicate its intended environment and upgrade path.
TKr Format Types ( see documentation )
• Legacy TKrs:
– Utilized an older format compatible with vSphere 7.x.
– Also supported on vSphere 8.x, but strictly for upgrade purposes.
– Identified by the legacy-tkr annotation label.
– Labeled as “for vSphere 7.x” in release notes and documentation.
• Non-Legacy TKrs:
– Introduced with vSphere 8.x, these TKrs support new features and enhanced compatibility.
– Exclusively compatible with vSphere 8.x.
– Labeled as “for vSphere 8.x” in release notes and documentation.
Previous Release Designations
Until recently, TKr releases included explicit version designations in their naming conventions and documentation, such
as:
• TKr v1.28.8 for vSphere 8.x (non-legacy)
• TKr v1.28.7 for vSphere 7.x (legacy)
This approach provided clear guidance on which TKr should be used for a given vSphere version and ensured smooth
upgrade paths.
Change in Versioning and Compatibility (Effective VKr 1.29)
Effective with VKr 1.29, the explicit “for vSphere m.n” designation will be discontinued, since the legacy TKrs are no longer
supported. A single VKr release (non-legacy) will now operate across both vSphere 8.x and 9.x platforms.
Compatibility and Upgrades
The VKrs for vSphere 8.x are updated to a package-based framework. While you can run vSphere 7.x VKrs on vSphere
8.x, you cannot take advantage of vSphere 8.x features unless you upgrade the cluster to use a VKr for vSphere 8.x.
Use the command to verify compatibility of VKrs with the vSphere Kubernetes Service. See also the
kubectl get tkr
Compatibility Matrix section. Upgrading VKS clusters to a VKr for vSphere 8.x is allowed starting with the vSphere 8.0a
release. You must update existing VKS clusters to a minimum VKr v1.21.x or later before upgrading your environment
to vSphere 8.0a. After you have upgraded to vSphere 8.0a, update clusters to a VKr for vSphere 8.x format to take
advantage of new features. See the Updating vSphere Supervisor documentation for details.
Important:
Upgrading is only supported when the origin and target VKrs are the same operating system. For example, you
cannot upgrade from a Photon OS VKr to an Ubuntu VKr.
Components and Packages
Use the command to list components and packages. The VKr format that
kubectl get kr VKR_NAME -o yaml
supports provisioning VKS clusters on vSphere 8.x uses a package-based framework to deliver VMware software and
Kubernetes components.
STIG Hardening
VMware provides Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIG) for each vSphere Kubernetes release. See STIG
Hardening for details.
VMware by Broadcom 139

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
CRITICAL REQUIREMENT for vSphere 8.0.0 Customers
If you have deployed vSphere Supervisor 8.0.0 GA, be aware of the following CRITICAL REQUIRMENT.
Before upgrading to vSphere 8 U1 you must create a temporary VKr content library to avoid a known issue that causes
VKS Controller pods to go into CrashLoopBackoff when VKrs are pushed to the existing content library. To avoid this
issue, complete the following steps.
NOTE: This requirement does not apply to content libraries you use for VMs provisioned through VM Service.
1. Create a new subscribed content library with a temporary subscription URL pointing to https://wp-content.vmware.com/
v2/8.0.0/lib.json.
2. Synchronize all the items in the temporary content library.
3. Associate the temporary content library with the VKS.
4. Run the command and verify that all the VKrs are created.
kubectl get tkr
5. At this point the VKS Controller should be in a running state, which you can verify by listing the pods in the vSphere
Namespace.
6. If the VKS Controller is in CrashLoopBackOff (CLBO) state, restart the VKS Controller deployment using the following
command:
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n vmware-system-tkg vmware-system-tkg-controller-manager
7. Upgrade to vSphere 8 U1.
8. Update the VKS configuration to use the original subscribed content library at https://wp-content.vmware.com/v2/
latest/lib.json. NOTE: The content library is not namespace-scoped, so when you update one VKS configuration, the
change should be propagated to all others. You should verify this by checking each vSphere Namespace.

Known Issues
TKr 1.24.9 for use with vSphere 8.x has the following known issues.
TKG 2.0 cluster creation fails if the cluster name contains more than 31 characters.
Due to an issue with the kapp controller, a TKG cluster cannot be created if the cluster name has more than 31 charaters.
This issue will be fixed in a future release when the underlying kapp controller issue is fixed.
Do not use a cluster name with more than 31 characters.
TKG cluster upgrades to TKR v1.24.9 from TKR v1.23.x may fail with CP node going into a NotReady state.
After upgrading a TKG cluster to TKR v1.24.9+vmware.1-tkg.4 from TKR v1.23.x, the TKG cluster may not be upgraded
and the CP node is stuck in a NotReady State.
The following upgrade paths are affected:
• FROM v1.23.15---vmware.1-tkg.4 (TKG 2 TKR Photon and Ubuntu) --TO--> v1.24.9+vmware.1-tkg.4 (TKG 2 TKR
Photon and Ubuntu)
• FROM v1.23.8+vmware.2-tkg.2-zshippable (TKG 2 TKR Photon and Ubuntu) --TO--> v1.24.9+vmware.1-tkg.4 (TKG 2
TKR Photon and Ubuntu)
• FROM v1.23.8+vmware.3-tkg.1 (TKG 1 TKR Photon) --TO--> v1.24.9+vmware.1-tkg.4 (TKG 2 TKR Photon)
On the control plane node, manually delete the kube-proxy pod that is stuck in ImagePullBackoff. This should restore
the kube-proxy pod to a running state. The kaap-controller should come up, followed by updated packages and finally a
running upgraded cluster.

Known Issues
TKr 1.23.8 for vSphere 8.x has the following known issues.
Known Issue with VKr v1.23.8---vmware.2-tkg.1-zshippable
VMware Tanzu Mission Control data protection does not work correctly when you use v1.23.8---vmware.2-tkg.1-
zshippable to provision a VKS cluster that uses Photon OS for cluster nodes. The issues is not present when using the
Ubuntu OS version of v1.23.8---vmware.2-tkg.1-zshippable.
As a result of service account permission issues, the tanzu-capabilities-controller-manager pod on the VKS cluster is
continually restarting and going into a Crash Loop back off (CLBO) state when using VKr version v1.23.8+vmware.2-tkg.2-
zshippable on vSphere with Tanzu 8.0.0a. To resolve the issue, add the required permissions to the capabilities service
account tanzu-capabilities-manager-sa on the TKC as described below.
To address the known issue with the Ubuntu OS version of v1.23.8---vmware.2-tkg.1-zshippable, complete the following
workaround.
1. Pause the reconciliation of the capabilities package on the TKC (replace 'tkc' with the name of the Tanzu Kubernetes
Grid cluster).
kubectl patch -n vmware-system-tkg pkgi tkc-capabilities -p '{"spec":{"paused": true}}' --type=merge
2. Create a new file named capabilities-rbac-patch.yaml.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
name: tanzu-capabilities-update-rbac
namespace: vmware-system-tkg
stringData:
patch-capabilities-rbac.yaml: |
#@ load("@ytt:overlay", "overlay")
#@overlay/match by=overlay.subset({"kind":"ClusterRole", "metadata": {"name": "tanzu-capabilities-manager-
clusterrole"}}),expects="1+"
---
rules:
- apiGroups:
- core.tanzu.vmware.com
resources:
- capabilities
verbs:
- create
- delete

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1

- patch
- update

- apiGroups:
- core.tanzu.vmware.com

3. Patch the capabilities cluster role on TKC (replace 'tkc' with the name of the VKS cluster).
4. Delete the tanzu-capabilities-controller-manager on the TKC.
kubectl patch -n vmware-system-tkg pkgi tkc-capabilities -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":
{"ext.packaging.carvel.dev/ytt-paths-from-secret-name.0":"tanzu-capabilities-update-rbac"}}}' --type=merge

VKR-v1.23.8 Ubuntu for TKG 1.0 clusters the system pod guest-cluster-auth-svc is in CLBO state on freshly

None
When upgrading from VKR v1.22.9 Ubuntu to VKR v1.23.8 Ubuntu, some VKS 1.0 clusters get stuck in False state

Known Issues
TKr 1.21.6 (Photon) for vSphere 7.x has the following known issues:
• Storage throughput regression caused by new QPS throttles with csi-attacher v3.2.1
TKr 1.21.2 upgraded the csi-attacher to v3.2.1 (in TKr 1.20.7 the csi-attacher is v2.0.0). There are more QPS throttles
with csi-attacher v3.2.1 that are causing a drop in throughput.
• An expansion of a Supervisor cluster PVC in offline or online mode does not result in an expansion of a
corresponding VKS cluster PVC
A pod that uses the VKS cluster PVC cannot use the expanded capacity of the Supervisor cluster PVC because the
filesystem has not been resized.
Workaround:
Resize the VKS cluster PVC to a size equal or greater than the size of the Supervisor cluster PVC.
• Size mismatch in statically provisioned VKS PVC when compared to underlying volume
Static provisioning in Kubernetes does not verify if the PV and backing volume sizes are equal. If you statically create a
PVC in a VKS cluster, and the PVC size is less than the size of the underlying corresponding Supervisor cluster PVC,
you might be able to use more space than the space you request in the PV. If the size of the PVC you statically create
in the VKS cluster is greater than the size of the underlying Supervisor cluster PVC, you might notice No space left on
device error even before you exhaust the requested size in the VKS cluster PV.
Workaround:
a. In the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster PV, change the persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy to Retain.
VMware by Broadcom 147

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
b. Note the volumeHandle of the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster PV and then delete the PVC and PV in the VKS cluster.
c. Re-create the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster PVC and PV statically using the volumeHandle and set the storage to the
same size as the size of the corresponding Supervisor cluster PVC.
• Attempts to create a PVC from a Supervisor namespace or a VKS cluster fail if the external
csi.vsphere.vmware.com provisioner loses its lease for leader election
When you try to create a PVC from a supervisor namespace or a VKS cluster using the kubectl command, your
attempts might not succeed. The PVC remains in the Pending state. If you describe the PVC, the Events field displays
the following information in a table layout:
– Type – Normal
– Reason – ExternalProvisioning
– Age – 56s (x121 over 30m)
– From – persistentvolume-controller
– Message – waiting for a volume to be created, either by external provisioner "csi.vsphere.vmware.com" or
manually created by system administrator
Workaround:
a. Verify that all containers in the vsphere-csi-controller pod inside the vmware-system-csi namespace are
running.
kubectl describe pod vsphere-csi-controller-pod-name -n vmware-system-csi
b. Check the external provisioner logs by using the following command.
kubectl logs vsphere-csi-controller-pod-name -n vmware-system-csi -c csi-provisioner
The following entry indicates that the external-provisioner sidecar container lost its leader election:
I0817 14:02:59.582663 1 leaderelection.go:263] failed to renew lease vmware-system-csi/csi-vsphere-
vmware-com: failed to tryAcquireOrRenew context deadline exceeded
F0817 14:02:59.685847 1 leader_election.go:169] stopped leading
c. Delete this instance of vsphere-csi-controller.
kubectl delete pod vsphere-csi-controller-pod-name -n vmware-system-csi
Kubernetes will create a new instance of the CSI controller and all sidecars will be reinitialized.
• All PVC operations, such as create, attach, detach, or delete a volume, fail while CSI cannot connect to
vCenter Server
In addition to operation failures, the Volume health information and the StoragePool CR cannot be updated in the
Supervisor cluster. The CSI and Syncer logs display errors about not being able to connect to vCenter Server.
CSI connects to vCenter Server as a specific solution user. The password for this SSO user is rotated by wcpsvc once
every 24 hours and the new password is transferred in to a Secret that the CSI driver reads to connect to vCenter
Server. If the new password fails to be delivered to Secret, the stale password remains in the Supervisor cluster, and
the CSI driver fails its operations.
This problem affects vSAN Data Persistence Platform and all CSI volume operations.
Workaround:
Typically the WCP Service delivers the updated password to CSI that runs in the Kubernetes cluster. Occasionally,
the password delivery doesn't happen due to a problem, for example, a connectivity issue or an error in earlier part
of the sync process. The CSI continues to use the old password and eventually locks the account due to too many
authentication failures.
Ensure that the WCP cluster is in a healthy and running state. No errors should be reported for that cluster on
Workload Management page. After problems causing the sync to fail are resolved, force a password refresh to unlock
the locked account.
To force reset of the password:
a. Stop wcpsvc:
vmon-cli -k wcp
b. Edit the time of the last password rotation to a small value, for example 1, by changing the 3rd line in /etc/vmware/
wcp/.storageUser to 1.
c. Start wcpsvc:
vmon-cli -i wcp
The wcpsvc resets the password, which unlocks the account and delivers the new password to the cluster.
TKr 1.21.6 (Ubuntu) for vSphere 7.x has the following known issues:
VMware by Broadcom 148

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
• Attempts to run the Remove Disk operation on a vSAN Direct Datastore fail with the VimFault - Cannot
complete the operation error
Generally, you can observe this error when one of the following scenarios occurs:
– As a part of the Remove Disk operation, all persistent volumes placed on the vSAN Direct Datastore are relocated
to another vSAN Direct Datastores on the same ESXi host. The relocation can fail if no space is available on
the target vSAN Direct Datastores. To avoid this failure, make sure that the target vSAN Direct Datastores have
sufficient storage space for running applications.
– The Remove Disk operation can also fail when the target vSAN Direct Datastores on the ESXi host have sufficient
storage. This might occur when the underlying persistent volume relocation operation, spawned by the Remove
Disk parent operation, takes more than 30 minutes due to the size of the volume. In this case, you can observe that
reconfiguration of the underlying vSphere Pod remains in progress in the Tasks view.
The in-progress status indicates that even though the Remove Disk operation times out and fails, the underlying
persistent volume relocation done by reconfiguration of the vSphere Pod is not interrupted.
– Workaround:
After the reconfiguration task for the vSphere Pod completes, run the Remove Disk operation again. The Remove
Disk operation successfully proceed.
• An expansion of a Supervisor cluster PVC in offline or online mode does not result in an expansion of a
corresponding VKS cluster PVC
A pod that uses the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster PVC cannot use the expanded capacity of the Supervisor cluster PVC
because the filesystem has not been resized.
Workaround:
Resize the VKS cluster PVC to a size equal or greater than the size of the Supervisor cluster PVC.
• Size mismatch in statically provisioned VKS PVC when compared to underlying volume
Static provisioning in Kubernetes does not verify if the PV and backing volume sizes are equal. If you statically create a
PVC in a VKS cluster, and the PVC size is less than the size of the underlying corresponding Supervisor cluster PVC,
you might be able to use more space than the space you request in the PV. If the size of the PVC you statically create
in the VKS cluster is greater than the size of the underlying Supervisor cluster PVC, you might notice No space left on
deviceerror even before you exhaust the requested size in the VKS cluster PV.
Workaround:
a. In the VKS cluster PV, change the persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy to Retain.
b. Note the volumeHandle of the VKS cluster PV and then delete the PVC and PV in the VKS cluster.
c. Re-create the VKS cluster PVC and PV statically using the volumeHandle and set the storage to the same size as
the size of the corresponding Supervisor cluster PVC.

Known Issues
TKr 1.20.12 for vSphere 7.x has the following known issues:
• Attempts to delete a stateful pod and reuse or delete its volume in the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster after an
inactive session might cause failures and unpredictable behavior
When you delete a stateful pod after a day or so of being inactive, its volume appears to be successfully detached from
the node VM of the VKS cluster. However, when you try to create a new stateful pod with that volume or delete the
volume, your attempts fail because the volume is still attached to the node VM in vCenter Server.
Workaround:
Use the CNS API to detach the volume from the node VM to synchronize the state of the volume in the VKS cluster
and vCenter Server. Restart the CSI controller in Supervisor cluster to renew the session.

corresponding VKS cluster PVC
A pod that uses the VKS cluster PVC cannot use the expanded capacity of the Supervisor cluster PVC because the
filesystem has not been resized.

csi/csi-vsphere-vmware-com: failed to tryAcquireOrRenew context deadline exceeded
F0817 14:02:59.685847 1 leader_election.go:169] stopped leading
c. Delete this instance of vsphere-csi-controller.
vsphere-csi-controller-pod-name
kubectl delete pod -n vmware-system-csi
Kubernetes will create a new instance of the CSI controller and all sidecars will be reinitialized.
• All PVC operations, such as create, attach, detach, or delete a volume, fail while CSI cannot connect to
vCenter Server
In addition to operation failures, the Volume health information and the StoragePool CR cannot be updated in the
Supervisor cluster. The CSI and Syncer logs display errors about not being able to connect to vCenter Server.
CSI connects to vCenter Server as a specific solution user. The password for this SSO user is rotated by wcpsvc once
every 24 hours and the new password is transferred in to a Secret that the CSI driver reads to connect to vCenter
Server. If the new password fails to be delivered to Secret, the stale password remains in the Supervisor cluster, and
the CSI driver fails its operations.
This problem affects vSAN Data Persistence Platform and all CSI volume operations.
Workaround:
Typically the WCP Service delivers the updated password to CSI that runs in the Kubernetes cluster. Occasionally,
the password delivery doesn't happen due to a problem, for example, a connectivity issue or an error in earlier part
of the sync process. The CSI continues to use the old password and eventually locks the account due to too many
authentication failures.
Ensure that the WCP cluster is in a healthy and running state. No errors should be reported for that cluster on
Workload Management page. After problems causing the sync to fail are resolved, force a password refresh to unlock
the locked account.
To force reset of the password:
a. Stop wcpsvc:
vmon-cli -k wcp
b. Edit the time of the last password rotation to a small value, for example 1, by changing the 3rd line in /etc/vmware/
wcp/.storageUser to 1.
c. Start wcpsvc:
vmon-cli -i wcp
The wcpsvc resets the password, which unlocks the account and delivers the new password to the cluster.

• Pods are not evenly scheduled across the nodes
This was a known regression that was introduced in upstream Kubernetes. The fix is included in this release.

Known Issues
TKr 1.20.9 for vSphere 7.x has the following known issues:
• Attempts to delete a stateful pod and reuse or delete its volume in the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster after an
inactive session might cause failures and unpredictable behavior
When you delete a stateful pod after a day or so of being inactive, its volume appears to be successfully detached from
the node VM of the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster. However, when you try to create a new stateful pod with that volume or
delete the volume, your attempts fail because the volume is still attached to the node VM in vCenter Server.
Workaround:
Use the CNS API to detach the volume from the node VM to synchronize the state of the volume in the Tanzu
Kubernetes cluster and vCenter Server. Restart the CSI controller in Supervisor cluster to renew the session.
• Pods are not evenly scheduled across the nodes
This is a known regression that was introduced in upstream Kubernetes. VMware will release an updated Tanzu
Kubernetes release once a fix is available upstream.
• An expansion of a Supervisor cluster PVC in offline or online mode does not result in an expansion of a
corresponding Tanzu Kubernetes cluster PVC
A pod that uses the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster PVC cannot use the expanded capacity of the Supervisor cluster PVC
because the filesystem has not been resized.
Workaround:
Resize the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster PVC to a size equal or greater than the size of the Supervisor cluster PVC.
• Size mismatch in statically provisioned TKG PVC when compared to underlying volume
Static provisioning in Kubernetes does not verify if the PV and backing volume sizes are equal. If you statically create a
PVC in a Tanzu Kubernetes cluster, and the PVC size is less than the size of the underlying corresponding Supervisor
cluster PVC, you might be able to use more space than the space you request in the PV. If the size of the PVC you
statically create in the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster is greater than the size of the underlying Supervisor cluster PVC,
you might notice error even before you exhaust the requested size in the Tanzu
No space left on device
Kubernetes cluster PV.
VMware by Broadcom 155

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Workaround:
a. In the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster PV, change the to .
persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy Retain
b. Note the volumeHandle of the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster PV and then delete the PVC and PV in the Tanzu
Kubernetes cluster.
c. Re-create the Tanzu Kubernetes cluster PVC and PV statically using the volumeHandle and set the storage to the
same size as the size of the corresponding Supervisor cluster PVC.

Verify Compatibility
In addition to reviewing the compatibility matrix, you should independently verify compatibility before using or upgrading
to a particular VKr. You must also verify compatibility before upgrading Supervisor. Note that upgrading Supervisor may
initiate a rolling update of provisioned VKS clusters.
Compatibility with Supervisor
To verify VKr compatibility with Supervisor, switch context to the target vSphere Namespace and run the command
. The COMPATIBLE column displays a Boolean value showing the compatibility of each VKr with
kubectl get tkr
Supervisor. True means the release is compatible with Supervisor. False means it is not.
Important:
For the VKr to be compatible, Supervisor must be upgraded to the latest patch version shipped with the
corresponding vCenter release.
Compatibility with vSphere 8.x and 7.x
There are two types of VKr formats: non-legacy VKrs and legacy VKRs.
• Non-legacy VKrs are purpose-built for vSphere 8.x and are only compatible with vSphere 8.x
• Legacy VKrs use a legacy format and are compatible with vSphere 7.x, and also with vSphere 8.x but for upgrade
purposes only.
To verify VKr compatibility with vSphere, run the command (or
kubectl get tkr TKR_NAME --show-labels
). To list only the VKrs that do not contain the legacy label, run the command
kubectl get tkr TKR-NAME -o yaml
. See examples below.
kubectl get tkr -l '!run.tanzu.vmware.com/legacy-tkr'
If the release includes the label annotation , the image is based on the vSphere
run.tanzu.vmware.com/legacy-tkr
7.x format. You can run a legacy VKr on vSphere 8.x, but you will not be able to take advantage of vSphere 8.x features
such as class-based clusters and Carvel packaging until you upgrade to a non-legacy VKr. For more information, refer to
the Using TKG Service with vSphere Supervisor documentation.
The following example shows that v1.24.11---vmware.1-fips.1-tkg.1 is a legacy VKr because the label is
legacy-tkr
present.
kubectl get tkr v1.24.11---vmware.1-fips.1-tkg.1 -o yaml
apiVersion: run.tanzu.vmware.com/v1alpha3
kind: TanzuKubernetesRelease
metadata:
creationTimestamp: "2023-07-14T04:25:04Z"
finalizers:
- tanzukubernetesrelease.run.tanzu.vmware.com
generation: 1
labels:
os-arch: amd64
os-name: photon
os-type: linux
os-version: "3.0"
run.tanzu.vmware.com/legacy-tkr: ""
name: v1.24.11---vmware.1-fips.1-tkg.1
The following example shows that v1.25.7---vmware.3-fips.1-tkg.1 is a non-legacy VKr because the label is
legacy-tkr
absent.
kubectl get tkr v1.25.7---vmware.3-fips.1-tkg.1 -o yaml

Introduction
VKS Add-ons
Check for additions and updates to these release notes.
About VKS Add-ons
Effective with the 3.7.0 release version, Broadcom has formally transitioned from the legacy "Core" and "Standard"
package terminology to a unified VKS Add-Ons framework. VKS Add-Ons are a collection of validated software
components that extend the core functionality of vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) clusters. You can seamlessly deploy,
manage, and track these add-ons on VKS clusters within a vSphere Supervisor environment via UI, CLI or API.
VKS Add-Ons Support Framework
To provide complete operational and runtime transparency, all software in the VKS Add-Ons portfolio is organized into a
single framework based on ownership, support commitment, and integration depth. Broadcom commits to maintaining
compatible, supported VKS Add-on package options throughout the entire 24-month General Support lifecycle of each
vSphere Kubernetes Release (VKr). To maintain active support eligibility, customers are expected to apply published add-
on updates and patch versions as documented in the VKS Add-on Support Matrix.
VKS Add-ons Support Tiers
• Product: Software curated, packaged, and validated by Broadcom engineering and deeply integrated with VKS and
the underlying infrastructure. Broadcom Global Support (GS) provides support for deployment, lifecycle management,
and runtime troubleshooting.
• Partner: Software curated and validated by Independent Software Vendors (ISVs). Broadcom GS provides support for
deployment and lifecycle management, and provides escalation to the partner who owns runtime troubleshooting.
• Ecosystem: Broadcom-curated open-source software (OSS) packages validated for base VKS infrastructure
compatibility. Broadcom support is limited to packaging, signing, and lifecycle management issues. Runtime bugs,
security patches, or feature requests must be addressed by the upstream community.
• Community: Unverified or user-built OSS packages managed outside the official VKS portfolio. Broadcom provides no
official support channel, lifecycle management, or runtime troubleshooting for this tier.
Scope of Support Boundaries & Exclusions
While Broadcom Global Support (GS) provides comprehensive support for Product Tier add-ons, support is limited to the
deployment, operational health and runtime stability of the add-on package itself as documented in the official Broadcom
Tech Docs.
Runtime Support Scope
• Resolving crashes, failures, or operational errors inherent to the add-on binary or service.
• Troubleshooting infrastructure integration between the add-on and the VKS and vSphere environment.
Lifecycle Support Scope
• Includes install, uninstall, and upgrade support.
Out of Scope
• Application or payload configuration: Support covers the operational health of the add-on package, not user-
created artifacts built using the tool. For example: Broadcom GS will troubleshoot issues with the Helm Controller add-
on itself, but will not assist in authoring, debugging or troubleshooting custom Helm charts or releases.
VMware by Broadcom 166

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
• Undocumented features & OSS documentation: Assistance, configuration guidance and troubleshooting are limited
exclusively to parameters and features published in Broadcom's official documentation. Broadcom GS will not review
or assist with configuration options found solely in upstream OSS project documentation or community blogs.
• Customer created YTT overlays: Custom YTT overlays used to modify or inject undocumented parameters fall
outside of Broadcom support.
• General "How-To" Consulting: Requests for advanced architectural design, custom scripting, or general usage
tutorials for underlying OSS tools are not covered under standard technical support.

Known Issues
Issue: Installing the Secret Store Supervisor Service on a Supervisor that hosts VKS clusters with Windows nodes causes
those clusters to enter an Addon Reconcile Failed state. This is not limited to newly created clusters — existing Windows-
node clusters are also affected once the service is installed.
Symptom: The vault-injector ClusterAddon resource on affected Windows-node clusters shows Reconciled: False /
Ready: False, with the deployment failing to roll out.
Root Cause (as reported): The vault-injector add-on deployed by the Secret Store Supervisor Service does not
currently support Windows nodes. Related pods fail to schedule on clusters with Windows worker nodes, causing vault-
injector add-on pod reconciliation failures.
Workaround: Run the following command on the impacted cluster:
• kubectl label cluster <cluster-name> -n <namespace-name> vault-injector.kubernetes.vmware.com/install=false --
overwrite
This command removes the vault-injector ClusterAddon resource from the namespace.
To confirm that vault-injector has successfully been removed, run the following command:
• kubectl -n <namespace-name> get clusteraddon | grep "vault-injector"

Resolved Issues
Helm Controller and NFS Client add-on deploy failed when resourceQuotaConfiguration is enabled on VKS
cluster.
Helm Controller and NFS Client have a default priority class system-cluster-critical and system-node-critical. When
resourceQuotaConfiguration is enabled as below, a resourceQuota CR must be created in the namespace for pods to use
system-* priorityClass.
For more details about configuring resourceQuotaConfiguration.enabled, please refer to this document.
The resourceQuota CR is missing in earlier Helm Controller and NFS Client add-on versions.  The issue is resolved in
Helm Controller 1.5.5+v4.02.00-vmware.2-vks.1 and NFS Client 4.13.4+vmware.1-vks.1
ClusterRoleBinding Namespace Mismatch in Headlamp Add-on
Resolved an issue where the ClusterRoleBinding subject namespace incorrectly defaulted to kube-system instead
of the target deployment namespace, which caused token authorization and privilege failures for the Headlamp
ServiceAccount. This issue is fixed in 0.44.0+vmware.1-vks.1.
OIDC Startup Flag Correction in Headlamp Add-on
Resolved the overlay argument from -oidc-cookie to -oidc-use-cookie to align with the Headlamp backend CLI flags,
enabling seamless cookie-based OIDC authentication. This issue is fixed in 0.44.0+vmware.1-vks.1.

Add-On Name Add-On Version Additional Details
Enhancements
Policy Bundle # 0.1.0+vmware.1-vks.1 Initial Release
The Policy Bundle add-on is
now available for VKS. This
add-on delivers a curated
set of Kubernetes admission
policies aligned with the NSA/
CISA Kubernetes Hardening
Guidance v1.2, enabling
operators to harden workload
clusters.
NSA/CISA v1.2 Policy Profile
- A comprehensive out-of-
the-box policy set covering
NSA/CISA v1.2 hardening
recommendations. Policies are
pre-packaged alongside the
cluster, eliminating the need to
author, manage, or distribute
constraint templates manually.
Operators have full control over
the active policy set:
• Policy selection — choose
which policies from the NSA
bundle are enforced on a
per-cluster basis.
• Enforcement actions
— configure each policy
independently as audit
(observe without blocking) or
deny (enforce at admission
time), allowing a phased
rollout approach.
• Exclusions — define
namespace-level or
workload-level exemptions
for trusted platform
components or workloads
that legitimately require
elevated privileges.
Prerequisites
• Broadcom curated
Gatekeeper add-on must
be installed and healthy on
the target cluster. The Policy
Bundle enforces policies
through Gatekeeper's OPA
constraint engine.

Known Issues
In VKS 3.7.0+ and Cilium 1.19.4+ clusters with kube-proxy disabled, enabling gatewayAPI.enabled: true will cause
the Cilium operator to CLBO on VKr 1.36. This occurs because VKr 1.36 introduces Gateway API v1.5.1, which is
incompatible with Cilium 1.19.4+. To provision a VKr 1.36+ cluster successfully with this feature, please follow the
workaround steps detailed in this document.
VKS Add-Ons v3.7.0+20260618
Effective with this release, VKS Standard Packages have officially transitioned to the unified VKS Add-ons framework.
• Artifact Delivery: To ensure that existing customer deployment scripts, air-gapped registry syncs, and CI/CD pipelines
continue to function without modification, the registry endpoint structure remains unchanged for this release cycle.
• Repository URL: The 3.7.0-validated VKS Add-ons are hosted at the historical distribution path:
projects.packages.broadcom.com/vsphere/supervisor/vks-standard-packages/3.7.0-20260618/vks-
addons:3.7.0-20260618
• Configuration Manifests: Customers can visit the Broadcom Support Portal (support.broadcom.com) to download
the associated AddonRepository YAML configuration files. Starting with VKS 3.7.0, customers can add multiple
AddonRepoInstalls.

Known Issues
If the Gatekeeper Product Add-on is deployed on your VKS cluster, customers must manually scale down or temporarily
disable the Gatekeeper validating/mutating webhooks before initiating a cluster upgrade. Failure to lower the webhooks
may block the cluster upgrade process.
Please refer to Broadcom Knowledge Base Article 433183 for detailed, step-by-step instructions on backing up and safely
disabling the webhooks prior to upgrading.

Gatekeeper # 3.22.2+vmware.1-vks.1 First release of OPA Gatekeeper
as a VKS add-on
• Provides validating and
mutating admission
webhooks plus continuous
audit for customer-defined
Constraint policies.
• Ships with VKS system
namespace protections
• failurePolicy: Ignore on the
main admission webhook
(so Gatekeeper outages do
not block workloads)
• Customers apply their own
ConstraintTemplate and
Constraint resources; no
policies are preloaded.
• Customers managing
policy using the VKS
cluster management
feature (requires VCF
Automation 9.0.1 or newer)
can continue to do so. In
this pattern, VKS cluster
management will continue
to manage Gatekeeper.
This is recommended to
avoid disruption in policy
enforcement.
• Customers with custom OSS
Gatekeeper installations
must remove existing
Gatekeeper installations
before installing the
Gatekeeper add-on.

phase, ensuring the seamless
cluster creation with Cilium CNI.

Package version compatibility on clusters is based on their Kubernetes version, not the vSphere with Tanzu version of
their Supervisor.

Kubernetes minor versions v1.34, v1.33, v1.32 and v1.31

-vks.1 should scale up the node group to its
Upstream Release configured minimum size if needed.
Notes • Default: true

New Parameter: startupTaint
• Specifies a taint to ignore in node templates
when evaluating whether to scale a node
group.
• Default: " node.cluster.x-k8s.io/
uninitialized "
• Prevents scale-up blocking caused by
temporary initialization taints on new nodes.
New Parameter: logLevel
• Introduces a configurable logLevel
parameter to control Cluster Autoscaler
logging verbosity.
• Default: 5
• Enables better observability and debugging
flexibility.

Known Issues
• Each package has default requests for CPU and memory, if you failed to install packages due to resource
issue, especially on X-Small clusters
You can update the default values when you install the packages.
Example:
deploymentMode:
resources:
limits:
cpu: ""
memory: ""
requests:
cpu: 100m
memory: 128Mi
• When you migrate packages to addon, specify the configuration with or - in vcf
-f values-config-file
addon migrate command
If you don't do this, the default configuration will overwrite the existing one after migration. Especially for Prometheus,
if you specified storage class.

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Managing VCF Services and Partner Services in Your VCF
Automation Provider Management UI
You can use the Service Management UI to extend your VCF Automation offering with value-added functionalities that
Broadcom and third-party vendors provide. Through the UI, you can manage the resources and life cycle of services that
are custom-built to extend the functionality of VCF Automation.
Note:
For known and resolved issues that are related to the VCF Automation Service Management UI, see the known
and resolved issues in the VCF Automation release notes.
A service can contain numerous elements: UI plugins, service accounts, Supervisor Services, roles, rights bundles,
runtime defined entities, and so on. There are two types of services - VCF services and partner services.
• VCF services are provided by Broadcom. Such VCF services are:
– VMware Data Services Manager
– VMware Encryption Management
– Harbor
– Protection and Recovery
– VKS Cluster Management
– Secret Store Service
• Partner services are services from external vendors.
When a new version of a service becomes available, you can upgrade your existing service instances to the new version.
VCF Automation maintains services in a working state by constantly enforcing their desired state. If you manually delete
or change a VCF service element, such as deleting a rights bundle, after a few minutes, VCF Automation detects that the
rights bundle is missing and tries to recreate it.
Upload a Partner Service to Your VCF Automation Provider
Management UI
Before you can install a partner service in the VCF Automation, you must first upload its file.
.tar
You can upload more than one version of a service. If a service has multiple uploaded versions and the installed version
is not the latest, you can upgrade to a later version. See Upgrade a VCF Service or a Partner Service Using Your VCF
Automation Provider Management UI.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
a) In a browser, enter the VCF Automation Provider Management URL of your VCF Automation.
The URL opens the login screen for the organization.
https://vcfa.example.com/provider System
b) Sign in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
• If there is no interaction, after 5 seconds the UI redirects you to the VCF SSO, if configured. If you click Stop or
select another option from the drop-down menu, you can sign in with a local or SAML user.
• To sign as a local user, enter the system administrator user name and password, and click Sign In.
• To log in for the first time, you must use the default administrator account with a local user. Enter username
admin
and the password which you set up during the installation.

3. Click the Partner Services tab.
4. Click Upload.
5. Browse to the service file, and click Open.

Install a VCF Service or a Partner Service Using Your VCF Automation
Provider Management UI
In the VCF Automation Provider Management UI, you can install a service with customized input parameters.
If you want to install a partner service, verify that you uploaded the service file that you want to install.
.tar
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
a) In a browser, enter the VCF Automation Provider Management URL of your VCF Automation.
The URL opens the login screen for the organization.
https://vcfa.example.com/provider System
b) Sign in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
• If there is no interaction, after 5 seconds the UI redirects you to the VCF SSO, if configured. If you click Stop or
select another option from the drop-down menu, you can sign in with a local or SAML user.
• To sign as a local user, enter the system administrator user name and password, and click Sign In.
• To log in for the first time, you must use the default administrator account with a local user. Enter username
admin
and the password which you set up during the installation.
2. In the left navigation pane, click Service Management.
3. Click the VCF Services or the Partner Services tab depending on the type of service that you want to install.
4. On the card of the service, click Install.
5. If multiple versions are available, select the version that you want to install from the drop-down menu and click Install.
The installation wizard opens.
6. If necessary, review the service bundle certificates and click Accept Certificate(s) and Continue.
Certificate Status Description
Trusted The certificate is valid and issued by a Certificate Authority (CA)
which is registered in the VCF Automation Certificate Library.
Not Trusted The certificate is valid but its CA certificate is not in the VCF
Automation Certificate Library. You must manually import the CA
certificate to establish trust.
Not Signed The service is not signed with a certificate.
Not Valid The certificate is invalid. This status deactivates all actions and
renders the version inoperable.

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Managing Supervisor Services
Managing Supervisor Services provides information for vSphere administrators about how to install and manage the life
cycle of Supervisor Services on Supervisors.
Supervisor Services Life Cycle Management and Consumption
Supervisor Services are vSphere certified Kubernetes operators that deliver Infrastructure-as-a-Service components and
tightly-integrated Independent Software Vendor services to developers. You can install and manage Supervisor Services
on Supervisors, and make them available for use with workloads.
When vSphere administrators install Supervisor Services on Supervisors, DevOps engineers can consume them in
different ways:
• Shared Supervisor Services such as Harbor, directly provide functionality to workloads running in VKS clusters,
vSphere Pods, or VMs.
• Supervisor Services that include an operator, such as MinIO, typically provide API or graphical interfaces, which
DevOps engineers can use to create and manage instances of the service in a vSphere Namespace through CRDs.
For example, to create a MiniIO bucket, you use a CRD to create the bucket in a vSphere Namespace.
Learn more about the supported Supervisor Services and how to download their service YAML files at https://vsphere-
tmm.github.io/Supervisor-Services/.
Supervisor Services Life Cycle Management
As a vSphere administrator, you manage Supervisor Services from the vSphere Client. You can install Supervisor
Services on Supervisors, upgrade their versions, or uninstall Supervisor Services from Supervisors. A Supervisor Service
can have multiple versions registered with vCenter, but you can install only one version at a time on a Supervisor.
