VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Managing the life cycle of a Supervisor Service includes the following operations:
Operation Description
Add a new Supervisor Service to vCenter When you add a new service to vCenter, the service and all
information about it is registered with vCenter. The service is not
yet installed on any Supervisor. After the service is registered with
vCenter, its state is Active, which means that you can install that
service on Supervisors.
Note:
Regional Harbor must be installed on at least one Supe
rvisor that is part of the same region where you want to
install Supervisor Services and it must have connection to
the software depot.
Add a new Supervisor Service version to vCenter Once, you have added a Supervisor Service to vCenter, you can
add new versions of that service. After the new service version
is registered with vCenter it becomes in Active state and you can
install the version on Supervisors
Install a Supervisor Service on Supervisors When you install a Supervisor Service on a Supervisor, the service
YAML file is applied on the Supervisor, and all the vSphere Pods
and necessary resources are created for the service to operate. A
vSphere Namespace is automatically created for each Supervisor
Service that you install on a Supervisor. You can manage the
service resources from that vSphere Namespace. Supervisor
Services might also have a UI plug-in for vCenter, where you can
manage the service configuration.
Upgrade a Supervisor Service You can upgrade a service that is installed on a Supervisor by
first adding a new service version to vCenter and then installing
the new version on the Supervisor. During the service upgrade,
the YAML file of the new version is applied to the Supervisor. Any
resources that are specified in the previous service version that
are not required by the new version will be deleted. For example,
if version 1 specifies pod A and version 2 specifies pod B, after the
upgrade to version 2 a new pod B is created and pod A is deleted.
No currently running workloads are impacted during the process.
Uninstall a Supervisor Service version Uninstalling a service version from a Supervisor leads to all of the
services resources being removed from the Supervisor including
the service namespace. Application instances of the service in
Kubernetes workloads will continue to run.
Delete a Supervisor Service version To delete a service version, first you must Deactivate that version
and uninstall it from the Supervisors where it runs. Then you can
delete the service version from vCenter
Delete an entire Supervisor Service To delete entire service, you must deactivate all of its versions,
then uninstall these versions from Supervisors, and finally delete
all the service versions.
Core Supervisor Services
Core Supervisor Services are services whose operators are pre-installed during the Supervisor activation. You can install
core Supervisor Services on Supervisors and upgrade their versions without the need of updating the Supervisor first.
However, you cannot remove the operators of core Supervisor Services from the Supervisor platform. Examples of core
Supervisor Services are VKS and the Velero vSphere Operator service.

As an administrator, you can add Supervisor Services to the vCenter system where your Supervisors run. After adding
services to vCenter, you install Supervisor Services on Supervisors so that your DevOps engineers can use the services
in their vSphere Namespace

Starting from VCF 9.0 and Supervisor. Version 9.0.0.0100, Supervisor Service prechecks verify the identity of the
developer that published each service version before the service is installed on a Supervisor. When installing an unsigned

1. From the vSphere Client home menu, select Supervisor Management.
2. Select Services.
3. In the card of the Supervisor Service that you want to install, select Actions > Manage Service.

You cannot install Supervisor Service versions that are Deactivated.
5. Select the Supervisor where you want to install the service.

Compatibility pre-checks are performed to determine whether the Supervisor Service version that you want to install

installation. In case the selected service version is not compatible with the Supervisor two types of messages are
displayed that describe the exact incompatibility:
• Warning messages. You can skip the warning messages, but you must acknowledge them to proceed with the
installation.
• Error messages. Error message indicate that the Supervisor Service version is incompatible with the Supervisor
and cannot be installed. In case of error messages, you must first resolve the incompatibility that was detected
before you are able to install the service on the particular Supervisor.
7. In the YAML Service Config field, enter configuration properties if the service requires any.
8. View the installation progress for the service on Supervisors.
a) Select the Supervisors tab and select a Supervisor where you install the service.
b) Click Configure and click Supervisor Services > Overview.
c) Select the Installed tab.
The Supervisor Service is in Configuring state, which means that all the necessary resources are being created in the
Supervisor and the service YAML is being applied to the cluster. Once the YAML is successfully applied to the Supervisor
with all its resources and namespace created or updated, the service state changes to Configured. The service is
available to all the namespaces in that cluster and DevOps engineers can use it with their workloads.

Deploying Supervisor Services from a Private Container Image
Registry
You can install and use Supervisor Services when the images are relocated to a private or self-hosted container image
registry
Supervisor Services are Kubernetes operators that are stored as collections of Kubernetes YAML manifests and container
images and may deploy resources across multiple namespaces. This requires a set of registry details that are common
to the Supervisor. Deploying Supervisor Services container images from a private image requires configuring trust
and authentication for the Supervisor if the private registry uses a self-signed Certificate Authority and/or requires
authentication for image pulls. If the private registry uses a TLS certificate signed by a public Certificate Authority, then the
Certificate Authority configuration is not required.
Relocate Supervisor Services to a Private Registry
Relocate Supervisor Services to a private container registry.
• Verify that you have upgraded vCenter to version 9.0 and later.
VMware by Broadcom 244

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
• Verify that you have a private container image registry.
• Verify that you have installed the VCF Consumption CLI.
1. Install the utility for the VCF Consumption CLI.
imgpkg
a) Install .
imgpkg
vcf plugin install imgpkg
b) Verify installation.
vcf imgpkg copy --help
2. Get the YAML manifest for your service.
Locate the reference in your YAML manifest. Read the image property under
imgpkgBundle
.
template.spec.fetch
The following is a Contour example:
template:
spec:
fetch:
- imgpkgBundle:
image: projects.packages.broadcom.com/vsphere/supervisor/contour/1.32.0/
contour:v1.32.0_vmware.1-vks.1
3. Download a tar of that bundle.
imgpkg
vcf imgpkg copy -b projects.packages.broadcom.com/vsphere/supervisor/contour/1.32.0/
contour:v1.32.0_vmware.1-vks.1 \
--to-tar contour-v1.32.0.tar \
--cosign-signatures
Important:
You must use the command and not the and commands to relocate the images as they do not pull
copy push pull
down all referenced images.
4. Upload the bundle to your private container image registry.
imgpkg
vcf imgpkg copy --tar contour-v1.32.0.tar \
--to-repo ${registry_url}/contour \
--cosign-signatures
Note:
honors the system's trust settings and Docker's configuration for authentication. If your registry requires
imgpkg
authentication, first log in with the Docker CLI command
docker login ${registry_url}
5. Update the Supervisor Service YAML with the new URL for the bundle.
imgpkg
For example:
template:
spec:
fetch:
- imgpkgBundle:
image: ${registry_url}/contour:v1.32.0_vmware.1-vks.1

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Managing vSphere Kubernetes Service with vSphere
Supervisor
Learn how to manage the life cycle of the vSphere Kubernetes Service through the vSphere Client as a vSphere
administrator. Also learn how to perform other administrative tasks to support DevOps engineers in running workloads by
using vSphere Kubernetes Service.
Running VKS Clusters
This section describes the components and lists the requirements for running VKS clusters.
VKS Components
VKS (formerly called TKG Service or TKGS) provides self-service life cycle management of Kubernetes workload clusters.
VKS with Supervisor is optimized for the vSphere environment and integrates with the underlying infrastructure, including
vCenter, ESX, virtual networking, and cloud native storage. With VKS, you can provision conformant Kubernetes clusters
and maintain upstream concurrency.
The VKS includes several components integrated with the vSphere Supervisor.
Note:
Regional Harbor must be installed and configured, because it serves as a central container registry for images
that are used for deploying Supervisor Services, VCF CLI Plugins, and VKS Standard Packages on VKS clusters.
See Install Regional Harbor through VCF Automation.
vSphere Supervisor
Supervisor is a critical control plane built into vSphere that integrates desired state and a single consistent API directly into
the hypervisor, enabling native deployment and management of Kubernetes clusters, declarative Virtual Machines, and
vSphere Pods alongside traditional workloads. It transforms vSphere into a extensible platform providing a declarative API
surface for self-service provisioning of modern infrastructure services within a resource boundary enabled by a vSphere
Namespace.
Supervisor Deployment: vSphere Zones
You can assign vSphere clusters to vSphere Zones to provide high availability and fault tolerance for Supervisor.
Deploying Supervisor across vSphere Zones lets you provision VKS clusters in specific availability zones.
In a deployment of Supervisor on a single vSphere cluster, there is a one-to-one relationship between the Supervisor and
the vSphere cluster. In a zoned Supervisor deployment, Supervisor stretches across three vSphere clusters to provide
high-availability and failure domains for VKS clusters on Supervisor.
A vSphere administrator creates the three vSphere Zone and associates them with a vSphere cluster. A Supervisor
deployment on three vSphere Zones has special requirements in addition to vSphere cluster requirements, including:
• Three vSphere Zones connected by a vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS)
• Each vSphere Zone contains a single vSphere cluster
• A Supervisor must deploy on exactly 3 vSphere Zones
• A vSphere storage policy is available on vSphere Zone
vSphere Namespace
A vSphere Namespace is a tenancy boundary that enables self-service consumption of 3 runtimes to include Virtual
Machines, VKS clusters, vSphere Pods and a number of other infra services. For each vSphere Namespace, you
configure role-based access control, persistent storage, resource limits, images library, and virtual machine classes.
VMware by Broadcom 249

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS)
VKS is an implementation of the open source Cluster API project that defines a set of custom resources and controllers to
manage the life cycle of Kubernetes clusters. VKS is a component of Supervisor.
VKS has three layers of controllers to manage the life cycle of VKS clusters, including Virtual Machine Service, Cluster
API, and Cloud Provider Plugin.
VM Operator The Virtual Machine Service controller provides a declarative, Kubernetes-style API for management of
VMs and associated vSphere resources. The Virtual Machine Service introduces the concept of a virtual
machine class that represents an abstract reusable hardware configuration. VKS uses the Virtual Machine
Service manage the life cycle of the control plane and worker node VMs hosting a workload cluster.
Cluster API The Cluster API controller provides declarative, Kubernetes-style APIs for cluster creation, configuration,
and management. The inputs to Cluster API include a resource describing the cluster, a set of resources
describing the virtual machines that make up the cluster, and a set of resources describing cluster add-ons.
Cloud Provider Plugin VKS provisions workload clusters that include the components necessary to integrate with the underlying
vSphere Namespace resources. These components include a Cloud Provider Plugin that integrates
with the Supervisor. VKS uses the Cloud Provider Plugin to pass requests for persistent volumes to the
Supervisor, which is integrated with VMware Cloud Native Storage (CNS).
vSphere Kubernetes release
A vSphere Kubernetes release (VKr) provides the Kubernetes software distribution and add-ons signed and supported by
VMware for use with VKS clusters.
Each VKr is distributed as a virtual machine template (OVA file). VKS uses the OVA format to construct the virtual
machine nodes for VKS clusters. VKrs are versioned according to Kubernetes versioning, and include OS customizations
and optimizations for vSphere infrastructure.
For a list of VKrs and compatibility with Supervisor, refer to the VKr Release Notes.
Content Library vSphere Kubernetes releases are made available to VKS clusters using a vCenter content library. You can
create a subscribed content library and automatically receive VKr versions when they are made available
by VMware.
VKS Cluster Components
The components that run in a VKS cluster provide functionality for four areas of the product: authentication, storage,
networking, and load balancing.
Authentication The authentication webhook runs as a pod inside the cluster to validate user authentication tokens.
Webhook
VKS clusters support authentication two ways: using vCenter Single Sign-On and using an external identity
provider that supports the Open ID Connect (OIDC) protocol.
VKS runs the Pinniped OIDC client on Supervisor and on VKS cluster nodes. Configuring an external OIDC
provider for Supervisor automatically configures the Pinniped components.
For authenticating with Supervisor, VKS supports VCF CLI.
Container Storage A paravirtual CSI plugin is a Kubernetes pod that runs inside a VKS cluster and integrates with VMware
Interface (CSI) Cloud Native Storage (CNS) through Supervisor. A Kubernetes pod that runs inside a VKS cluster can
mount three types of virtual disks: ephemeral, persistent volume and container image.
Transient Storage
A pod requires transient storage to store ephemeral data such Kubernetes objects as logs, volumes, and
configuration maps. Transient storage lasts while the pod exists. Ephemeral data persists across container
restarts, but once the pod is deleted, the virtual disk storing ephemeral data disappears.
Persistent Storage
VKS leverages the vSphere storage policy framework for defining storage classes and reserving persistent
volumes. VKS clusters pass requests for persistent volumes to the Supervisor, which is integrated with
VMware Cloud Native Storage (CNS). Persistent volumes are provisioned on cluster nodes dynamically
using a storage class, or manually.
Container Image Storage
VMware by Broadcom 250

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Containers inside a Kubernetes pod use images that contain the software to be run. The pod mounts
images used by its containers as image virtual disks. When the pod completes its life cycle, the image
virtual disks are detached from the pod. Kubelet is responsible for pulling container images from the image
registry and transforming them into virtual disks to run inside the pod.
Container Network The Container Network Interface Plugin is a CNI plugin that provides pod networking.
Interface (CNI)
VKS clusters support the following Container Network Interface (CNI) options: Antrea (default) and Calico.
In addition, VKS provides the Antrea NSX Routed CNI to implement routable pods networking.

VKS Cluster API
VKS provides an API for provisioning and managing the life cycle of VKS clusters. The API lets you create conformant
Kubernetes clusters of type Cluster based on a default ClusterClass provided by VMware.
VKS Cluster Clients
VKS on Supervisor supports various client interfaces for provisioning, monitoring, and managing VKS clusters.
• vSphere Client for configuring Supervisor and monitoring deployed VKS clusters.
• VCF CLI for authenticating with Supervisor and VKS clusters using vCenter Single Sign-On.
• kubectl to provision and manage the life cycle of VKS clusters declaratively, and to interact with Supervisor.
• VCF Automation interface for managing VKS clusters.
Deploying VKS Clusters
To deploy VKS clusters, you install or upgrade the VKS, use a content library to store VKS releases, and configure
one or more vSphere Namespaces to host VKS clusters. Regional Harbor is a mandatory requirement for VKS cluster
deployment, because it serves as a central container registry for images that are used for deploying Supervisor Services,
VCF CLI Plugins, and VKS Standard Packages on VKS clusters. See Install Regional Harbor through VCF Automation.

Reference Architectures for VKS Clusters
This topic provides a set of reference architectures for VKS clusters with various deployment topologies.
VKS Cluster with NSX Topology
The reference architecture consists of a VKS cluster on Supervisor with NSX networking. In such an environment, the
management plane hosts vCenter and NSX Managers. The compute plane hosts NSX Edge Nodes and Supervisor
nodes.
The following NSX network objects are present:
• Tier-1 gateway (router)
• Segment (switch) linked to the gateway
• Load balancer server
• Server pool for each VKS cluster control plane virtual server
• Virtual server for each Kubernetes service load balancer instance
VKS Cluster with VDS Topology
The reference architecture consists of a VKS cluster with VDS networking and an external load balancer. In such an
environment, the following networks are present:
• Management network for Supervisor control plane VMs
• Workload network for VKS clusters
• Frontend network through which developers connect to VKS clusters
VKS Cluster with vSphere Zones Topology
The reference architecture consists of a VKS cluster deployed across vSphere Zones. Each vSphere Zone maps to a
vSphere Cluster, which is a collection of ESX hosts managed by vCenter and connected by a vSphere Distributed Switch,
with shared storage and qualities of service enabled.
In a zoned topology, you deploy Supervisor across three vSphere Zones. The system locates a Supervisor control plane
in each vSphere Zone, providing for high-availability if a failure occurs.
When you provision a VKS cluster on Supervisor, the cluster is aware of the vSphere Zones. The zone topology supports
failure domains for highly available workloads. If needed you can run a workload in a specific zone using annotations.
Installing and Upgrading VKS
This section provides information for installing and upgrading the VKS.
Lifecycle and Support Policy for VKr Releases
Use the lifecycle and support policy to understand support timelines, scope, and dependencies, and to plan and maintain
your production workloads on VCF.
VMware by Broadcom 253

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Minor and Patch Releases
Each vSphere Kubernetes release (VKr) encapsulates a base operating system, a Kubernetes version, and core
dependencies (such as CNI, CPI, and CSI), distributed by Broadcom as a set of VM images. There are two types of
releases:
Minor version upgrade Unlocks new Kubernetes features, maintains support eligibility as older releases reach End of Service
(EOS), and ensures compatibility with updated applications.
Patch release Delivers essential bug and security fixes with an upstream Kubernetes guarantee that the API/ABI
compatibility remains unchanged. Patch versions are complete, self-contained VM images, not additive
or incremental updates. Like minor releases, each patch packages the full OS, Kubernetes runtime, and
dependency stack.
VKr Support Period
Starting with VKr minor version 1.33, Broadcom supports each VKr minor version for 24 months following General
Availability (GA), delivering ongoing patch releases for bug fixes and security vulnerabilities during this period. Specific
lifecycle dates are published on the Broadcom Product Lifecycle page. Patch releases for a given minor version do not
reset or extend the 24-month support window.
Patch Cadence
VKr and Add-ons follow a frequent asynchronous release process with several releases in a year. When a vulnerability
is assessed to critically impact VKr or an Add-on, Broadcom will address it in the shortest commercially reasonable time
possible.
Support Scope
Patch releases contain bug fixes and address Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) across the base OS and
core Kubernetes components in accordance with Vulnerability Management for VKr and VKS Add-ons.
If Broadcom determines that an issue or security vulnerability is resolved in a newer patch version (for example, 1.33.14),
the official resolution for the ticket is to upgrade to that patch release. Broadcom will not issue custom hotfixes or backport
code to older patch releases.
Support for Custom Node OS Images
Customers can create custom Node OS images using the imagebaker tool to bring in their choice of operating systems,
such as Windows Server 2022, RHEL, or customized versions of Photon OS and Ubuntu. Customers can patch the
custom OS layer of these images independently using the imagebaker tool while leveraging the Kubernetes layer provided
by Broadcom.
Broadcom supports custom Node OS images as long as the underlying Kubernetes version remains within an active
support window. Broadcom's support scope is strictly limited to Kubernetes and core platform components. Any functional
or security issues pertaining to the custom operating system layer remain the customer's responsibility.
Add-on Support Policy
To provide complete operational and runtime transparency, all software in the VKS Add-Ons portfolio is organized into a
single framework based on ownership, support commitment, and integration depth. Broadcom commits to maintaining
compatible, supported VKS Add-on package options throughout the entire 24-month General Support lifecycle of each
vSphere Kubernetes release (VKr). To maintain active support eligibility, customers are expected to apply published add-
on updates and patch versions as documented in the VKS Add-on Support Matrix captured in the add-ons release notes.
Infrastructure Requirements
Applying certain VKr patch releases may require upgrading VKS , and occasionally the Supervisor, as newer patch
releases are not always compatible with existing VKS versions.
VMware by Broadcom 254

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
End of Service Dates
VKS regularly drops compatibility for unsupported VKr versions. It is therefore recommended to plan VKr upgrades before
a version reaches End of Service. To view current End of Service dates for VKr versions, consult the Broadcom Product
Lifecycle Tool.
VKS clusters running on a VKr version past its End of Service period fall out of official support. To restore to an active
support state, upgrade the VKS Cluster to a supported VKr version.
Using the vSphere Kubernetes Service
VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) lets you deploy Kubernetes workload clusters on the vSphere Supervisor.
The VKS provides independent releases and asynchronous upgrades without workload disruptions.
Introducing the VKS
In vSphere 9, VKS is installed as a Supervisor Service. This architectural change decouples VKS from vSphere
Supervisor releases and lets you upgrade the VKS independent of vCenter and Supervisor.
VKS runs on Supervisor control plane nodes. The VKS is delivered as a nested collection of Carvel packages. As a Core
Supervisor Service, the VKS can be upgraded, even in internet-restricted environments, but it cannot be uninstalled
or downgraded. You can monitor and manage the VKS from the Supervisor Management > Services tab. See the
Upgrading the VKS Service Version section below.
VKS registration and upgrade are separate processes.
Installing VKS
Installing the VKS is done automatically when you upgrade vSphere Supervisor components to their required versions.
Refer to the VKS release notes for details.
Registering New VKS Versions with vCenter
The VKS package is published with vCenter and pushed to the VMware public registry. VKS registration is performed at
the vCenter level. You have two options to register new versions of the VKS: synchronous and asynchronous.
Table 5: VKS Version Registration Options
Registration Method Description
Synchronous with vCenter Update Wait for an update to the latest vCenter release to auto-register a new version of the VKS,
then update Supervisor to populate the embedded registry with the new versions.
Asynchronous Public Download a new VKS version definition from the public registry, then manually register it with
vCenter.
Asynchronous Private Relocate the VKS package from the public registry to a private registry that you host, then
manually register the service with vCenter.
Synchronous registration requires a system update. Updating vCenter automatically registers new VKS versions with
Supervisor. However, to use a auto-registered (new) version, you must then update Supervisor to the version that ships
with the vSphere Namespaces release delivered by that vCenter. On update of Supervisor, the Carvel package bundle
for the VKS is available in the Supervisor embedded registry and ready for deployment. A Supervisor upgrade does not
automatically upgrade the VKS. You must choose to deploy the version you want.
Asynchronous registration does not require vCenter and Supervisor updates, assuming the current Supervisor version is
within the support window. Asynchronous registration has the following workflow:
1. Download the service definition YAML file from the public registry site for Supervisor Services.
2. If air-gapped installation is required, relocate the package to your private registry.
3. Register the new version of the VKS by uploading the service definition to vCenter.

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1

VKS Property vCenter Bundled Registry
Registration of new versions Auto-registered Manual registration
Deletion of newly registered versions Not allowed Allowed

Upgrading the VKS Version
VKS version upgrades are performed at the Supervisor level. Once the VKS is registered, you upgrade the VKS by
deploying it as a Supervisor Service on the target Supervisor. See Upgrade the VKS Version.
When you upgrade the VKS version, the system performs pre-checks and reports two levels of severity:
• WARNING which is non-blocking
• ERROR which is blocking
A Kubernetes version check is an example of a non-blocking warning check. A Supervisor version check is an example of
a blocking error. For more information, refer to the Supervisor Services documentation.
Air-Gapped Upgrades
To upgrade the VKS in an air-gapped environment, you have two choices: synchronously with a vCenter update or
asynchronously when a new version is available.
For synchronous air-gapped updates, you wait for a vCenter release then register the new VKS version by updating
vCenter. See the Registering New VKS Versions with vCenter section.
For asynchronous air-gapped updates, use the VCF Download Tool to download the new VKS release images and upload
them to the Software Depot. You then register the new VKS version with vCenter. You can use the same service package
YAML as in an online deployment. For the download and upload steps, see Deploying VKS in Air-Gapped Environments.
Once the new VKS version is registered, the system upgrads the VKS from the registered images.

Administering Kubernetes Releases for VKS Clusters
vSphere Kubernetes releases (VKrs) provide the Kubernetes software distribution for VKS clusters. VKrs are distributed
as virtual machine templates which you synchronize with the platform using a vCenter Content Library.
VMware by Broadcom 260

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Using Kubernetes Releases with VKS Clusters
A vSphere Kubernetes release provides the Kubernetes software distribution signed and supported by VMware for use
with VKS clusters. The VKr formats and multiple operating systems.
VKr Release Notes
Refer to the VKr Release Notes for the complete list of available VKr distributions, what's new for each release, known
issues, and compatibility.
VKr Distribution and Consumption
VMware distributes vSphere Kubernetes releases through a content delivery network. You use a vSphere content library
to associate VKrs with vSphere Namespaces. To automate the consumption of VKrs, use a subscribed content library. For
internet-restricted environments, use a local content library.
Each vSphere Kubernetes release is distributed as an OVA template. The VKr Controller on Supervisor uses the OVA
template to construct the VMs for VKS cluster nodes. The VM disk size is set by the VKr OVA template. You specify CPU
and RAM resources using VM classes.
The VKr content library is not namespace-scoped. All vSphere Namespaces use same content library for VKS with
Supervisor. Editing the content library for one vSphere Namespace will update it for all others.
VKr Name String

matches the NAME string. See local content library for details.
VKr Compatibility with VKS
VKrs are released and updated independent from the VKS and from Supervisor.
To provision a VKS cluster, the VKr must be compatible with the VKS. You cannot use a VKr that is not compatible with
the VKS. In addition, you must make sure that you are running a compatible VKr for the version you target for upgrade.
You can check VKr compatibility using the command . The COMPATIBLE column returns a boolean.
kubectl get tkr
means the VKr is compatible, means it is not compatible.
True False

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
VKr Operating System Image Format
The VKr OS image format allows a single VKr for a specific Kubernetes version to support multiple operating systems.
Currently, PhotonOS, Ubuntu 22.04, Ubuntu 24.04, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, and Microsoft Windows Server 2022 are
supported. The default OS image format is PhotonOS.
By default, VKS cluster nodes use the PhotonOS edition of the specified VKr.
To use Ubuntu OS, add the annotation. For
run.tanzu.vmware.com/resolve-os-image: os-name=ubuntu
information, see VKr and OS Image Resolution Process.
VKr Packages
VKr images compatible with vSphere are updated to a package-based framework for core components, such as the
container storage interface (CSI) and container network interface (CNI). If you are using the v1beta API, changing or
updating these components is done using custom resource definitions.
To view the packages that comprising a VKr, run the following command:
kubectl get kr VKR-NAME -o yaml
For example:
kubectl get kr v1.28.8---vmware.1-fips.1-tkg.2 -o yaml
The command returns all the packages. For example:
spec:
bootstrapPackages:
- name: antrea.tanzu.vmware.com.1.13.3+vmware.3-tkg.2-vmware
- name: vsphere-pv-csi.tanzu.vmware.com.3.1.0+vmware.1-tkg.6-vmware
- name: vsphere-cpi.tanzu.vmware.com.1.28.0+vmware.1-tkg.1-vmware
- name: kapp-controller.tanzu.vmware.com.0.48.2+vmware.1-tkg.1-vmware
- name: guest-cluster-auth-service.tanzu.vmware.com.1.3.3+tkg.1-vmware
- name: metrics-server.tanzu.vmware.com.0.6.2+vmware.3-tkg.5-vmware
- name: secretgen-controller.tanzu.vmware.com.0.15.0+vmware.1-tkg.1-vmware
- name: pinniped.tanzu.vmware.com.0.25.0+vmware.2-tkg.1-vmware
- name: capabilities.tanzu.vmware.com.0.32.1+vmware.1
- name: gateway-api.tanzu.vmware.com.1.0.0+vmware.1-tkg.1-vmware
- name: calico.tanzu.vmware.com.3.26.3+vmware.1-tkg.1-vmware
See v1beta1/v1beta2 Example: Cluster with Calico CNI for an example use case.
Migrating VKr OS Types
In-place cluster updates between VKr operating systems are not supported. This means, for example, that you cannot
upgrade a VKS cluster using VKr v1.27.11 Photon to VKr v1.28.8 Ubuntu.
If you want to change the VKr OS type that a VKS cluster is using, consider the following procedure. In this example, the
origin cluster is using Photon and the target is Ubuntu.
• Using Velero, backup the Photon-based VKS cluster workloads.
See Backing Up and Restoring VKS Clusters and Workloads in the Supervisor documentation.
• Provision a new VKS cluster using the Ubuntu VKr.
See Provisioning VKS Clusters.
• Using Velero, restore the VKS cluster workloads to the Ubuntu cluster.
See Backing Up and Restoring VKS Clusters and Workloads in the Supervisor documentation.
VKr Hardening
Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIG) for system components, including Supervisor and VKrs, are available.
See Tanzu STIG Hardening for details.

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Build a Custom VKr Machine Image
You can build custom VKr machine images for VKS clusters on vSphere. A custom machine image packages a supported
operating system and version, a Kubernetes version based on a released VKr, and any customizations you make.
Beginning with VKr 1.35, use Image Baker to build custom machine images for VKS cluster nodes. See Building a Custom
VKr Machine Image.
For VKr 1.34 and earlier, use the Image Builder to build customer machine images for VKS cluster nodes. Refer to the
documentation for details on building custom images, supported VKr versions, and supported customizations.
Building a Custom VKr Machine Image
The Kubernetes Image Baker from Broadcom is a specialized tool for creating reproducible and customizable VM images
for VKS use while ensuring full compliance with VCF requirements.
Unlike traditional approaches that create exact copies of live VMs, Image Baker uses an OCI-based Buildkit backend for
Linux environments to systematically curate the filesystem. This offers a more efficient and controlled alternative to the
existing vSphere Tanzu Kubernetes Grid Image Builder.
The subcommand is integrated into the (kr) plugin of the VCF CLI to enable baking
bake kubernetes-release
vSphere Kubernetes Release (VKr) images directly from the VCF command-line interface.
The tool creates OVA files containing operating system images with Kubernetes distributions, suitable for deployment on
vSphere environments. It uses a BuildKit-based Low-Level Build format to create images from:
• Base OS OCI images (Ubuntu, Photon, RHEL, Windows)
• Kubernetes Distribution OCI images
When you run the command, the following processes occur:
bake
• Pre-bake checks: Validation of the configuration file, output directory, and BuildKit availability.
• Configuration Parsing: Reads and validates the YAML configuration.
• Image Baking: Creation of the OVA file with:
– OS layer from base OCI image
– Kubernetes distribution layer
• OVA Generation: Produces VMDK, OVF, and OVA files.
• Cleanup: Clears cache (unless is specified).
--keepCache
Image Baker Prerequisites
For all operating system environments:
• Root/Administrator access. Required for disk operations and system-level modifications.
• At least 50 GB of free disk space for image building and caching.
To build Linux images, the following prerequisites must be installed in your environment:
• VCF CLI with kubernetes-release plugin installed, and upgraded to the latest 3.6 version.
• Linux AMD64 (Ubuntu 22.04+ recommended) installed on the host machine
• Docker (https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/)
• BuildKit Version 0.21.0+ (https://github.com/moby/buildkit/releases)
• xsfprogs (provides mkfs.xfs)
• open-vmdk Version 0.3.11+ (https://github.com/vmware/open-vmdk)
• Python Version 3.10+ with packages: semver, jinja2, jinja2-time, pyyaml
To build Windows images, the following prerequisites must be available in your environment:
• VCF CLI with kubernetes-release plugin installed, and upgraded to the latest 3.6 version
• Windows 10/11 must be installed on the host machine
• Windows Server 2022 ISO (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/evalcenter/evaluate-windows-server-2022)
• QEMU >= 9 (https://www.qemu.org/download/)
VMware by Broadcom 263

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
• Hyper-V with an External vSwitch configured (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/virtualization/hyper-v/
get-started/create-a-virtual-switch-for-hyper-v-virtual-machines)
Networking Requirements for Image Baker
• Access to OCI registries containing:
– Base OS images
– Kubernetes distribution images
– Any custom package repositories
Image Baker Configuration File
The bake command accepts a configuration file to specify the settings needed for building the image. The configuration
file uses a Kubernetes-style YAML format with the API version.
imagebaker.vmware.com/v1alpha1
The basic file structure is as follows:
apiVersion: imagebaker.vmware.com/v1alpha1
kind: Image
metadata:
name: <image-name>
spec:
osSpec: { ... }
kubernetesSpec: { ... }
# Optional fields
packages: { ... }
repositorySpec: { ... }
services: [ ... ]
customOVFProperties: { ... }
diskSize: <size>
The required fields for the configuration file are as follows:
metadata.name
Name of the image (used for output directory naming).
Type: String
Example:
metadata:
name: ubuntu-2204-amd64-v1.35.0---vmware.1-vkr.1
spec.osSpec
Defines the base operating system layer.
Supported OS Configurations:
• Ubuntu: 22.04, 24.04
• Photon: 5
• RHEL: 9
• Windows: 2022
osSpec:
<os-name>
name: # ubuntu, photon, rhel, or windows
<os-version>
version: # 22.04, 24.04, 5, 9, or 2022
<oci-image-ref>
image: # OCI image reference or ISO path
<path>
vmtoolsPath: # (Windows only) Path to VMware Tools installer
<name>
virtualSwitch: # (Windows only) Hyper-V virtual switch name
spec.kubernetesS
Defines the Kubernetes distribution layer.
pec
kubernetesSpec:
image: <oci-image-ref> # Kubernetes distribution OCI image
The optional fields for the configuration file are as follows:
spec.packages
Install or remove packages during image baking.

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Example:
packages:
present: # Packages to install
- name: nfs-common
- name: curl
absent: # Packages to remove
- name: tuned

Using the bake command
The command is part of the plugin of the VCF CLI.
bake kubernetes-release
Usage:
vcf kubernetes-release bake -f <config-file> [flags]
sudo vcf kr bake -f <config-file> [flags] # using alias
VMware by Broadcom 266

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Important:
The kubernetes-release plugin needs to be installed with , and must be used whenever you invoke the
sudo sudo
bake subcommand.
Global flags:
These flags control the behavior of the bake command.
--log-format
• Type: String
• Default: json
• Values: plain, json
• Description: Output format for log entries
• Example: vcf kr bake -f config.yaml --log-format plain
--log-level
• Type: String
• Default: INFO
• Values: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR
• Description: Sets the logging verbosity level
• Example: vcf kr bake -f config.yaml --log-level DEBUG
--no-cache
• Type: Boolean
• Default: false
• Description: Ignores and clears the image baker cache before execution
• Example: vcf kr bake -f config.yaml --no-cache
Required flags:
-f, --file
• Type: String
• Description: Path to the Image Configuration YAML file
• Example: vcf kr bake -f config/photon5-kr-image.yaml
Optional flags:
-o, --output
• Type: String
• Default: artifacts
• Description: Output directory for the baked Kubernetes Release Image
• Example: vcf kr bake -f config.yaml -o /path/to/output
-s, --keepCache
• Type: Boolean
• Default: false
• Description: Keeps the cache directory after baking completes
• Example: vcf kr bake -f config.yaml -s
Image Baker Output
The bake command creates the following output structure:
artifacts/
└── <image-name>/
├── <image-name>.ova # Bootable VM image (final deliverable)
├── <image-name>.vmdk # Virtual disk
├── <image-name>.ovf # Open Virtualization Format descriptor
├── <image-name>.mf # Manifest file
├── metadata.json # Kubernetes metadata
└── manifest.json # Image manifest
Configuring Image Baker for Private Registries with Self-Signed Certificates
Additional configuration may be required to use Image Baker with private registries using self-signed certificates.
VMware by Broadcom 267

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
When using VKD Image Baker with a private container registry that uses self-signed certificates (for example, Harbor),
you may encounter the following error:
tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
This occurs because BuildKit (used internally by the image baker) does not use Docker's certificate configuration. Even
if Docker can successfully connect to your registry, BuildKit maintains its own certificate trust store. You have multiple
options for configuring Image Baker to be able to access your registry.
Prerequisites
Before configuring your registry, extract the CA certificate:
<your-registry-hostname>
openssl s_client -showcerts -connect :443 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -
outform PEM > harbor-ca.crt
Replace <your-registry-hostname> with your actual registry hostname (for example, ).
bitnami.workernode.lab
Option 1: Add CA Certificate to System Trust Store (Recommended)
This option is the simplest and recommended approach.
1. Install the certificate to the system trust store.
sudo cp harbor-ca.crt /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/harbor-ca.crt
sudo update-ca-certificates
2. Restart BuildKit to pick up the new certificates.
sudo systemctl restart buildkit.service
3. Verify that the certificate was added.
grep -r "<your-registry-hostname>" /etc/ssl/certs/ || echo "Certificate added to bundle"
Option 2: Configure BuildKit with Registry-Specific Settings
This approach provides more granular control by configuring BuildKit specifically for your registry.
1. Install the certificate to the system trust store.
sudo cp harbor-ca.crt /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/harbor-ca.crt
sudo update-ca-certificates
2. Create the BuildKit configuration directory.
sudo mkdir -p /etc/buildkit
3. Create the BuildKit configuration file ( ).
/etc/buildkit/buildkitd.toml
sudo tee /etc/buildkit/buildkitd.toml > /dev/null <<EOF
# Configure registry with self-signed certificate
<your-registry-hostname>
[registry." "]
http = false
insecure = false
ca = ["/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt"]
EOF
4. Update the BuildKit service to use the config file.
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/buildkit.service.d
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/buildkit.service.d/override.conf > /dev/null <<EOF
[Service]
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/buildkitd --addr fd:// --config /etc/buildkit/buildkitd.toml
EOF
5. Reload and restart BuildKit.
systemd
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart buildkit.service
VMware by Broadcom 268

Create a Subscribed Content Library
To provision VKS clusters on Supervisor, you can create a subscribed content library and synchronize vSphere
Kubernetes releases. A subscribed content library lets you automate the distribution of a VKr and stay current with the
latest releases.
• The content library functionality is a feature of vCenter that Supervisor relies on. For general information, see Using
Content Libraries in the vSphere Virtual Machine Administration documentation.
• Ensure you have the correct subscription endpoint URL for your environment:
– Environments with the Software Depot, such as VCF or VMware vSphere Foundation with Management Services
Ensure that the Software Depot is installed and configured and that you have the Software Depot subscription
endpoint URL.
To find your subscription URL, log in to the vCenter Developer Center, open the API Explorer, and execute a GET
request on the lcm/depot/services API.
Use the returned and values to format your URL as: https://
VcenterLcmDepotServicesAddress base_url
{VcenterLcmDepotServicesAddress}{base_url}/PROD/COMP/VKR/lib.json.
VMware by Broadcom 273

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
See Configure a Software Depot Connection Mode.
– VCF or VMware vSphere Foundation deployments earlier than 9.1 that do not have the Software Depot, such as
VMware vSphere Foundation without Management Services
Use the standard Broadcom public repository URL: https://wp-content.broadcom.com/v2/latest/lib.json.
For VKS on Supervisor, VMware publishes vSphere Kubernetes releases to a content delivery network. You can create
a content library that subscribes to these image publications. You choose the synchronization mode: immediate or on
demand.
Warning:
Immediate synchronization on the public content delivery network can take substantial time and disk space.
1. Log in to the vCenter using the vSphere Client and navigate to Menu > Content Libraries.
2. Create a subscribed content library.
a) Click Create.
The system displays the New Content Library wizard.
b) Specify the Name and location of the content library and click Next.
For example, you can enter a descriptive name, such as and include a description, such as
VKr-local
.
Subscribed library for VKS
c) On the Configure content library page, select the Subscribed content library option.
d) Enter the Subscription URL address of your Software Depot.
e) For the Download content option, select one of the following:
Option Description
Immediately The subscription process synchronizes both the library metadata
and images. If items are deleted from the published library, their
contents remain in the subscribed library storage, and you have to
manually delete them.
When needed The subscription process synchronizes only the library metadata.
The system downloads the images when published. When you
no longer need the item, you can delete the item contents to free
storage space. To save storage this option is recommended.
f) When prompted, accept the SSL certificate thumbprint.
The SSL certificate thumbprint is stored on your system until you delete the subscribed content library from the
inventory.
g) On the Apply security policy page, configure the OVF security policy and click Next.
When you select the Apply security policy option, the system verifies the OVF signing certificate during the
synchronization process. An OVF template that does not pass certificate validation is marked with the Verification
Failed tag. The template metadata is kept, but the OVF files cannot be synchronized.
Note:
Currently the OVF default policy is the only supported security policy.
h) On the Add storage page, select a datastore as a storage location for the content library contents and click Next.
i) On the Ready to complete page, review the details and click Finish.
3. On the Content Libraries page, select the new content library you created.
4. Confirm or complete the synchronization of the library contents.
Synchronization Option Description
Immediately If you chose to download all content immediately, confirm that the
library is synchronized.
To view the synchronized library contents, select Templates > OVF &
OVA Templates.
VMware by Broadcom 274

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Synchronization Option Description
When needed If you chose to synchronize the library on demand, you have two
options:
• Use Actions > Synchronize to synchronize the entire library
• Right-click an item and select Synchronize to synchronize only it.
To view the synchronized library contents, select Templates > OVF &
OVA Templates.
5. If you chose the When needed option, download the OVF templates you want to use.
If you chose the When needed option, you see that the image files are not stored locally, only the metadata is stored.
To download the template files, select the item, right-click, and select Synchronize item.
6. To update the subscribed content library settings, choose Actions > Edit Settings.
Setting Value
Subscription URL The Subscription URL address of your Software Depot
Authentication Not enabled
Library content Download when needed
Security policy OVF default policy
Associate the content library for the VKS clusters with the Supervisor. See Update VKS Content Libraries Associated with
Supervisor.
Create a Content Library for the Air-Gapped Environment
To provision VKS clusters on Supervisor in an air-gapped environment, set up a content library to serve vSphere
Kubernetes releases.
The content library functionality is a feature of vCenter that VKS on Supervisor relies on. For general information, see
Using Content Libraries in the vSphere Virtual Machine Administration documentation.
Use one of the following approaches to set up a content library in the air-gapped environment.
• For VCF 9.1.1 and later. You can upload the VKr images to the Software Depot and create a subscribed content library.
After the VKr images are uploaded to the Software Depot, the subscribed content library serves them automatically.
For the steps to upload VKr images to the Software Depot in an air-gapped environment, see Deploying VKS in Air-
Gapped Environments.
For the steps to create the subscribed library, see Create a Subscribed Content Library.
Create a subscribed library only if no existing subscribed library with the same subscription URL is already configured
for VKS.
Note:
If you change the Software Depot from online to disconnected or offline mode, make sure that all artifacts and
images currently in use are available in the offline depot. Missing artifacts can cause workload failures and, for the
VKr content library, flood vCenter with image download task errors.
• For VCF earlier than 9.1.1, or for environments where you do not upload VKr images to the Software Depot. Use the
following procedure to create a local content library. Creating a local content library involves configuring the library,
downloading the OVA files, and importing them to the local content library.
1. Log in to the vCenter using the vSphere Client and navigate to Menu > Content Libraries.
2. Create a local content library.
a) Click Create.
The system displays the New Content Library wizard.
VMware by Broadcom 275

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
b) Specify the Name and location of the content library and click Next.
For example, you can enter a descriptive name, such as and include a description, such as
VKr-local Local
.
library for VKS
c) On the Configure content library page, select the Local content library option and click Next.
For local content libraries you manually import the OVF templates you want to use.
d) On the Apply security policy page, configure the OVF security policy and click Next.
When you select the Apply security policy option, the system verifies the OVF signing certificate during the
synchronization process. An OVF template that does not pass certificate validation is marked with the Verification
Failed tag. The template metadata is kept, but the OVF files cannot be synchronized.
Note:
Currently the OVF default policy is the only supported security policy.
e) On the Add storage page, select a datastore as a storage location for the content library contents and click Next.
f) On the Ready to complete page, review the details and click Finish.
3. Download the OVA files for each VKr you want to import to the local content library.
The download method depends on your VCF version.
• For VCF 9.1.1 and later, use the VCF Download Tool.
The VCF Download Tool downloads the VKr OVF files to a local depot-store directory.
For the prerequisites and download procedure, see Deploying VKS in Air-Gapped Environments.
• For VCF 9.1.0 and earlier, use the following steps to download from wp-content.broadcom.com.
Note:
Some VKrs released after VCF 9.1.0 might not be published to wp-content.broadcom.com. You can access them
through the VCF Download Tool.
a) Using a browser, navigate to the following URL:
https://wp-content.broadcom.com/v2/latest/
b) Click the directory for the image you want.
Typically this directory is the latest or most recent version of the Kubernetes distribution.
For example:
ob-25439943-photon-5-amd64-v1.35.5---vmware.1-vkr.1
Important:
You use the distribution name to import the files to the local content library.
For the above example, the portion of the name string that you need is:
ob-25439943-photon-5-amd64-v1.35.5---vmware.1-vkr.1
Copy the destination name to a file or keep the browser open until you complete the procedure.
c) For each of the files in the package, right-click and select Save link as.
For example:
•
photon-ova-disk1.vmdk
•
photon-ova.cert
•
photon-ova.mf
•
photon-ova.ovf
VMware by Broadcom 276

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
d) Verify that each file successfully downloads to your local file system.
Note:
The files you import are the OVF and VMDK files. However, if a security policy is applied, all four files, including
the certificate ( ) and manifest ( ), must be present in the source directory during import. If the
*.cert *.mf
certificate and manifest files are not available during import, the imported VKS release is not usable.
4. Import the OVA and VMDK files to the local content library.
a) Select Menu > Content Libraries.
b) From the list of Content Libraries, click the link for local content library you created.
c) Click Actions > Import Items.
d) In the Import Library Item window, select Local File and click Upload Files.
e) Select both files and .
photon-ova.ovf photon-ova-disk1.vmdk
You see the message . Each file is listed with a green check mark beside its name.
2 files ready to import
f) Change the Destination Item name to be the OS image version plus the Kubernetes version from the directory
where you downloaded the files.
For example:
ob-25439943-photon-5-amd64-v1.35.5---vmware.1-vkr.1
Warning:
The content library Destination Item name must match exactly the folder name string for the desired VKS
release. If the names do not match, Supervisor cannot resolve the image to a valid VKS release.
g) Click Import.
VMware by Broadcom 277

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
5. Verify that the local content library is populated with the vSphere Kubernetes release.
a) In the Recent Tasks pane, monitor the uploading task for the library item and verify that it is successfully
Completed.
b) In the local content library view, select Templates > OVF & OVA Templates.
c) Verify that the vSphere Kubernetes release metadata is listed and its content is stored locally.
Associate the content library for the VKS clusters with the Supervisor. See Update VKS Content Libraries Associated with
Supervisor.
Enable Publishing of a Local Content Library
You can create a local content library and enable publication, allowing other content libraries to subscribe. This approach
lets you control the vSphere Kubernetes release images that are available for use, while providing VKS cluster operators
with a subscription-style service.
Instead of subscribing to the VMware Content Delivery Network for vSphere Kubernetes releases, where all images
are published and remain, you can create a local content library that provides a limited subset of vSphere Kubernetes
releases. Such an approach is convenient when you want to control which images are available, such as in continuous
build environments.
Starting with VCF 9.1.1, the recommended way to obtain VKrs is to create a subscribed content library subscribing to the
Software Depot directly. For information, see Create a Subscribed Content Library.
Note:
Some VKrs released after VCF 9.1.0 might not be published to wp-content.broadcom.com. All new VKrs are
published to the Broadcom online depot and are accessible through the VCF Download Tool. For information
about creating a local content library for air-gapped environments, see Create a Content Library for the Air-
Gapped Environment.
1. Create a local content library, or edit the settings for an existing one.
2. Select the check box to Enable publishing.
You receive a subscription URL for this local content library.
3. Create one or more subscribed content libraries using the subscription URL.
When you upload vSphere Kubernetes releases to the local content library enabled with publishing, all subscribed content
libraries will receive the images on synchronization.
Add or Update VKS Content Libraries on a Supervisor
To provision VKS clusters, you have to associate a content library with vSphere Kubernetes Service on a Supervisor. You
can later change the library or add additional libraries, if your environment supports this action. You might also need to
remove an associated library.
To be able to add or remove a content library, make sure your environment meets the following requirements:
• vSphere version 9.0 or later.
• VKS version 3.3 or later installed.
To create a content library for hosting VKr images, see Create a Subscribed Content Library.
Complete these steps to change an existing content library, add a new one for use with the VKS clusters, or remove a
content library associated with the VKS cluster.
VMware by Broadcom 278

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
When you make changes to your content library, keep in mind the following:
• The content library you use for VKS clusters is not scoped to individual vSphere Namespaces. The same content
library is used for all vSphere Namespaces on a Supervisor instance. For this reason, changing the content library is
only allowed at the Supervisor level.
• The content library referenced in the VM Service tile can be used only with standalone VMs. Do not add the VKS
content library to the VM Service tile.
• If a content library associated with VKS is deleted from vCenter, the library remains linked to VKS. You must first
remove this library from VKS to proceed with any operations. If you try to add or remove any other content library, you
see an error message prompting you to unlink the library that was deleted from vCenter.
1. Log in to the vCenter using the vSphere Client.
2. Select Supervisor Management > Supervisors, and select the Supervisor instance.
3. Select Configure > General.
4. Under Kubernetes Service, edit, add, or remove a content library.
Option Description
Add or remove a content library. 1. Click Add and select one or more content libraries that you
want to associate.
With vSphere version 9.0 and VKS version 3.3 installed.
2. Wait for all selected content libraries to show up in the list.
3. To remove one or more content libraries, select them from
the list and click Remove.
4. Wait for the selected content libraries to be removed from
the list.
Edit a content library. 1. Select Content Library > EDIT, and select a content library
you want to use.
With vSphere version 8.x or earlier.
2. Wait for the content library name to change to the one that
you selected.
The content library you select is used for the VKS across all vSphere Namespaces created on Supervisor.

 VKr and OS Image Resolution Process
This topic describes how the system resolves VKr images.
VKr Resolution
When you create or update a cluster, the system selects a compatible, ready VKr and corresponding OS images
for the control plane and each machine deployment. The selection is based on annotations and the cluster's
 you set.
spec:topology:version
You can set the following annotations:
 run.tanzu.vmware  (Optional). The annotation is set to filter candidate VKrs. An empty string selects all VKrs.
.com/resolve-tkr
 run.tanzu.vmware  Label selector that chooses OS images from the resolved VKr. If omitted, resolve-os-image defaults
to os-name=photon. Set these annotations in the Cluster topology, under the control plane and each
.com/resolve-os-i
machine deployment.
mage
In VKS earlier than 3.4, you can set these annotations in a ClusterClass. Starting with VKS 3.4, annotations defined in a
ClusterClass are no longer applied to clusters.
In VKS 3.4 and later, specify them in the Cluster topology. For more information, see Using builtin-generic-v3.4.0
ClusterClass with VKS 3.4.0 and Later.
spec:
  topology:

If no matching VKr or OS images are found, the cluster create or update request is denied.
On success, the following happens:
• The cluster is labeled with the resolved VKr, .
run.tanzu.vmware.com/tkr
• is set to the Kubernetes version of the resolved VKr.
spec.topology.version
Understanding VKr Deactivated Status
Sometimes a VKr might not be ready and the reason indicates that it is . A deactivated VKr can still be
deactivated
compatible with the current VKS release. A VKr is marked as deactivated if it has been superseded by a new VKr patch.
This occurs only if a critical bug is identified in an existing patch.
Always refer to the VKr Release Notes for details.
If a VKr is deactivated, clusters currently using that VKr remain operational. Adding a new nodepool to the cluster requires
an upgrade to a new VKr patch. New clusters cannot be created with a deactivated VKr.
Example Scenario: Deactivated VKr
In this scenario, VKr 1.35.2 supersedes VKr 1.35.0. When both VKrs are present in the VKS content library, VKr 1.35.0
is marked as . If you query the VKrs, you see that VKr 1.35.0 is compatible but not ready. Also there is a
deactivated
column to indicate the superseding VKr, in this case 1.35.2.
DEACTIVATED BY
# kubectl get kr
# kubectl get kr
NAME VERSION READY COMPATIBLE DEACTIVATED BY
CREATED
v1.35.0---vmware.2-vkr.4 v1.35.0+vmware.2-vkr.4 False True v1.35.2---vmware.1-vkr.3
4d2h
v1.35.2---vmware.1-vkr.3 v1.35.2+vmware.1-vkr.3 True True
8d
v1.35.4---vmware.1-dev.1 v1.35.4+vmware.1-dev.1 True True
4d2h
When you describe the VKr, the status.conditions field confirms that it is deactivated.

Handling Missing VKr Upgrade Versions
The condition on a cluster determines the VKr version to which the cluster can be upgraded.
updatesAvailable
The evaluation takes the annotation into account. As a result, you might
updatesAvailable resolve-os-image
encounter a situation where you expect to see a new compatible VKr for an upgrade, but the list is
updatesAvailable
empty or missing expected versions.
This behavior typically occurs if the new VKr image is published to a different content library than the one explicitly set in
the annotation during the cluster's creation.
Note:
When you provision a VKS cluster using the Cloud Consumption Interface (CCI) UI, the system automatically sets
the annotation on your cluster, which makes this issue more
run.tanzu.vmware.com/resolve-os-image
likely to occur. However, even without CCI, you can encounter this behavior if a new VKr is published to a content
library different from the one currently configured in the cluster's annotation.
Resolution
If your list is missing expected VKr images, verify the annotation on your
updatesAvailable resolve-os-image
cluster object. To proceed with the upgrade when the new image resides in a different content library, perform one of the
following actions while updating the VKr version in the cluster spec:
• Unset the content library: Remove the key from the annotation entirely if no image conflicts exist
content-library
across your linked libraries.
• Update the content library: Change the value to match the ID of the new content library that
content-library
contains the target VKr image.
Example Scenario
You created a cluster named test-cluster using the CCI UI with an image from a content library named cl-11. The UI
automatically sets the following annotation on your cluster's control plane and worker nodes:
run.tanzu.vmware.com/resolve-os-image: content-library=cl-11
VMware by Broadcom 288

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Later, a new compatible VKr version becomes available in your environment.
v1.35.2---vmware.1-fips-vkr.1
You expect to be able to upgrade, but when you check the cluster's status, the new version is missing from the
condition.
updatesAvailable
1. Identify the new image and its content library.
Use kubectl to list the available OS images for the new version in your environment:
$ kubectl get osimage -A | grep v1.35.2
vmi-843b236a8f02c5e42v1.35.2+vmware.1-fips photon5 amd64 vmi 2d9h
Next, use the ID of the image (vmi-843b236a8f02c5e42) or the version string to look up the corresponding
ClusterContentLibraryItem (cclitem):
$ kubectl get cclitem -A | grep v1.35.2
clitem-843b236a8f02c5e42ob-24537963-photon-5-amd64-v1.35.2---vmware.1-fips-vkr.1 cl-22 OVF True true
8083576284 true 2d10h
From the output above, you can see that the new OS image resides in a new content library: cl-22. Because your
cluster is constrained to only look for images within cl-11, the update is not available.
2. Update the cluster spec.
To resolve this and upgrade your cluster, modify the cluster spec to update the annotation to point to the new content
library while simultaneously updating the cluster's topology version:
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
name: test-cluster
namespace: test-ns
spec:
topology:
# 1. Update the version to the new Kubernetes Release
version: v1.35.2---vmware.1-fips-vkr.1
controlPlane:
replicas: 1
metadata:
annotations:
# 2. Update the annotation to point to the new content library
run.tanzu.vmware.com/resolve-os-image: content-library=cl-22
workers:
machineDeployments:
- class: node-pool
name: node-pool-1
metadata:
annotations:
# 3. Ensure worker node annotations are updated as well
run.tanzu.vmware.com/resolve-os-image: content-library=cl-22
Resolve VKr Image Conflicts When Using Multiple Content Libraries
When you create or update a VKS cluster, the VKr resolver might deny the request if it can’t find a matching VKr image, or
if it finds multiple matching images with the same Kubernetes version, name, VKr version, and architecture. This conflict
can occur when multiple content libraries linked to the Supervisor environment contain the same VKr images. You can
resolve this issue by adding an annotation to the cluster spec to specify which library to use.
To avoid conflicts, you need to add the following annotation when you create or update clusters:
,
run.tanzu.vmware.com/resolve-os-image: content-library=cl-****
where is the name of the ClusterContentLibrary resource from the Supervisor.
cl-****
If this annotation is omitted and duplicates exist, the operation fails with the error:

Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "<yaml_name>": admission webhook "tkr-
resolver-cluster-webhook.tanzu.vmware.com" denied the request: Could not resolve KR/
OSImage
For existing clusters, depending on the operation, one the following applies:
• If you upgrade the cluster and the target image belongs to multiple content libraries associated with VKS, you must
specify the annotation.
resolve-os-image
• In VKS earlier than 3.5, for classy clusters created with ClusterClass 3.2.0 and later, if you scale up the cluster and
the image belongs to multiple content libraries associated with VKS, you must specify the
resolve-os-image
annotation.
• If you scale up the cluster and the resolved image no longer exists, for example, if the content library association was
removed from VKS, the image resolution fails.

Vulnerability Management for VKr and VKS Add-ons
Learn how Broadcom identifies, assesses, and remediates security vulnerabilities in vSphere Kubernetes Releases (VKr)
and VKS Add-ons. The process follows a structured lifecycle from artifact analysis to technical resolution.
Overview
VKS clusters are built on top of VKrs. The VKrs provides the infrastructure, OVF packages, and container images used for
cluster nodes. VKS Add-ons include open source add-ons such as container registry, monitoring tools, and CNI plug-ins.
To address the challenges of securely shipping these open source components, Broadcom complements existing VCF
security controls. Broadcom ensures that both base distributions and additive packages go through a vetting process
before deployment.
Build to Ship: Vulnerability Lifecycle
Each publicly announced vulnerability follows a continuous lifecycle from artifact analysis to technical resolution. This
structured approach applies equally to VKr and VKS Add-ons . VKrs provide pre-baked node OS and container images.
VKS Add-ons provide container images.
Configuring vSphere Namespaces for Hosting VKS Clusters
A vSphere Namespace provides the runtime environment for VKS clusters. To provision a VKS cluster, you first configure
a vSphere Namespace with users, roles, compute, storage, content library, and virtual machine classes. This configuration
is inherited by VKS clusters that run in that namespace.
Using vSphere Namespaces with VKS Clusters
A vSphere Namespace is a network-scoped tenancy on Supervisor. vSphere Namespaces are used to host VKS
clusters, and provide networking, role permissions, persistent storage, resource quota, and content library and VM class
integration.
vSphere Namespace Network
A vSphere Namespace network is a subnet carved from the Supervisor > Workload Network > Namespace Network.
The Namespace subnet prefix defines the size of the subnet reserved for each vSphere Namespace. The default is /28.
VMware by Broadcom 291

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
The vSphere Namespace network provides connectivity for VKS clusters to Supervisor. By default, the vSphere
Namespace will use cluster level network configurations and allocate IP addresses from its subnet. When you create a
vSphere Namespace, a /28 overlay segment and corresponding IP pool is instantiated to service pods in that vSphere
Namespace.
When the first VKS cluster is provisioned in a vSphere Namespace, the VKS cluster will share the same subnet as its
vSphere Namespace. For each subsequent VKS cluster that is provisioned in that vSphere Namespace, a new subnet is
created for that cluster and connected to its vSphere Namespace gateway.
There is a shared load balancer instance in the vSphere Namespace that is responsible for routing kubectl traffic to each
VKS cluster control plane. In addition, for each Kubernetes service load balancer that is resourced on the VKS cluster, a
layer-4 load balancer instance is created for that service.
VKS clusters within the same vSphere Namespace share a SNAT IP for north-south connectivity. East-west connectivity
between namespaces is no SNAT.
The vSphere Namespace is typically non-routable. However, if you are using NSX networking, you can override
the vSphere Namespace Network with a routable subnet. See Override Workload Network Settings for a vSphere
Namespace.
vSphere Namespace Resource Pools
In a single vSphere Zone Supervisor deployment, when you create a vSphere Namespace, a resource pool backing that
namespace is created. The vSphere Namespace provides a logical unit of resources on Supervisor, including compute,
storage, permissions, classes, and images. When you configure a CPU or memory limit on a vSphere Namespace, for
example, the same resource limits are applied to the resource pool backing that namespace. In this fashion vSphere
Namespaces enable multi-tenancy in Supervisor.
The same multi-tenant experience applies to Supervisor deployed across three vSphere Zones. When a vSphere
Namespace is created on a zoned Supervisor, the system creates a resource pool in each of the vSphere clusters
supporting that Supervisor. This enables a VKS cluster provisioned in that vSphere Namespace to be deployed in any of
the zones belonging to this Supervisor.
Using the vSphere Client, you can view the vSphere Namespace resource pool and objects by selecting the Hosts and
Clusters perspective, and also by selecting the VMs and Templates view. When you provision a VKS cluster, it is created
in the target vSphere Namespace. In a zoned Supervisor deployment, you will have the same resource pool in each
vSphere cluster.
VMware by Broadcom 292

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
vSphere Namespace Creation
There are several ways in which to create vSphere Namespaces.
Administrators can create vSphere Namespaces using the vSphere Client. See Create a vSphere Namespace for Hosting
VKS Clusters.
vCenter Single Sign-On users who are granted the Owner role permission for a vSphere Namespace can create vSphere
Namespaces in a self-service manner using . See Enable vSphere Namespace Creation Using Kubectl.
kubectl
VMware exposes vCenter APIs for managing the life cycle of vSphere Namespaces, and provides software development
kits (SDKs), including:
• The Namespace Management APIs provide REST-based resources for managing vSphere Namespaces.
• The Namespaces APIs provide REST-based resources to manage access control of subjects on vSphere
Namespaces.
• The vSphere Automation SDK for Java provides several packages for automating the creation and life cycle
management of vSphere Namespaces.
• Likewise the vSphere Automation SDK for Python provides several packages for automating the creation and life cycle
management of vSphere Namespaces.
vSphere Namespace Storage for VKS Clusters
VKS clusters rely on the Container Storage Interface (CSI), the industry standard interface used to lifecycle persistent
storage.
In a VCF environment, storage provisioning across the platform uses a hierarchical, two-driver orchestration model across
the infrastructure and developer layers:
VMware by Broadcom 293

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
• Supervisor Layer (CNS-CSI): The Supervisor runs the core vSphere CNS-CSI driver. The driver communicates
directly with the CNS control plane on vCenter to execute storage tasks. This driver connects vSphere storage to the
Kubernetes environment through individual vSphere Namespace.
• VKS Cluster Layer (pvCSI): VKS clusters run a specialized, modified version of the driver called the Paravirtual
CSI (pvCSI) driver. The pvCSI handles all storage requests originating from within the VKS cluster. Unlike the
infrastructure-level CNS-CSI, the pvCSI does not require global vSphere credentials. It authenticates securely using a
local service account bounded to its designated namespace.
The diagram shows the relationship between the vSphere Namespace, Supervisor, and VKS cluster storage mechanisms.

For more information, see Storage for Supervisor and VKS Clusters.
StorageClass Propagation on VKS Clusters
Storage availability across the platform is controlled through vSphere storage policies. When configuring a vSphere
Namespace, you assign one or more vSphere storage policies. The Supervisor the converts the policy into a Kubernetes
StorageClass and replicates it to every VKS cluster in that namespace. Each assigned policy generates two StorageClass
objects in the VKS cluster: one with the user-defined name specified when the vSphere storage policy was created, and
the other with appended to the name.
*-latebinding
For more information on which storage class to use and when, see Using Storage Classes for Persistent Volumes.
To create the storage policies, see Create a vSphere Storage Policy for VKS Clusters.
Follow these guidelines when creating and assigning the storage policies to the namespace:
• For multi-zone namespaces on a zonal Supervisor deployment, always assign storage policies with the Zonal
topology attribute. The StorageClass ensures volumes land in the same zone as the scheduled Pod,
-latebinding
preventing cross-zone attachment failures.
• Assign at least one storage policy to every vSphere Namespace. Without a policy assignment, no StorageClass is
available in the VKS cluster and all PVC creation requests fail.
• Set a storage consumption limit per policy per namespace to prevent a single namespace from exhausting shared
datastore capacity.
• Do not remove a storage policy from vCenter or from a namespace while PVCs reference it. The StorageClass
remains in Kubernetes but becomes non-functional, causing unpredictable provisioning behavior.
Persistent Storage Volumes for VKS Clusters
Persistent volumes are required for stateful applications in Kubernetes. For more information about persistent volumes,
refer to the Kubernetes documentation.
In the vSphere environment, persistent volume objects are backed by virtual disks that reside on datastores. Datastores
are represented by storage policies. When you assign a vSphere storage policy to a vSphere Namespace, the storage
policy is made available as a Kubernetes storage class for each VKS cluster in that namespace.
VKS supports dynamic and static provisioning of persistent volumes.
Dynamic Provisioning With dynamic provisioning, the persistent volume does not need to be pre-provisioned. You issue a
persistent volume claim (PVC) that references a storage class available in the vSphere Namespace. VKS
automatically provisions the corresponding persistent volume with a backing virtual disk. See Creating
Persistent Storage Volumes Dynamically.
VMware by Broadcom 294

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Static Provisioning With static provisioning, you use an existing storage object and make it available to a cluster. You define
the persistent volume by providing the details of the existing storage object, its supported configurations,
and mount options. See Creating Persistent Storage Volumes Statically.
The diagram illustrates the dynamic persistent volume provisioning workflow. You create a PVC using on the
kubectl
VKS cluster. This action generates a matching PVC on Supervisor and triggers the CNS-CSI driver, which invokes the
CNS create volume API.
