CNS-CSI
PVe Cors llauis imm teent PVe Cors llauis imm teent Volume
pvCSI CNS
Two-Layer PVC Binding Model
When a VKS workload creates a PVC, storage is provisioned through two binding layers working together:
1. VKS cluster layer. The PVC and bound PV are created in the VKS cluster. They are the objects visible to the workload
and the Kubernetes scheduler.
2. Supervisor layer. A corresponding PVC and PV are automatically created in the Supervisor namespace. The
Supervisor PVC maps to the actual First Class Disk (FCD) on the vSphere datastore.
Each VKS PVC maps to exactly one Supervisor PVC. The underlying FCD is owned and managed at the Supervisor
layer, not the VKS layer.
Important:
Always delete storage objects from the VKS cluster layer first. Attempting to delete Supervisor PVCs or PVs
before removing the VKS objects leaves the FCD on the datastore in an inconsistent state that requires manual
remediation. Never delete FCDs directly from the datastore. Doing so might corrupt the FCD catalog in vCenter.
For more information, see Reconcile the FCD Catalog.
This two-layer model is the foundation for all operations that involve PVC deletion, volume migration, backup and restore,
and cluster decommission.
For information on viewing and monitoring Supervisor persistent volumes and their FCD backing in vCenter, see Monitor
Persistent Volumes Using the vSphere Client.
vSAN File Services (Required for ReadWriteMany)
ReadWriteMany (RWX) volumes require vSAN File Service. vSAN File Services must be activated on the Supervisor
before you assign a file service storage policy to a namespace. Verify that File Services is enabled on the vSAN cluster
before creating or assigning file service policies.
4Kn Storage Format Support
Starting with VCF 9.0, you can deploy pods with persistent volumes using 4Kn storage format. Specify the sector size,
4Kn or 512n, in the storage policy. VKS supports 4Kn format for pod volumes only. Control plane and worker nodes do not
support 4Kn format.
To deploy pods with 4Kn persistent volumes, ensure the namespace uses VM classes compatible with ESX 9.0 and later.
Create a vSphere Namespace for Hosting VKS Clusters
You provision VKS clusters in a vSphere Namespace.
Create a vSphere Namespace to host one or more VKS clusters.

The name must be in a DNS-compliant format and the name must be unique across all Supervisor instances managed
by vCenter.

Configure a vSphere Namespace for VKS Clusters
You deploy one or more VKS clusters in a vSphere Namespace. VKS clusters automatically inherit configuration settings
from the vSphere Namespace, including storage access, resource quotas, and permissions.
Configure Persistent Storage for the vSphere Namespace
You can assign one or more vSphere storage policies to a vSphere Namespace. An assigned storage policy controls
datastore placement of persistent volumes in the vSphere storage environment.
Typically a vSphere administrator defines a vSphere storage policy. If you are using vSphere Zones, the storage policy
must be configured with the topology. See Create a vSphere Storage Policy for VKS Clusters.
Zonal
To assign a vSphere storage policy to a vSphere Namespace:
1. Select Supervisor Management > Namespace and the target vSphere Namespace.
2. From the Storage tile, select Add Storage.
3. Select one or more storage policies from the available options.
For each vSphere storage policy you assign to a vSphere Namespace, the system creates two matching Kubernetes
storage classes in that vSphere Namespace. These storage classes are replicated to each VKS cluster deployed in that
vSphere Namespace. For more information, see Using Storage Classes for Persistent Volumes and vSphere Namespace
Storage for VKS Clusters.
Set Capacity and Usage Limits for the vSphere Namespace
When you configure a vSphere Namespace, a resource pool for the vSphere Namespace is created on vCenter. By
default this resource pool is configured without any capacity and usage quota; resources are limited by the infrastructure.
In the Capacity and Usage tile for the vSphere Namespace, you can configure the following Limits.
CPU The amount of CPU resources to reserve for the vSphere
Namespace.
Memory The amount of memory to reserve for the vSphere Namespace.
VMware by Broadcom 296

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Storage The total amount of storage space to reserve for the vSphere
Namespace.
Storage Policy Limit Set the amount of storage individually to each of the storage
policies that are associated with the vSphere Namespace.
Note:
Always set a storage consumption limit per policy per
namespace. Without a limit, a single namespace can
exhaust shared datastore capacity and affect provisioning
for all other namespaces on the same Supervisor.
Typically, for VKS cluster deployments, you do not need to configure resource quota on the vSphere Namespace. If you
do assign quota limits, it is important to understand their potential impact on VKS clusters deployed there.
CPU and Memory Limits CPU and Memory limits configured on the vSphere Namespace have no bearing on a VKS cluster
deployed there, if the VKS cluster nodes are using the guaranteed VM class type. However, if the VKS
cluster nodes are using the best effort VM class type, the CPU and Memory limits can impact the VKS
cluster.
Because the best effort VM class type allows resources to be overcommitted, you can run out of resources
if you have set CPU and memory limits on the vSphere Namespace where you are provisioning VKS
clusters. If contention occurs and the VKS cluster control plane is impacted, the cluster may stop running.
For this reason you should always use the guaranteed VM class type for production clusters. If you cannot
use the guaranteed VM class type for all production nodes, at a minimum you should use guaranteed for
the control plane nodes.
Storage and Storage A Storage limit configured on the vSphere Namespace determines the overall amount of storage that is
Policy Limits available to the vSphere Namespace for all VKS clusters deployed there.
A Storage Policy limit configured on the vSphere Namespace determines the amount of storage available
for that storage class for each VKS cluster where the storage class is replicated.

Override Workload Network Settings for a vSphere Namespace
When you deploy Supervisor, you configure the default settings for the workload network. If you have enabled Supervisor
with NSX networking, you can override the default workload network settings when you create a vSphere Namespace.
Overridden workload network settings apply only to this vSphere Namespace segment.
Override Workload Network Settings (NSX Only)
When you create a vSphere Namespace, a network segment is created. By default, this network segment is derived from
the Workload Network configured in Supervisor. See vSphere Namespace Network for more information.
If Supervisor is configured with NSX networking, during the creation of a vSphere Namespace, you have the option of
choosing to Override cluster network settings for the vSphere Namespace. Choosing this option lets you customize the
vSphere Namespace network by adding CIDRs to the Ingress, Egress, and Namespace Network fields. The new CIDRs
you add override existing CIDRs for this vSphere Namespace instance.
If you have configured NSX version 4.1.1 or later, and have installed, configured, and registered the version 22.1.4 or
later with Enterprise license on NSX, the load balancer that is used with NSX is . If you have configured versions of NSX
earlier than 4.1.1, the NSX load balancer is used. For more information, see Supervisor Networking in the Supervisor
documentation.
The typical use case for overriding Supervisor network settings is to provision a VKS cluster with routable pod networking.
Refer to the configuration settings in the table for details on how to do this and links to examples.

of NSX must include an Edge Cluster dedicated for Tier-0 Gateways (routers) and another
Edge Cluster dedicated for Tier-1 Gateways. Refer to the NSX installation guide Installing and

enabled. In this case you must configure new CIDR ranges. If you select a VRF Gateway that
is linked to the Tier-0 Gateway, the network and subnets are automatically configured.
Once you select a Tier-0 Gateway and complete its configuration, you cannot change the Tier-0
Gateway.
Load Balancer Size Select the size of the load balancer instance on the Tier-1 gateway for the vSphere
Namespace.
Set the size of the load balancer to small (default), medium or large. Only a set number of Load
balancer instances per Edge Node can be defined. Refer to Config Max for details.
Note:
If you are using the , this setting is supported beginning with vSphere 8 U2 and
avi-22.1.5.
NAT Mode NAT mode is selected by default. This means that the Namespace Network subnet is expected
to be non-routable, and you must configure the Namespace Network, Ingress, and Egress
CIDRs.
Deselecting NAT mode tells the system you are going to provide a routable CIDR range for
the Namespace Network. If you deselect NAT mode, the VKS cluster node IP addresses are
directly accessible from outside the Tier-0 Gateway, and you do not have to configure the
Egress CIDR.
To provision a cluster using no NAT mode, deselect NAT mode and refer to the examples:
Provisioning VKS Clusters.
Namespace Network CIDR The Namespace Network CIDR is a subnet that operates as an IP pool whereby the
Namespace Subnet Prefix describes the size of any subsequent CIDR block that is carved out
from that IP pool.
Each time a vSphere Namespace is created, a subnet from the Namespace Network is
allocated. The subnet size carved out from this block is /24, which means a maximum of 256
pods can be created per vSphere Namespace. Refer to Config Max for details.
The Namespace Network CIDR is used to allocate IP addresses to VKS clusters attached to
vSphere Namespace segments.
If NAT mode is selected, the CIDR is expected to be non-routable. If NAT mode is unchecked,
Namespace Network CIDR must be routable.
VMware by Broadcom 300

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Component Configuration
Namespace Subnet Prefix Enter the subnet prefix that specifies the size of the subnet reserved for namespaces
segments. Default is 28.
Namespace subnet prefix defines the IP subnet created for each vSphere Namespace
segment. For example, setting a /24 prefix would result in a vSphere Namespace segment with
an IP subnet of 254 IP addresses to allocate to VKS clusters deployed there.
Additional example:
Namespace Network CIDR = 192.168.1.0/24
Namespace Subnet Prefix = /28
In this case, VKS can provide 16x 192.168.1.x/28 CIDR blocks from the 192.168.1.0/24 subnet.
This allows the instantiation of 16 VKS cluster Namespace networks to which your VKS-
managed VMs are connected to. For example, every cluster receives a dedicated Namespace
CIDR and in this case that could be 192.168.1.0/28 and the next cluster namespace subnet
would be 192.168.0.16/28 and so on.
Ingress Ingress IP CIDR block is used to allocate IP addresses for Kubernetes services that are
published by a service type load balancer and by an ingress controller across all vSphere
Namespaces. VKS cluster services and ingress get their IP addresses from this CIDR block.
Enter a CIDR annotation that determines the ingress IP range for the virtual IP addresses
published by the load balancer service for VKS clusters.
Note:
This setting is not applicable for the .
Egress Egress IP CIDR is used to allocate IP addresses for SNAT (Source Network Address
Translation) for traffic exiting the vSphere Namespace to access external services.
Enter a CIDR annotation that determines the egress IP range for the SNAT IP addresses.
Using VM Classes with VKS Clusters
To size VKS cluster nodes, you specify the virtual machine (VM) class. The platform provides default VM classes, and you
can create your own. To use a VM class, you associate it with the target vSphere Namespace and reference the class in
the cluster manifest.
About VM Classes
A virtual machine (VM) class is a request for resource reservations for processing power on the virtual machine (VM),
including CPU and memory (RAM). For example, the VM class type named "guaranteed-large" reserves 4 CPU and 16
GB RAM.
Note:
The VM disk size is set by the OVA template, not the VM class definition. For vSphere Kubernetes releases, the
disk size is 16 GB.
There are two reservation types for VM classes: guaranteed and best effort. The guaranteed class fully reserves its
configured resources. This means that for a given cluster the matches the
spec.policies.resources.requests
settings. The best effort class allows resources to be overcommitted. For production workloads it is
spec.hardware
recommended that you use the guaranteed VM class type.
Warning:
Because the best effort VM class type allows resources to be overcommitted, you can run out of resources if you
have set limits on the vSphere Namespace where you deploy the VKS cluster. If contention occurs and the control
plane is impacted, the cluster may stop running. For this reason use the guaranteed VM class type for production
clusters. If you cannot use the guaranteed VM class type for all production nodes, at a minimum use guaranteed
for the control plane nodes.
Using VM Classes with VKS Clusters
To use a VM class with a VKS cluster, the VM class must be bound to the vSphere Namespace where the cluster is
provisioned. To do this, you associate the class with the target namespace. See Configure a vSphere Namespace for VKS
Clusters.
VMware by Broadcom 301

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
To list the VM classes available in the target vSphere Namespace, use the command  kubectl get
.
virtualmachineclass
Note:
If you experience issues with this command, see Troubleshoot VM Class Binding Errors.
VM class definitions are not immutable. Any VM class can be edited, including the default VM class definitions. If a VM
class is edited, existing VKS cluster nodes remain unaffected. New VKS clusters use the modified class.
CAUTION:
If you edit a VM class that is in use by a VKS cluster, and then scale out that cluster, the new node(s) will use the
edited class definition, but the existing nodes will use the initial class definition, resulting in a mismatch of classes.
Default VM Classes
The table lists default VM class types that are used as deployment sizes for VKS cluster nodes.
To avoid overcommitting resources, production workloads should use the guaranteed class type. To avoid running out of
memory, do not use the small or extra small class size for any worker node where you are deploying workloads in any
environment (development, test, or production).
Note:
If your storage class specifies 4KN as a target storage format for persistent volumes, make sure to use VM
classes compatible with ESX 9.0 and later.

System Resource Reservations in VKS Nodes
VKS nodes reserve a portion of CPU and memory for system components that are required for Kubernetes and VKS to
function reliably. These reservations ensure that critical system processes do not compete with application workloads for
resources.
Because of these reservations, the allocatable CPU and memory available to workloads is lower than the total capacity
defined by the VM class used for the node.
Node Resource Reservations
To ensure cluster and node stability, VKS reserves resources for essential system daemons. These reservations ensure
that critical system components do not compete with user workloads for CPU and memory.
Note:
System resource reservations are supported on Linux nodes only. This functionality is not available for Windows
nodes.
Because of these reservations, a difference exists between the node's total resources, which are based on the underlying
VM class, and the resources available for application requests.
CPU Reservations
The CPU in a VKS node is calculated using the following formula, which is based on the total capacity
systemReserved
of the underlying virtual machine. This calculation determines the amount of CPU resources reserved exclusively for
system daemons.
• 6% of first 1000m (first core)
• 1% of next 1000m (up to 2000m, or two cores)
• 0.5% of next 2000m (up to 4000m, or four cores)
• 0.25% of cores above 4000m (above four cores)
The following example illustrates how to calculate the CPU reserved for a best-effort-large VM class (four cores) used in a
node:
• Total CPU: 4000m
• Calculations for :
systemReserved
– First 1000m x 6% = 60m
– Next 1000m x 1% = 10m
– Next 2000m x 0.5% = 10m
– CPU reserved = 80m (~0.08 CPU)
• Allocatable CPU:
4 CPU - 0.08 CPU = 3.92 CPU
Memory Reservations
By default, the reserved memory in a VKS node is calculated using the following method to determine the
value.
systemReserved
• For memory < 1024 Mi: 255 MiB reserved
• For memory = >24 MiB:
– 25% of first 4096 MiB
– 20% of next 4096 MiB (up to 8192 MiB)
– 10% of next 8192 MiB (up to 16384 MiB)
– 6% of next 114688 MiB (up to 131072 MiB)
– 2% of any memory above 131072 MiB
If you want to change the default value, keep in mind the following:

Create a vSphere Storage Policy for VKS Clusters
A vSphere storage policy that you assign to a vSphere Namespace is converted to a Kubernetes storage class. DevOps
engineers use this storage class to control how VKS cluster nodes and persistent volumes are placed within vSphere
datastores.
Prerequisites
• Confirm that the underlying datastores (VMFS, NFS, or vSAN) are fully configured and accessible from all hosts in the
cluster.
• For multi-zone deployments, verify that the datastore spans all vSphere Zones that the namespace covers.
• For ReadWriteMany workload, verify that vSAN File Services is activated on the Supervisor before creating the file
service policy.
• For 4Kn volumes, confirm that the namespace uses VM classes compatible with ESX 9.0 and later.
• For storage policy naming requirements and general best practices, see Best Practices for Storage in Supervisor and
VKS Environments.
• For more information about storage in VKS clusters, see vSphere Namespace Storage for VKS Clusters.
1. Using the vSphere Client, select Policies and Profiles.
2. Select VM Storage Policies > Create.
3. Select the vCenter.
4. Name the storage policy descriptively, such as name-cluster-storage-class.
The storage policy name becomes the Kubernetes StorageClass name in the namespace and all VKS clusters
deployed within it. Use a descriptive, RFC 1123–compliant name.
5. On the Policy structure page, enable rules for a target storage entity.
a. Under Datastore specific rules, select the rule type appropriate for your storage backend.
For example, Enable rules for "VMFS" storage.
b. Under Storage format, select Enable storage format to be able to select a sector size.
c. To create a topology aware policy, under vSphere Kubernetes Service Storage topology, select Enable Zonal
topology for Supervisor.
Note:
This step is necessary if you are creating topology aware policies to be used for persistent storage on a
namespace in a three-zone Supervisor. Three-zone namespaces reject storage policies that lack this attribute.
6. Configure the selected rules:
– vSAN rules: set Failures to Tolerate (FTT) and site disaster tolerance to match your OSA or ESA cluster
configuration.
– VMFS rules: select Conserve space when possible.
– Tag-based rules: select the tag category and datastore tags that define this storage tier.
7. If you enabled storage format, on the Storage format page, select the sector size.
Option Description
512n Sector size of 512 bytes (default).
4Kn Sector size of 4096 bytes.
8. For Storage compatibility, review and click Next.
9. Click Finish to complete the storage policy creation.
Assign the storage policy to a vSphere Namespace. The Supervisor generates two Kubernetes StorageClass objects,
(Immediate) and (WaitForFirstConsumer), in the namespace and
<policy-name> <policy-name>-latebinding
propagates them to all VKS clusters in that namespace.

Connecting to VKS Clusters on Supervisor Using an External Identity
Provider
You can connect to VKS clusters on Supervisor using an external identity provider and the Pinniped authentication service
for Kubernetes.
Configure an External Identity Provider for VKS Clusters
You can configure Supervisor with any OIDC-compliant identity provider (IDP), such as Okta. To complete the integration,
you configure the IDP with the callback URL for Supervisor.
Supported External Identity Provider
You can configure Supervisor with any OIDC-compliant identity provider. The table lists common ones and includes links
for configuration instructions.
External IDP Configuration
Okta Configure Okta as an OIDC provider for Pinniped
Workspace ONE Configure Workspace ONE Access as an OIDC provider for
Pinniped
Dex Configure Dex as an OIDC provider for Pinniped
GitLab Configure GitLab as an OIDC provider for Pinniped
Google OAuth Using Google OAuth 2
Configuring the IDP with the Callback URL for Supervisor
Supervisor acts as an OAuth 2.0 client to the external identity provider. The Supervisor callback URL is the redirect URL
used to configure the external IDP. The callback URL takes the form https://SUPERVISOR-VIP/wcp/pinniped/callback.
If the IP portion of the callback URL is represented as a fully qualified domain name (FQDN), ensure that the DNS server
used by both the Supervisor and the VKS can resolve the FQDN to the correct virtual IP (VIP).
Note:
When performing the IDP registration, the callback URL might be called the "redirect URL" in the OIDC provider
you are configuring.
When configuring the external identity provider for use with VKS on Supervisor, you supply the external identity provider
with the Callback URL that is available in vCenter at Supervisor Management > Supervisors > Configure > Identity
Providers screen.

Okta lets users sign-in to applications using the OpenID Connect protocol. When you configure Okta as an external
identity provider for VKS on Supervisor, the Pinniped pods on Supervisor and on VKS clusters control user access to both
vSphere Namespaces and workload clusters.

Using the vSphere Client, get the Identity Provider Callback URL at Supervisor Management > Supervisors >
Configure > Identity Providers. Copy this URL to a temporary location.

Register an External Identity Provider with Supervisor
To connect to VKS clusters on Supervisor using an external identity provider, register your identity provider with
Supervisor.
Prerequisites
Before you register an external identity provider with Supervisor, complete the following prerequisites:
• Enable Supervisor Management and deploy a Supervisor instance.
• Configure an external OpenID Connect identity provider with the Supervisor callback URL. See Configure an External
Identity Provider for VKS Clusters.
• Get the Client ID, Client Secret, and Issuer URL from the external IDP. See Configure an External Identity Provider for
VKS Clusters.
Register an External Identity Provider with Supervisor
Supervisor runs as pods the Pinniped Supervisor and the Pinniped Concierge components. VKS clusters run as pods the
Pinniped Concierge component only. For more information about these components and how they interact, refer to the
Pinniped authentication service documentation.
Once you register an external identity provider with Supervisor, the system updates the Pinniped Supervisor and Pinniped
Concierge pods on Supervisor and the Pinniped Concierge pods on VKS clusters. All VKS clusters running on that
Supervisor instance are automatically configured with that same external identity provider.
To register an external ODIC provider with Supervisor, complete the following procedure:
1. Log in to the vCenter using the vSphere Client.
2. Select Supervisor Management > Supervisors > Configure > Identity Providers.
3. Click the plus sign to begin the registration process.
4. Configure the provider. See Identity Provider Configuration.

Configure vSphere Namespace Permissions for External Identity Provider Users
and Groups
To configure VKS cluster access for OIDC users, you configure the vSphere Namespace with role permissions for external
identity provider users and groups.
Configure vSphere Namespace Permissions for External Identity Provider Users and Groups
A VKS cluster on Supervisor is provisioned in a vSphere Namespace. After you register an external OIDC provider with
Supervisor, you configure the vSphere Namespace with role permissions for external OIDC provider users and groups.
This action creates the role bindings for the external OIDC provider on each cluster in that vSphere Namespace . If the
vSphere Namespace already exists, the role bindings are updated.
Note:
Once you have registered an external IDP on a Supervisor, all clusters created on that Supervisor will be
configured automatically with the external IDP via the Pinniped components.
1. Register an external identity provider with Supervisor.
See Register an External Identity Provider with Supervisor.
2. Create a vSphere Namespace for a cluster, or select an existing vSphere Namespace.
3. Configure users and roles for the vSphere Namespace.
Select the external OIDC provider as an identity source, and add users and assign roles.
1. Select the vSphere Namespace.
2. Select Actions > Add Permissions.
3. Identity Source: Select the external identity provider registered with Supervisor.
The Provider Name you used to register the external IDP should appear in the drop-down menu. If it does not,
check the configuration.
4. User/Group Search: Type in the user or group name. The text input is a free-form string.
Users and groups from an external identity provider are not synchronized with vCenter and cannot be selected.
You must type in the string value, usually an email address. There is no prefix, so you can type "jdoe@acme.com,"
for example.
5. Role: Assign the user or group to a role by selecting the role, either Can View or Can Edit.
Note:
The Owner role is not available for use with an external identity provider.
4. Complete the configuration of the vSphere Namespace.
See Configure a vSphere Namespace for VKS Clusters.

Vulnerability Management for VKr and VKS Add-ons.
Learn how Broadcom identifies, assesses, and remediates security vulnerabilities in vSphere Kubernetes releases (VKr )
and VKS Add-ons. The process follows a structured lifecycle from artifact analysis to technical resolution.
VMware by Broadcom 326

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Overview
VKS clusters are built on top of vSphere Kubernetes releases (VKr). A VKr provides the infrastructure, OVF packages,
and container images used for VKS cluster nodes. VKS Add-ons include open source add-ons such as container registry,
monitoring tools, and CNI plug-ins.
To address the unique challenges of securely shipping these open source components, Broadcom complements existing
security controls. Broadcom ensures that both base distributions and additive packages go through a vetting process
before deployment.
Build to Ship: Vulnerability Lifecycle
Each publicly announced vulnerability follows a continuous lifecycle from artifact analysis to technical resolution. This
structured approach applies equally to VKr and VKS Standard Packages. VKr provides pre-baked node OS and container
images. VKS Add-ons provide container images.
Figure 15:
Perform Regular Identify and Analyze Vulnerabilities; Assess and Remediate Vulnerabilities
Scanning for Review Reports and Scans
Vulnerabilities
Remediate
Decision
Scan A Identify B Analyze C Assess D Patch F
E
Accept Risk
Document G
Scan: Automated Artifact Analysis
Every release of a VKr image or VKS Add-ons goes through automated identification of security vulnerabilities.
• Infrastructure image inspection. For a VKr, the system inspects the VMDK files. The system mounts the file systems
directly to analyze OS packages, for example, Ubuntu or Photon OS.
• Component and binary analysis. For VKS Add-ons, the system analyzes individual binaries and archives, for
example, container archives for Harbor or Istio. The system checks these artifacts for vulnerable language specific
dependencies.
Identify: Contextual Risk Filtering
After the system identifies flaws, Broadcom filters the flaws to isolate actionable risks from theoretical exposures.
• Severity thresholding. Broadcom scores findings based on impact. High and critical severity items receive automatic
flagging for immediate attention. Broadcom defines severity based on CVSS scoring methodology.
• Release based aggregation. Broadcom consolidates results into standardized reports. The reports categorize
vulnerabilities by the specific product version, for example, VKr 1.34 or VKS Add-ons v3.7.0+20260827.
Analyze: Verification and Ticket Generation
Broadcom documents automatically generated findings in an issue tracking system to ensure a clear chain of custody.
• Automated tracking. Broadcom aggregates vulnerabilities by release to manage the cumulative security posture of a
product version.
• Ownership assignment. The system automatically routes issues to responsible engineering and component owners.
VMware by Broadcom 327

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Assess: Technical Reachability and Exploitability
Engineers analyze each vulnerability to determine whether a theoretical vulnerability presents an actual risk in the
product.
• Reachability analysis. Engineers verify whether the vulnerable code path is actively utilized. For example, engineers
mark a flaw in a database library as invalid if the component, such as a pause container image or CNI plug-in, does not
interact with that library.
• Configuration safeguards. Assessments determine whether product defaults, for example, disabled modules or
restricted root access, effectively block an exploit, even if the vulnerable library is present.
Patch or Document
Broadcom determines the final response based on the assessment results.
• Remediation, patch. Broadcom resolves confirmed risks through peer reviewed updates to base images or
dependency versions. When available, Broadcom consumes the fix from upstream projects. If required, Broadcom
engineers contribute these fixes to the upstream open source projects.
• Impact assessment, document. If remediation is not feasible, Broadcom documents the assessed impact with a formal
status justification.
Disclaimer
Each deployment is unique, and the impact of a CVE can differ depending on several factors. If you have any questions or
want to learn more about how a specific CVE affects how you use VKr and VKS Add-ons, contact your Broadcom support
representative.
Product Release Cadence
VKr and VKS Add-ons follow a frequent asynchronous release process, with releases several times a year. For more
information about the cadence of releases, see the VMware VKr release notes and the VKS Add-Ons release notes.
Note:
When a vulnerability critically affects VKr or a VKS Add-on, Broadcom addresses the vulnerability in the shortest
commercially reasonable time possible.
Conclusion: Added Value
By applying this unified process to both VKr and VKS Add-ons, Broadcom ensures that the product releases follow
secure by design principles. You benefit from reduced maintenance noise and the assurance that Broadcom vets every
component, from the node OS to the container image, against the VCF security controls described in this topic.
VMware by Broadcom 328

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Installing and Configuring Harbor
As a Provider Administrator, you can install Harbor as a VCF Service that spans across one or more regions. As a VI
Administrator, you can install Harbor on individual Supervisor instances as a Supervisor Service.
Harbor as a VCF Service Versus Harbor as a Supervisor Service
Two ways exist to deploy Harbor in VCF and Supervisors:
• Harbor as a VCF Service or regional Harbor, where you deploy Harbor on one or more regions in VCF Automation.
Regional Harbor is a mandatory requirement for VCF because it serves as a central container registry for images that
are used for deploying Supervisor Services, VCF CLI Plugins, and VKS add-ons on VKS clusters.
• Harbor as a Supervisor Service on individual Supervisor instances.
Note:
The Harbor instance that you install manually as a Supervisor Service on individual Supervisors does not have
connectivity with the software depot and cannot handle the same use cases as the regional Harbor.
Installing and Configuring Harbor as a VCF Service in VCF Automation
Learn how to deploy Harbor to all available regions in the VCF fleet by using the VCF Automation Provider UI. VCF
Automation deploys and manages a dedicated Harbor instance for every region in the environment. This regional Harbor
is the OCI registry that VCF uses to distribute container images and OCI artifacts that are Supervisor Services, VCF CLI
plugins, VKS clusters, and VKS add-ons, to every Supervisor and VKS cluster in that region.
Overview
Key characteristics of the Regional Harbor:
• One Harbor instance runs per region, on one Supervisor that belongs to that region.
• Every Supervisor and VKS cluster in the region is automatically configured to trust this Harbor instance under a
constant, well-known name: .
depot.kube-system.svc
• Consumers do not need to know the real hostname or IP address of the registry. They always resolve and trust it
through this fixed name, which VCF Automation keeps pointed at the right place even if the underlying infrastructure
changes.
• After installation, Harbor is automatically initialized as a caching proxy in front of the software depot service, the
upstream source of VKS system images.
During initialization, the following occurs:
• A remote registry entry is created pointing to the software depot endpoint, as configured on the Supervisor under
Config > Networking > Management Proxy with entry name .
vcf-depot
• A project named is created in Harbor and configured as a proxy cache for that remote registry.
vcf
This means artifacts are pulled from Broadcom once, cached regionally in Harbor, and served locally to every Supervisor
and VKS cluster in the region. This reduces external bandwidth use and keeps deployments fast even with limited Internet
connectivity.
Why this matters to you:
• Harbor is a prerequisite for deploying Supervisor Services, VCF CLI plug-ins, VKS clusters, and VKS add-ons in a
region. If the regional Harbor insance is not healthy, those workflows fail.
• You manage Harbor per region, not per Supervisor. You select which Supervisor hosts the regional Harbor, and VCF
Automation configures trust to the rest of the region automatically.
• You can install Harbor can be fresh (greenfield) or adopted from an existing installation (brownfield).
• Once installed, Harbor is self-healing. VCF Automation continuously reconciles its configuration and corrects drift
automatically.

One Supervisor in each region runs Harbor behind an NGINX load balancer. Every other Supervisor in the region and
every VKS cluster on those Supervisors is configured to trust and resolve Harbor by using the fixed name
depot.kube-
Harbor itself functions as a caching proxy for the software depot service.

Installation Modes
The Harbor lifecycle management operations such as installation, reconfiguration, upgrade, and uninstallation are self-
service and on-demand for the Provider Administrator.
Important:
If you change the host Supervisor for a region during reconfiguration,VCF Automation removes the existing
Harbor installation and all of its cached content from the previous Supervisor. VCF Automation then performs a
fresh install or brownfield adoption on the newly selected Supervisor.
Installing Harbor or the Select a region and a host Supervisor without an existing Harbor installation. VCF Automation installs and
first time configures a new Harbor instance on the host Supervisor that you selected.
Other, unrelated Harbor instances can continue to exist elsewhere in the region but not on the Supervisor
that you selected to host the regional Harbor.
Adopting an existing If the Supervisor you select already has a Harbor Supervisor Service installed, VCF Automation detects
Harbor installation that Harbor instance and suggests adopting the instance. The outcome depends on the version of the
existing installation relative to the versionVCF Automation installs.
• Older than the target version - Automatically upgraded and reconfigured in a single step.
VMware by Broadcom 330

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
• Same as the target version - Reconfigured in place to bring it under VCF Automation management.
• Newer than the target version - Adoption is blocked. You must remove the Supervisor Service manually
before a green field installation can happen.
Important:
Always back up Harbor before starting an adoption workflow.
When an existing instance is adopted, VCF Automation performs the following steps:
1. Validates the admin password.
The recorded in the Supervisor Service installation parameters must match the current
harborAdminPassword
Harbor admin password. If the password is changed from the Harbor UI or API after installation, that change is not
reflected in the Supervisor Service configuration. You must update the password in the Harbor UI or API before
starting the VCF Automation adoption process, or the adoption will fail.
2. Reissues the TLS certificate.
A new certificate is issued containing the fixed trust name and the current Load Balancer
depot.kube-system.svc
IP in the Subject Alternative Name, with the current hostname as the CN. Any registry clients that are configured with
the old certificate must be updated.
3. Moves to an NGINX Load Balancer.
Adoption only supports NGINX. If the existing instance uses a different Load Balancer type, its external IP might
change as part of the adoption. Plan to update any DNS records that pointed at the old IP.
4. Registers the software depot service as a remote registry and creates the project, exactly as in a
vcf proxy-cache
greenfield installation.
The adoption pulls the existing Harbor configuration, adjusting only the TLS and networking sections to match the VCF
Automation requirements, and applies that adjusted configuration as the new desired state. Your existing projects,
images, and other Harbor configuration are preserved.
Normal Day 2 Operation
After VCF Automation installs or adopts a Harbor instance, the instance comes under continuous management.
• VCF Automation constantly checks the actual state of Harbor against the desired configuration and automatically
corrects any drift that VCF Automation detects.
• When Supervisors join or leave the region, VCF Automation automatically adds or removes the Supervisors from the
Harbor trust configuration.
• Reconfiguration, upgrade, and uninstall remain available as self-service actions at any time.
Important:
Secrets and passwords cannot be rotated through Day 2 reconfiguration. You cannot change any of the the
Harbor secret fields - Harbor admin password, secret key, XSRF key, core, jobservice, or registry secrets. If you
edit one of these values in the form, the change is not applied to the running Harbor instance.
To rotate a password or any other component-level secret, perform the following steps.
1. Change the value directly on the affected component. For example, change the Harbor admin password from the
Harbor UI or API.
2. Update that same value in the Harbor VCF service configuration so that the value matches.
If you perform only step 1, the Harbor VCF service holds a stale value, which will cause a future adoption or reconciliation
to fail. See the password note under Brownfield adoption. If you perform only step 2, the change has no effect on the
actual component. You must perform both steps, in that order.
Install Regional Harbor Through VCF Automation
You can install Harbor through the Service Management in the VCF Automation Provider Management UI. You can install
Harbor in all available or only to specific regions that you select. A Harbor instance is installed to only one Supervisor
instance per region and the same Harbor instance is configured as a container registry to the rest of the Supervisors
and VKSClusters in the region. Regional Harbor is a foundational requirement for VCF because it serves as a central
VMware by Broadcom 331

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
container registry for images that are used for deploying Supervisor Services, VCF CLI Plugins, and VKS add-ons on VKS
clusters.
• Both vCenter and Supervisor must be running version 9.1.0 or later. This requirement applies to regional Harbor
deployments in both new and upgraded environments.
• The Supervisor where you install the Harbor service, must have connectivity to the rest of the Supervisors in the
region. Providing connectivity to all Supervisors in a region may require some advanced NSX VPC configuration, see
Managing Networking in VCF Automation Organizations for more information.
• The software depot service must be up and running. The Supervisor where you want to install Harbor must already
have thee software depot service configured under Config > Networking > Management Proxy. The entry name
is , and the entry includes the FQDN, port, and CA certificate. Fleet LCM typically configures this entry
vcf-depot
automatically during the Supervisor setup.
• Routable Load Balancer IP addresses. The IP addresses in the Load Balancer pool on the Supervisor that will host
Harbor must be routable from every Supervisor and VKS cluster in the region.
• Sufficient storage. The StorageClass that Harbor uses must have enough capacity to cache the OCI artifacts that
Harbor pulls from the software depot service.
• vCenter service account permissions. The service account that VCF Automation uses to connect to vCenter and
its Supervisors must be a member of the group. Fleet LCM typically
SupervisorProviderAdministrators
configures this membership automatically.
As part of Harbor as a VCF service installation, a project in Harbor is created and named where the software depot
VCF
is set as a proxy cache. The Harbor project proxies to the software depot requests for Supervisor Services, VCF
VCF
services, VKS clusters, VKS add-ons, and VCF CLI. This Harbor instance is configured as a container registry to the rest
of the Supervisors in the region.
Note:
If you do not install Harbor as a VCF Service in a region, you are unable to install and upgrade Supervisor
Services, VKS add-ons, or download VCF CLI.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. In the left navigation pane, click Service Management.
3. In the VCF Services tab, scroll down to the Not installed list of services.
4. On the Harbor card, select Install.
5. Review the certificates and click Accept Certificates to Continue.
6. On the Select Deployment Scope page, you can select the regions where you want to install Harbor.
7. On the Service Properties page, you can manually override the Harbor installation options by editing the service
definition YAML file.
a) On the left of the screen, click YAML View, which is orientated vertically on the screen.
The YAML containing the Harbor installation properties is displayed.
Once Harbor is installed, you can log in to the regional Harbor instance on it's IP address. You can find the IP
address under the External IP column of the service properties.
b) Select the Edit Service Configuration toggle.
c) Click Save when you are done with your edits.
8. On the Review and Finalise page, review the configured service properties and click Submit.
Uninstall Regional Harbor as a VCF Service in VCF Automation
Learn how to uninstall Harbor from the regions where it's running by using VCF Automation.
Note:
After the regional Harbor is uninstalled from a region, you might not be able to install Supervisor Services, VCF
services, VKS add-ons, and VCF CLI, on Supervisors and VKS clusters in the region from the VCF software
depot .
VMware by Broadcom 332

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management Portal.
2. In the left navigation pane, click Service Management.
3. Click VCF Services.
4. Select Harbor and click Uninstall.
Harbor is uninstalled from all regions where it was previously installed.
Edit a Harbor Instance in VCF Automation
Learn how to change the configuration of a Harbor instance through the VCF Automation Provider Management Portal,
deploy Harbor to additional regions, or change some of the service properties.
Check out the Harbor configuration values at Harbor VCF Service Configuration Properties Reference.
1. Log in to the VCF Automation Provider Management UI.
2. In the left navigation pane, click Service Management.
3. Click VCF Services.
4. Select Harbor and click Edit.
5. In Select Deployment Scope, add or remove regions where Harbor is installed.
6. In Service Properties, you can change the configuration properties of Harbor.
a) On the left of the screen, click YAML View, which is orientated vertically on the screen.
The YAML containing the Harbor installation properties is displayed.
b) Select the Edit Service Configuration toggle.
c) Click Save when you are done with your edits.
7. On the Review and Finalise page, review the configured service properties and click Submit.
Change the Default Password of Regional Harbor Service
Learn how to change the default password of the regional Harbor service after the initial installation.
1. Log in to the Harbor console as an admin and change the password.
2. In the left navigation pane, click Service Management.
3. Click VCF Services.
4. Select Harbor and click Edit.
5. In Service Properties, change the Harbor password in the service configuration properties.
a) On the left of the screen, click YAML View, which is orientated vertically on the screen.
The YAML containing the Harbor installation properties is displayed.
b) Select the Edit Service Configuration toggle.
c) Change the Harbor password accordingly.
d) Click Save when you are done with your edits.
6. On the Review and Finalise page, review the change and click Submit.

 Supervisor Service Supported Input Parameters and Day 2 Alternations
Learn how each Harbor Supervisor Service input parameter responds to a Day 2 change. Understand which parameters
you can safely reconfigure after installation and which parameters require fresh installation.
The following status indicators describe how each parameter responds to a Day 2 change.
•
YES - The change is written to a live  ConfigMap/Secret/pod-spec  field.  kapp-controller  reconciliation
updates the object. The consuming workload rolls automatically. Alternatively, the field is reconciled without pod
involvement.
• PARTIAL - The rendered manifest changes, but the underlying data is not migrated, a component does not auto-
restart, or the change applies only going forward and not retroactively.
• NO - The value is applied only at first boot or is baked to an already-persisted state. Changing the value post-
installation has no effect on the running system, or the system rejects the value as an immutable field.
• NOT EDITABLE - You must not change this value after initial installation. Changing the value does not migrate or move
the existing deployment and causes orphaned resources or data loss.

Installing and Configuring Harbor as a Supervisor Service
You can deploy Harbor as a Supervisor Service in your Supervisor environment. Harbor is an open-source, trusted cloud-
native registry project that stores, signs, and scans content. It extends the open-source Docker Distribution by adding key
capabilities such as security, identity, and management.
In the Supervisor environment, Harbor acts as the container image registry. It stores and provides container images for
workloads running as vSphere Pods or in VKS clusters on the same Supervisor. Having a registry closer to your build and
runtime environments improves image transfer efficiency.
Capabilities and Features
When deployed as a Supervisor Service, Harbor provides the following capabilities and features:
• The latest version of the Harbor open-source registry.
• Full feature parity with the upstream Harbor registry.
• Access through Ingress using DNS.
• Support for replication of images between registries.
• Advanced security features such as user management, access control, and activity auditing.
Considerations
When you install Harbor, keep in mind the following items:
• Use the Harbor Supervisor Service for shared Supervisor cluster deployments. Harbor is not suitable for multi-tenancy
because it does not provide the isolation that is required for tenant-specific use cases.
For multi-tenant environments, deploy Harbor as a VKS Addon on a dedicated VKS cluster that is used for shared
services. This cluster can host Harbor and provide container (OCI) images to workloads across the tenant. For
installation steps, see Install the Harbor Registry.
• When Harbor and VKS run on the same Supervisor, VKS clusters automatically trust the Harbor registry certificates
and can pull container images directly from it. For details, see Using Harbor as a Private Registry.
• Since version 2.11.2, the Harbor Supervisor Service supports exposing the registry by using a load balancer.
Depending on your configuration, you can expose Harbor through either an NGINX-based load balancer or by using
Contour.
– If you use an NGINX-based load balancer, ensure you have a load balancer configured for the Supervisor.
– If you use Contour as an Ingress controller, install it before installing Harbor on the same Supervisor where you
want to install Harbor. See Installing Contour as a Supervisor Service.
VMware by Broadcom 342

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Harbor Versions
The Harbor versions available in the vSphere Supervisor environment are curated and supported package releases based
on the official open-source Harbor project.
VMware at Broadcom bundles, tests, and certifies specific Harbor releases for integration with Supervisor, ensuring
compatibility with its networking, storage, and authentication.
Supervisor supports multiple Harbor versions as Supervisor Services. The versions offer full feature parity with upstream
Harbor while being optimized for the vSphere platform.
To access Harbor versions, log in to support.broadcom.com, search for vSphere Supervisor Services, and download an
appropriate version of Harbor from the vSphere Supervisor Services page.
Install Harbor as a Supervisor Service
You can install Harbor as a Supervisor Service through the Supervisor Management option in the vSphere Client. You
can then use Harbor as a registry for workloads running on VKS clusters and vSphere Pods. Harbor requires a load
balancer or an Ingress controller. You can use either an NGINX-based load balancer or Contour.
• Verify that you have upgraded to vCenter 8.0a or higher. Harbor Supervisor Service is supported with vCenter 8.0a and
higher.
• Verify that you have the Manage Supervisor Services privilege on the vCenter system where you add the services.
• Since version 2.11.2, the Harbor Supervisor Service supports exposing the registry by using a load balancer.
Depending on your configuration, you can expose Harbor through either an NGINX-based load balancer or by using
Contour.
– If you use an NGINX-based load balancer, ensure you have a load balancer configured for the Supervisor.
– If you use Contour as an Ingress controller, install it before installing Harbor on the same Supervisor where you
want to install Harbor. See Installing Contour as a Supervisor Service.
• Designate an FQDN for accessing the Harbor admin UI.
Note:
In environments that do not use regional Harbor deployed through VCF Automation, you can integrate Harbor
Supervisor Service with the Software Depot management service on the Supervisor. This configuration allows
Harbor to proxy images from Software Depot and provide them to services, vSphere Pods, and VKS clusters. See
Deploy Harbor Supervisor Service in vSphere Foundation.

Map the Harbor FQDN to the Ingress IP Address
After Harbor is installed successfully, create a DNS record that maps the Harbor FQDN to the ingress IP address used
for external access. VKS clusters, vSphere Pods, and the Supervisor must be able to resolve the Harbor FQDN to pull
images from the registry.
The location of the ingress IP address depends on your configuration:
• If you are using Contour, obtain the Envoy ingress IP address from the Contour namespace. In the UI, navigate to the
Contour namespace, select Network, and select Services.
• If you are using an NGINX-based load balancer, use the external IP address configured for your NGINX service.
Migrate Images from the Embedded Registry to Harbor in Supervisor
Environment
If you are using the embedded Harbor registry with your Supervisor, you can migrate the images from the embedded
registry to the Harbor registry that you have installed as a Supervisor Service.
• If you are migrating images to a regional Harbor deployment, verify that both vCenter and Supervisor are running
version 9.1.0 or later in both new and upgraded environments.
• Verify that Harbor and Contour, if you use it, are installed on the Supervisor.
• Verify that the DNS that you use with your Supervisor includes an entry of the Harbor FQDN that is mapped to the
Envoy service ingress IP.
• Verify that trust is established between the Supervisor and Harbor. If images are being referenced by VKS clusters that
run on Supervisors different than the one where Harbor runs, verify that there is trust between these VKS clusters and
the Harbor.

namespace of Harbor, which can be named for example.

kind: NetworkPolicy

Deploy Harbor Supervisor Service in vSphere Foundation
In VCF and vSphere Foundation 9.1 and later, Harbor Supervisor Service can be configured to provide OCI images
for VCF components and services running on the workload network. In environments that do not use regional Harbor
deployed through VCF Automation, you can integrate Harbor Supervisor Service with the Software Depot management
service on the Supervisor. This configuration allows Harbor to proxy images from Software Depot and provide them to
services, vSphere Pods, and VKS clusters.

Taking and Managing Snapshots of VMs Created Through the VM
Service
You can take snapshot of VMs created by using the VM Service and revert to these shapshots. You can take one or more
snapshots of a virtual machine to capture the settings state, disk state, and memory state at specific times. When you take
a snapshot, you can also quiesce the virtual machine files and exclude the virtual machine disks from snapshots.
When you take a snapshot, other activity that is occurring in the virtual machine might affect the snapshot process when
you revert to that snapshot. The best time to take a snapshot from a storage perspective is when you are not incurring a
large I/O load. The best time to take a snapshot from a service perspective is when no applications in the virtual machine
are communicating with other computers. The potential for problems is greatest if the virtual machine is communicating
with another computer, especially in a production environment. For example, if you take a snapshot while the virtual
machine is downloading a file from a server on the network, the virtual machine continues downloading the file and
communicating its progress to the server. If you revert to the snapshot, communications between the virtual machine
and the server are confused and the file transfer fails. Depending on the task that you are performing, you can create a
memory snapshot or you can quiesce the file system in the virtual machine.
Memory Snapshots The default selection for taking snapshots. When you capture the virtual machine's memory state, the
snapshot retains the live state of the virtual machine. Memory snapshots create a snapshot at a precise
time, for example, to upgrade software that is still working. If you take a memory snapshot and the upgrade
does not complete as expected, or the software does not meet your expectations, you can revert the virtual
machine to its previous state.
When you capture the memory state, the virtual machine's files do not require quiescing. If you do not
capture the memory state, the snapshot does not save the live state of the virtual machine and the disks
are crash consistent unless you quiesce them.
Quiesced Snapshots When you quiesce a virtual machine, VMware Tools quiesces the file system of the virtual machine. A
quiesce operation ensures that a snapshot disk represents a consistent state of the guest file systems.
Quiesced snapshots are appropriate for automated or periodic backups. For example, if you are unaware of
the virtual machine's activity, but want several recent backups to revert to, you can quiesce the files.
If the virtual machine is powered off or VMware Tools is not available, the parameter is not
Quiesce
available. You cannot quiesce virtual machines that have large capacity disks.
Important:
Do not use snapshots as your only backup solution or as a long-term backup solution.
VMware by Broadcom 359

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Take a Snapshot of a VM Created by Using the VM Service
Learn how to create a snapshot of a VM created by using the VM Service through the Local Consumption Interface on the
vSphere Supervisor. You can take a snapshot when a virtual machine is powered on, powered off, or suspended. If you
are suspending a virtual machine, wait until the suspend operation finishes before you take a snapshot.
• Verify that you have access to a namespace.
• Verify that the namespace must have access to the content library that contains the VM image.
• Verify that the Local Consumption Interface service is installed on the vSphere Supervisor.
• If you are taking a memory snapshot of a virtual machine that has multiple disks in different disk modes, verify that the
virtual machine is powered off. For example, if you have a special purpose configuration that requires you to use an
independent disk, you must power off the virtual machine before taking a snapshot.
• To capture the memory state of the virtual machine, verify that the virtual machine is powered on.
• To quiesce the virtual machine files, verify that the virtual machine is powered on and that VMware Tools is installed.
• Verify that you have the Virtual machine > Snapshot management > Create snapshotprivilege on the virtual
machine.
When you create a memory snapshot, the snapshot captures the state of the virtual machine memory and the virtual
machine power settings. When you capture the virtual machine memory state, the snapshot operation takes longer to
complete. You might also see a momentary lapse in response over the network.
When you quiesce a virtual machine, VMware Tools quiesces the file system in the virtual machine. The quiesce operation
pauses or alters the state of running processes on the virtual machine, especially processes that might modify information
stored on the disk during a revert operation.
Application-consistent quiescing is not supported for virtual machines with IDE or SATA disks.
Note:
If you take a snapshot of a Dynamic Disk (a Microsoft-specific disk type), the snapshot technology preserves the
quiesce state of the file system, but does not preserve the quiesce state of the application.
1. Log in to the interface you are using by following the steps in Access the IaaS Services Console or Local Consumption
Interface.
2. In the Resources tab, select a VM and select Snapshots.
3. Click Take snapshot.
4. Enter a name and description for the snapshot.
5. (Optional) To capture the memory of the virtual machine, select Include virtual mahine's memory.
6. (Optional) To pause running processes on the guest operating system so that file system contents are in a known
consistent state when you take a snapshot, select the Quiesce guest file system.
Note:
You can quiesce the virtual machine files only when the virtual machine is powered on and the Snapshot the
virtual machine's memory check box is deselected.
For more information about the virutal machine behavior when you quiesce a virtual machine, see the KB article
https://kb.vmware.com/s/article/5962168.
7. Click Create.
Revert to a Snapshot of VM Created by Using the VM Service
To return a VM created by using the VM Service to its original state, or to return to another snapshot in the snapshot
hierarchy, you can use the revert options
When you revert a snapshot, you return the virtual machine's memory, settings, and the state of the virtual machine disks
to the state they were in when you took the snapshot. You can revert any snapshot in the snapshot tree and make that
snapshot the parent snapshot of the current state of the virtual machine. Subsequent snapshots from this point create a
new branch of the snapshot tree.
VMware by Broadcom 360

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Restoring snapshots has the following effects:
• The current disk and memory states are discarded, and the virtual machine reverts to the disk and memory states of
the parent snapshot.
• Existing snapshots are not removed. You can revert those snapshots at any time.
• If the snapshot includes the memory state, the virtual machine will be in the same power state as when you created the
snapshot.
Table 29: Virtual Machine Power State After Restoring a Snapshot
Virtual Machine State When Parent Snapshot Is Taken Virtual Machine State After Restoration
Powered on (includes memory) Reverts to the parent snapshot, and the virtual machine is powered
on and running.
Powered on (does not include memory) Reverts to the parent snapshot and the virtual machine is powered
off.
Powered off (does not include memory) Reverts to the parent snapshot and the virtual machine is powered
off.
Virtual machines running certain kinds of workloads can take several minutes to resume responsiveness after reverting
from a snapshot.
When you revert to a snapshot, disks that you added or changed after the snapshot was taken are reverted to the
snapshot point. For example, when you take a snapshot of a virtual machine, add a disk, and revert the snapshot, the
added disk is removed.
Independent disks are also removed when you revert to a snapshot that was taken before the disk was added. If the latest
snapshot includes an independent disk, its contents do not change when you revert to that snapshot.
1. Log in to the interface you are using by following the steps in Access the IaaS Services Console or Local Consumption
Interface.
2. In the Resources tab, select a VM and select Snapshots.
3. Navigate to a snapshot in the snapshot tree, click Revert, and click the Revert button.
Delete a Snapshot of a VM Created by Using the VM Service
Deleting a snapshot permanently removes the snapshot from the snapshot tree. The snapshot files are consolidated and
written to the parent snapshot disk and merge with the virtual machine base disk. You can delete a single snapshot or all
snapshots in a snapshot tree.
• Familiarize yourself with the delete and delete all actions and how they affect virtual machine performance.
• Required Privilege: Virtual machine > Snapshot management > Remove Snapshot on the virtual machine.
Deleting a snapshot does not change the virtual machine or other snapshots. Deleting a snapshot consolidates the
changes between snapshots and previous disk states. Then it writes all the data from the delta disk that contains the
information about the deleted snapshot to the parent disk. When you delete the base parent snapshot, all changes merge
with the base virtual machine disk.
To delete a snapshot, a large amount of information must be read and written to a disk. This process can reduce the
virtual machine performance until the consolidation is complete. Consolidating snapshots removes redundant disks, which
improves the virtual machine performance and saves storage space. The time to delete snapshots and consolidate the
snapshot files depends on the amount of data that the guest operating system writes to the virtual disks after you take
the last snapshot. If the virtual machine is powered on, the required time is proportional to the amount of data the virtual
machine is writing during consolidation.
VMware by Broadcom 361

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
1. Log in to the interface you are using by following the steps in Access the IaaS Services Console or Local Consumption
Interface.
2. In the Resources tab, select a VM and select Snapshots.
3. Navigate to and select a snapshot in the snapshots tree.
4. Click Delete and click the Delete button.
The snapshot data is consolidated to the parent snapshot and the selected snapshot is removed from the snapshot tree.
Deploying and Managing Virtual Machines in vSphere Supervisor
With the VM Service functionality, DevOps engineers can deploy and run VMs, in addition to containers, in a common,
shared Kubernetes environment. You can use the VM Service to manage the lifecycle of virtual machines in a
namespace. VM Service manages stand-alone VMs and VMs that make up VKS clusters.
The VM Service addresses the needs of DevOps teams that use Kubernetes, but have existing VM-based workloads that
cannot be easily containerized. It also helps users reduce the overhead of managing a non-Kubernetes platform alongside
a container platform. When running containers and VMs on a Kubernetes platform, DevOps teams can consolidate their
workload footprint to just one platform.
Note:
In addition to stand-alone VMs, the VM Service manages the VMs that make up VKS clusters. For information
about the clusters, Managing vSphere Kubernetes Service Clusters and Workloads.
Figure 17: VM Service Architecture
vSphere

ESX Cluster Networking Storage
Each VM deployed through the VM Service functions as a complete machine that runs all the components, including its
own operating system, on top of the Supervisor infrastructure. The VM has access to networking and storage that the
Supervisor provides, and is managed using the standard Kubernetes command. The VM runs as a fully isolated
kubectl
system that is immune to interference from other VMs or workloads in the Kubernetes environment.
When to Use Virtual Machines on a Kubernetes Platform?
Generally, a decision to run workloads in a container or in a VM depends on your business needs and goals. Among the
reasons to use VMs appear the following:
• Your applications cannot be containerized.
• You have specific hardware requirements for your project.
• Applications are designed for a custom kernel or custom operating system.
• Applications are better suited to running in a VM.
VMware by Broadcom 362

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
• You want to have a consistent Kubernetes experience and avoid overhead. Rather than running separate sets of
infrastructure for your non-Kubernetes and container platforms, you can consolidate these stacks and manage them
with a familiar command.
kubectl
Concepts of VM Service
To describe the state of a VM to be deployed in a vSphere Namespace, you use such parameters as a VM class, a VM
image, and a storage class. The VM Service then brings together these specifications to create stand-alone VMs or VMs
that support VKS clusters.
VM Service The VM Service provides a declarative, Kubernetes-style API for management of VMs and associated
vSphere resources. The VM Service enables the vSphere administrators to deliver resources and provide
templates, such as VM classes and VM images, to Kubernetes. DevOps engineers can use these
resources to describe the desired state of a VM. After the DevOps engineers specify the VM state, the VM
Service converts the desired state in to a realized state against backing infrastructure resources.
A VM created through the VM Service can be managed only from the Kubernetes namespace with the
commands. vSphere administrators cannot manage the VM from the vSphere Client, but can
kubectl
display its details and monitor resources it uses. For information, see Monitor Virtual Machines Available in
vSphere Supervisor.
VM Class The VM class is a VM specification that can be used to request a set of resources for a VM. The VM
class is controlled and managed by a vSphere administrator, and defines such parameters as the number
of virtual CPUs, memory capacity, and reservation settings. The defined parameters are backed and
guaranteed by the underlying infrastructure resources of a Supervisor.
A vSphere administrator can create custom VM classes.
In addition, the Supervisor offers several default VM classes. Generally, each default class type comes
in two editions: guaranteed and best effort. A guaranteed edition fully reserves resources that a VM
specification requests. A best effort class edition does not and allows resources to be overcommitted.
Typically, a guaranteed type is used in a production environment.
Examples of default VM classes include the following.
Reserved CPU and
Class CPU Memory (GB)
Memory
guaranteed-large 4 16 Yes
best-effort-large 4 16 No
guaranteed-small 2 4 Yes
best-effort-small 2 4 No
The vSphere administrator can assign any number of existing VM classes to make them available to
DevOps engineers within a specific namespace.
The VM class provides a simplified experience for the DevOps engineers. The DevOps don't need to
understand the full configuration of each VM that they plan to create. Instead, they can select a VM class
from available options, and the VM Service manages the VM configuration.
On the Kubernetes side, the VM classes appear as resource.
VirtualMachineClass
VMware by Broadcom 363

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
VM Image A VM image is a template that contains a software configuration, including an operating system,
applications, and data.
When DevOps engineers create VMs, they can select images from the content library associated with the
namespace. To the DevOps, the images are exposed as objects.
VirtualMachineImage
A vSphere administrator can create VM images that are compatible with vSphere and upload them to a
content library.
Content Library A DevOps engineer uses a content library as a source of images to create a VM. Similar to VM classes,
a vSphere administrator assigns existing content libraries to a namespace or a cluster to make them
available to DevOps engineers. The vSphere administrator can also make the namespace content library
writable. This additional permission allows DevOps users to publish their images to the library.
Storage Class VM Service uses storage classes for placing virtual disks and dynamically attaching persistent volumes.
VM Specification DevOps engineers describe the desired state of a VM in a YAML file that brings together the VM image, the
VM class, and the storage class.
VM Operator for VM operator enables management of virtual machines with a Kubernetes-style, declarative API.
Kubernetes
Note:
Starting with VCF 9.0, the v1alpha1 version of the VM Operator API is deprecated. Use v1alpha2
or v1alpha3 instead, as both are supported on Supervisor and are fully backward compatible.
Support for v1alpha1 will be phased out.
For information about the VM Operator API, see https://vm-operator.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ref/api.
Networking VM Service does not have any specific requirements and relies on the network configuration available in
the Supervisor. VM Service supports both types of networking, the vSphere networking or NSX. When VMs
are deployed, an available network provider allocates static IP addresses to the VMs. For information, see
the Supervisor documentation.
VM Service and Supervisor with vSphere Zones
When you create VMs on a three-zone Supervisor, the VM instance is replicated across all available zones. To control the
VMs placement through the YAML file, the DevOps team can use the Kubernetes label
topology.kubernetes.io/
. For example, .
zone topology.kubernetes.io/zone: zone-a02

Supervisor
To deploy virtual machines in the Supervisor environment, DevOps users must have access to VM images, or templates,
that contain software configurations, including operating systems, applications, and data. To provide access to images,
a vSphere administrator configures a VM content library, and then associates it with the namespace where the VMs

are deployed. Starting with vSphere 8.0 Update 2, the vSphere administrator can also assign the content library at a

Create a Content Library for Stand-Alone VMs in the Supervisor Environment
As a vSphere administrator, create a content library to store and manage VM templates.
Create a Content Library for Stand-Alone VMs
You can create a local content library and populate it with templates and other types of files. You can also create a
subscribed library to use the contents of an already existing published local library.
Required privileges:
• Content library > Create local library orContent library > Create subscribed library on the vCenter instance where
you want to create the library.
• Datastore > Allocate space on the destination datastore.
To protect the items of a content library, you can apply an OVF security policy. The OVF security policy enforces strict
validation when you deploy or update a content library, import items to a content library, or synchronize templates. To
make sure that the templates are signed by a trusted certificate, you can add the OVF signing certificate from a trusted CA
to a content library.
For more information about content libraries and VM templates in vSphere, see Using Content Libraries in vSphere
Virtual Machine Administration.

a) From the vSphere Client home menu, select Supervisor Management.
b) Click the Services tab and click Manage on the VM Service card.
2. On the VM Service page, click Content Libraries > Create a content library.
This action takes you to the content library section in the vSphere Client.
3. Click Create.
The New Content Library wizard opens.
4. On the Name and location page, enter a name, select a vCenter instance for the content library and click Next.
Make sure to use an informative name for the content library, so that your DevOps team can easily find and access the
library items.
5. On the Configure content library page, select the type of content library that you want to create and click Next.

Local content library A local content library is accessible only in the vCenter instance where you create it
by default.
1. To make the content of the library available to other vCenter instances, select
Enable publishing.
2. If you want to require a password for accessing the content library, select Enable
authentication and set a password.
Subscribed content library A subscribed content library originates from a published content library. Use this
option to take advantage of existing content libraries.
You can synchronize the subscribed library with the published library to see up-to-
date content, but you cannot add or remove content from the subscribed library. Only
an administrator of the published library can add, modify, and remove contents from
the published library.
Provide the following information to subscribe to a library:
1. In the Subscription URL text box, enter the URL address of the published
library.
2. If authentication is enabled on the published library, select Enable
authentication and enter the publisher password.
3. Select a download method for the contents of the subscribed library.

After you create the content library, populate it with VM templates in OVA or OVF format. Your DevOps engineers can use

• Create VM images that are compatible with the vSphere Supervisor environment.
The image specification requires that all VM images include VMware Tools or an equivalent open source package. The
images must use one of the following to bootstrap the guest OS and its networking stack. For more information, see
Bootstrap Providers.
– Linux + Cloud-Init version 17.9-21.2 with DataSourceVMwareGuestInfo.
– Linux + Cloud-Init version 21.3+
– Windows + Cloudbase-Init version 1.1.0+
– Windows + Sysprep (System Preparation)
For information about Cloud-Init, see the official documentation at The standard for customising cloud instances.
For information about Sysprep, see the official documentation at Sysprep overview.
• If your library is protected by a security policy, make sure that all library items are complaint. If a protected library
includes a mix of compliant and non-compliant items, the fails to present VM

Add and Manage VM Content Libraries in vSphere Supervisor
After you create the content library and populate it with VM templates, use the vSphere Client to add the library to the
namespace. By adding the library to the namespace, you give your DevOps users access to the library. In addition, you
can use the Data Center CLI (DCLI) commands to add a writable or read-only content library to the namespace, or assign
a read-only library at a cluster level.
Add a VM Content Library to a Namespace Using the vSphere Client
The content library that you add with the vSphere Client is read-only. The DevOps users can access images from this
content library, but cannot publish VM images to this library.
Required privileges:
• Namespaces > Modify cluster-wide configuration
• Namespaces > Modify namespace configuration
You can add multiple content libraries to a single namespace. You can add the same content library to different
namespaces.

VMware Cloud Foundation Service Administration and Development 9.1
Note:
This procedure applies only to content libraries for VM Service. A content library for VKS must be managed from
the VKS card.
1. In the vSphere Client, go to the namespace.
a) From the vSphere Client home menu, select Supervisor Management.
b) Click the Namespaces tab and click the namespace.
2. Add a content library.
a) On the VM Service card, click Add Content Library.
b) Select one or several content libraries and click OK.
Manage VM Content Libraries on a Namespace Using the vSphere Client
After you associate the library with the namespace, you can use the vSphere Client to remove it from the namespace. You
can also add more libraries.
Required privileges:
• Namespaces > Modify cluster-wide configuration
• Namespaces > Modify namespace configuration
Removing a content library from a namespace does not affect VMs that were previously deployed with the library images.
Note:
This procedure applies only to content libraries for VM Service. VKS content libraries must be managed from the
VKS card.
1. In the vSphere Client, go to the namespace.
a) From the vSphere Client home menu, select Supervisor Management.
b) Click the Namespaces tab and click the namespace.
2. Add or remove a content library.
a) On the VM Service card, click Manage Content Library.
b) Perform one of the following operations.
Remove a content library Deselect the content library and click OK.
Add a content library Select one or several content libraries and click OK.
OVF templates from the library become available in the Kubernetes namespace as VM images and can be used by
DevOps to self-service VMs. See Deploy a VM on a Namespace in Supervisor.
Note:
Only OVF templates from the library show up in the namespaces. Other types of content do not show up in the
namespace.
